A Third of America is On Fire

It’s an enduring mystery: despite the plain fact that Donald Trump is the most hopeless President America has ever had, something like one-third of American adults cling to his leadership. Are they delusional? Do they like the idea of having such a vain, impulsive, grafting, mean, none-too-bright, vulgar, compulsively lying, self-absorbed leader? It’s finally come to me.

Look at it this way. The persistence of Donald Trump’s viability on the national stage is a laser-like spotlight on one thing: how toxic the Democratic brand has become across a wide swath of the population. Imagine: so many people put Trump on one side of the scale, and the appeal of the Democratic party on the other, and decide that it’s pretty much a wash.

Rather than focusing on the corrupt figure in the White House, we should be wondering how the hell Democrats figure so poorly as to not constitute an appealing alternative. It’s a staggering index of failure.

Is it because the Democratic Party has a disastrously poor record?

Is it because of corruption?

It’s true that the Biden administration failed to seriously address widespread concerns about immigration, either by taking steps to secure the border or speak up for the contributions immigrants past have made to the country, in the manner of Ronald Reagan and others. But the Biden administration didn’t start a historically stupid and hopeless war, they didn’t throw upwards of a hundred billion dollars sending armed thugs into the streets, and they didn’t enrich themselves and their children to the tune of billions of dollars. 

How can the scales be this off? I have a theory.

item.title: Against the Canonical Ideal
item.description: Unalloyed striving is almost always a bad idea
item.content:encoded:
Against the Canonical Ideal

Unalloyed striving is almost always a bad idea

We human beings want matters to be clear. A big part of organizing yourself for life is deciding what you believe and what matters the most to you. This is such an important job that we hardly notice when we take it one step further, into a hunt for general principles that we can depend on to be true; goals we can pursue relentlessly; ideals we can use to measure ourselves solely by how much we serve them. The opposite of tradeoffs and paradoxes.

Does that seem like a meaningless distinction? It turns out to be anything but. 

We all know people who take it too far.

Most of us even have an essential skill: pretending that a principle is absolute while realizing that exceptions are hard to avoid. (murder)

Traumatizing children? How about chemo? Saving them from abuse by removing them from their parents?


  • not taking up too much space
  • not offending anyone or bruising their feelings. (rupture and repair)

item.content:encoded:
Connection, Made Easy

I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but the hive mind has been waking up to the problem/opportunity of simple human connection, the fact of life which brings us joy and makes us feel we are not alone in this world.

Here’s a thought worth thinking about: the need for connection is behind a whole symphony of modern quagmires; if not the cause, it’s a major contributing factor to so much of what ails us. And on the upside, properly serving that fundamental drive goes a long way to making life worth living. Pretty good thing to think about when you think about it.

The most salient, if not the most pervasive, is the so-called loneliness epidemic.

It’s been decades in the making

  • the “loneliness epidemic”
  • the decline of connective structures

I was recently visiting with an impending divorcé who has been diligently trying to develop a social network with, e.g., book groups, meetups and the like. 

So if making connection is such a problem, both for individuals and the society at largeBut I bring you good news. This is not a hard problem to solve

COVID Skepticism is Genocide for Republicans

As the Delta variant of SARS-Cov-2 sweeps across America, red states are seeing surging numbers of hospitalizations and deaths. This is all according to plan. Since the beginning of the pandemic, Democrats have plotted to use the virus to reduce the number of Republican voters, and now that strategy is paying off big time.

Rejecting Masks

The story starts in early 2020, when wearing masks was first proposed as a way to staunch the spread of the virus. From the beginning, Democratic strategists advocated wearing masks in a way that appealed to liberals’ faith in science and social empathy. The effect? Republican lovers of liberty, who do their own research, quickly came to reject the very idea as government overreach imposing a regime of Socialist oppression. Furthermore, since older voters are disproportionately Republican, mask resistance left many older Republicans especially exposed.

Rejecting Vaccination

Later in 2020, when vaccines were approved, 

To further stoke the fires, the prospect of vaccine “passports” and requirements to get vaccinated ensured that Republicans would shy away, or join mass protests against more 

Enter Delta

After conditioning Republicans to reject masks and vaccination, now comes the coup de grace: the Delta variant. Currently, 99% of serious cases of COVID are among the unvaccinated. But even more nefariously, Delta uses vaccinated citizens to spread the virus to the unvaccinated. 

The mRNA vaccines do an excellent but not complete job of suppressing the Delta variant. While vaccinated people can and do get COVID, their cases are far milder than if they were vaccinated. But that’s okay, because they remain excellent carriers. Vaccinated people may be carrying an extraordinary viral load in their mouths and throat even without showing any symptoms. In other words, the vaccinated are being used to spread the virus to the unvaccinated.

The Bottom Line

The Democratic stealth program to get Republicans to refuse masks left them open to infection. The program continued by sowing doubt about vaccination among Republicans, so that Democrats got protected. And now that the majority of the US is vaccinated, out comes the Delta variant which uses vaccinated people to spread itself like wildfire among the unvaccinated.

Count on it: Republicans will be dying out in the latter half of 2021 as this program reaches its final phases. You read it here first.

item.content:encoded:
Don’t Be So Sure

We don’t see things as they are. We see things as we are. — Anais Nin
Between believing a thing and thinking we know is a short step and easily taken.— Mark Twain

Looking around at public discourse nowadays, two things stand out: 1) the tsunami of nonsense that has found widespread acceptance, from decisive voter fraud in the 2020 election, to QAnon, to the dismissal of public health guidance on the COVID pandemic; and 2) the intolerance with which all views, nonsensical or not, are bandied about. Collectively these are an existential threat to democracy, and individually, it seems that the lamer we get, the angrier we get. Could there be a connection?

I submit that the common thread between epidemic ignorance and ideological intransigence is unwarranted confidence. We have a plague of certainty. Certainty lubricates the spread of bad ideas in a community, and transmutes opinions into dogma; intolerance is just certainty with thorns.

Everyone immediately concurs with that assessment…as long as it’s about Them, the fools out there who refuse to see the light. The trick is to realize that this isn’t just true of other people. We’re all experts at spotting and denouncing unwarranted confidence in others, but that position assumes that some of us are right and some of us are wrong, and that politics is for sorting out one from the other. But what if we’re all wrong? What if none of us has the first clue about reality as it is?

I propose that we could throw some cold water on the overheated political climate by looking at this certainty that has us beating each other over the head.

Ignorance as a Way of Life

If there’s one thing we’re certain about, it’s certainty itself: we may make the odd mistake, but by and large our senses and our minds give us a pretty complete, pretty reliable picture of the world as it is. After all, we don’t spend our days metaphorically stumbling blindly into doors or falling downstairs, so how far off base could we be? But avoiding the worst collisions with reality (and surviving to propagate our genes) is a pretty low bar. 

We have an unshakeable faith that our senses deliver an accurate picture of the world to our brains, and that the limits of what we can know are as clear-cut as the boundary between light and shadow. Both of those are not just untrue, but so ludicrously untrue that it makes us look like a pack of monkeys running around thinking they’re at the top of the world.

Think for a moment about our limitations comprehending size, scale, and complexity. Does a nanometer (1 billionth of a meter) mean anything to you? Imagine taking a yardstick, taking a tenth of it, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that, then taking a tenth of that. Either you gave up before the end of that sentence or your head imploded. Yet a single water molecule is a fraction of that size. And you’d have to do that whole process another nine times to get down to the scale of a quark. 

Now go in the opposite direction: multiply the size of the yardstick by ten, nine times. You’ve barely gotten to the size of the moon’s orbit around earth. Go another eight times and you’re at about the distance between the sun and its nearest neighbor star. And you’re still only one ten-thousandth the size of the Milky Way. It takes nine more iterations to get to the size of the observable universe.

Does that all fit in your head? It doesn’t fit in mine.

One reason people resist the theory of evolution is their utter inability to conceive of the vast time scale over which a microbe evolves into, say, us. They just can’t imagine there’s enough time. If you think of the age of the earth (4.5 billion years) as a day, the entire history of the human species would fit in 3 seconds. A human lifespan would be a micro-blink: about 1/500th of a second.

It’s not that some people can fit such an eternity into their heads and the doubters can’t. Nobody can; it’s just that some can accept that such scales exist whether we can conceive of them properly or not.

In our minds, we catalog things and give them names, and that catalog is how we deal with the world. We see boundaries and identities, and we interact with things one at a time. But what is invisible to us in any meaningful sense is the web of relationships that make up the natural world. The word ecology was coined just a few decades ago to give a name to the complexity with which natural entities interact. If you have a system of three entities, there are only three possible relationships between pairs. A system of five has 120 pairings to contend with, and after that, the number gets just as unfathomable as the size or age of the universe.

As with the universe, and with systems, so with quantum physics. Here we are, on our little island of clarity, straining our facilities — which were provided solely to help us survive — and dismally failing to comprehend anything much smaller, larger, more enduring, distant or complex than us, our puny, puny selves.

The Universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we can suppose.” (J.S. Haldane)

But taking it back to where we live. Think about where you are — literally, where your self resides: in your skull. Your mind is confined to a capsule of meat within a bone shell atop another pile of meat and bones. Your brain is utterly isolated: it’s only way of knowing anything about the world is via electrical impulses fired by sense organs on the outside, carried on neural pathways in the body and then laboriously interpreted by the brain. Our eyes, for example, have a low-resolution array of sensors on the retina, only a small part of which (the fovea) is dense enough to be of much use, the remainder of the visual field being filled in by mental reconstruction. There’s literally a blind spot where the nerve fibers pass out of the eye, and we are blind to it because of this filling-in process. Most of the eye is insensible to color, and the bits outside the fovea provide mainly information about motion. Yet we “see” a complete picture of the world — or so our brain would have us believe.

What accounts for this gulf between the amount/quality of the data we sense and the richness of the world we perceive? Our brains literally fill in the blanks, using incoming data as cues that trigger patterns that live in our memory. The brain merges the data and the memories, synthesizing a complete, detailed picture that it then blesses with confidence, clarity and certitude. Perception is less a matter of reception than it is of conception.

Optical illusions are a vivid (as it were) reminder of how strong this filling-in process is. One of my favorite experiments involved showing subjects a screen full of text — or so it appeared. In reality, the screen was almost all gobbledygook: only the small fraction that the subject viewed at a given time (an eye tracker was used to tell where that was) actually showed clear text. In the time it took for the viewer’s eye to shift from one place to another and settle in place, the screen could be re-drawn. The subjects were unshakably convinced that they were viewing a perfectly ordinary screen of text.

Getting a true picture of the world outside via neurophysiology is like getting the play-by-play of the Super Bowl over a telegraph: some information gets through, to be sure; recipients will unfailingly marshall all their resources of verbal interpretation, prior experience and imaginative visualization to bring it to life. They will surely construct a far more compelling picture than what they’re getting, but, unlike brains in skulls, no one getting the telegraphic version would mistake it for the whole story.

…and that’s just what we can see, feel, etc. directly. Almost everything else we know about the world has to come to us from other brains through language with untold passings through words and other minds on the way to us. Yes, our vision and hearing extend outward through communications technologies, but how much do we learn over the wire without accompanying words?

Now turn your attention inward, and think about who you are on the inside: the richness, intensity and variety of your interior life. How much of that is available to others? Does anybody else have the first clue what’s really going on in there? To feel that gap directly, recall the rush of joy and elation that wells up whenever we come to feel, however fleetingly, that someone else “really gets me”. This marks as well as anything how much we’re locked inside our own skins. 

But turn that around. Do you imagine that you understand other people any better than they understand you? If you’re a mystery to others, then every one of us lives in a dark wood full of inscrutable shadow-figures. What claim does any one of us have to know more than the wispiest fraction of the human life around us?

…and what do we know about ourselves, anyway? Think of the half-million mental health professionals in the US whose job is to help people figure themselves out. And yet we walk around sublimely convinced that we have a clue.

Recall a moment in your life when you were thunderstruck by revelation. A time when you opened your eyes just the right way and awe rushed over you as you contemplated something in the vastness of nature, or a moment when another person revealed themselves, truly, and you understood something profound about the human condition. Everyone has those moments (I hope), and any one of them will do. That blinding flash of revelation is nothing more or less than your default blinkers slipping momentarily.

Do you think that the thing you suddenly understood sprang into being the moment you had your revelation? Don’t you think there is an infinite number and variety of other revelations to which you are walking around utterly oblivious? Those magic moments not only throw a spotlight on some hitherto dark portion of the world, it should tell us how much darkness still lies outside.

In the end, our position isn’t that different from the hookworm. We compare our exquisite senses with its near-zero levels of sensation and cognition, and it’s easy to imagine that we are looking down from some privileged position. But what if we could look up? What makes us think that we’re at the limit of that scale? Surely we can’t look up and apprehend creatures who are as far above us as we are above the hookworm, but we can get a glimpse of other such worlds in the visual acuity of the hawk; the frequency sensitivity of dogs; the unfathomable spectrum of color available to the bluebottle butterfly with its 15 types of color receptors; the mental capabilities of a savant like John von Neumann. But really, the scale vanishes into darkness pretty quickly.

You get the idea. Compared to what we don’t know, what we do know is not just the tip of the iceberg, more like a snow cone on the tip of the iceberg. We wander an infinite landscape of possible knowledge, in total darkness except for a few dapples of light, but we somehow remain unaware of the dark and think we’re in broad daylight.

Why this ludicrous gulf between what we think we know and what we actually deserve to believe? What’s the advantage of being so blissfully ignorant? It helps to ask a second question: what is the purpose of understanding what’s going on? We evolved the capacities we have for a reason: survival. And surviving requires two things: recognizing threats and opportunities in the environment; and acting on those understandings. These can become competing concerns. It doesn’t pay to act on unreliable information, but it also doesn’t pay to worry too much about imperfect information if it delays acting. And in a life-or-death situation, the important thing is not just to act, but to act quickly. With conviction. Accuracy and completeness are secondary concerns.

In other words, our senses and our cognition didn’t evolve to give us a clear and complete picture of reality. They evolved to give us a good enough picture of reality, as defined and strictly limited by the needs of survival. But at the same time, we evolved a sense of certainty, a faith in that accuracy, so that we could act to live another day.

Now take that ocean of ignorance and delusion in which we swim, and apply it to the modern political debate, if you can call it that. I don’t know about you but I hear nothing but the voices of people who are trying to prove that they’re right that they have the way. It reminds me of a giant game of King of the Hill played on a mountain of shit.

It gets worse. Suppose we decided to reform, to call out our inner philosopher, set reflexive certainty aside, put our beliefs through the wringer, and reserve our confidence for beliefs that actually hold water. Here’s the shocking thing: making that assessment is actually, literally impossible. To begin with, much of our thinking — by far the bulk of it — is actually unconscious/intuitive, and thus not even available for inspection. But assessing even the thoughts that you can get to is also a matter of thinking, which thinking must also be assessed, and so forth, infinitely down the rabbit hole. 

No, a truly valid decision on what to believe is just beyond us.

A personal note: I belong to a community that has a privileged, if embarrassing, view into the workings of a brain on certainty: software developers. Every programmer has this experience: your gleaming image of a perfectly functioning program is colliding with the reality that it just isn’t working. The refrain here is something along the lines of “how can this possibly not work?” There ensues an extended period of banging the image and the reality together, as stress, frustration, perplexity and profanity proliferate. Finally, after titanic struggles with the demons of the dark, the world shifts, the brain unlocks, all is revealed, and a new thought moves in: “How could this EVER have worked, AT ALL?!?”

Confidence is not and cannot be a reliable indicator of correctness.

If your purpose is to get a complete and accurate picture of the world, your brain is not your friend. It has its own agenda, shaped by our own evolutionary history, which only seems to be leading us to the truth — and notice the double-edged sword in that statement. Your brain presents itself — convincingly — as a reliable witness, and it covers the ideas it presents you with in a sugary coating of conviction and certainty. We need to get a better handle on both.

Out of the Bind

Before I make you completely hopeless about this aspect of the human condition, I have some good news. It turns out that, a few centuries ago, humanity as a whole developed an ingenious hack to deal with the problem of unwarranted certainty, one that both improves the accuracy of our conclusions and limits excess confidence: Science.

On a nuts and bolts level, science provides a practical bullshit detector for ideas: probing for logical inconsistencies, shaking them down for clashes between the theory and the facts of the matter, testing predictions to see if they pan out. These are amazingly powerful tools that account for the staggering progress of science and technology over the last few centuries.

But the real lesson of Science is more subtle. It directly addresses the “paradox of knowledge”, the need to proceed confidently as if you were correct, while remaining cognizant of the possibility of being wrong.

When confronting a paradox, the natural urge is to make a choice and commit to one pole or the other. In the case of the Knowledge Paradox, it’s easy to see the damage done by people who seize on either pole: those who will not question their beliefs under any circumstances, and those who won’t believe any expert who ever made a misstatement or a mistake, as well as the postmodernist for whom no idea is worth investing in.

But, as is often the case with paradox, there is a third possibility hidden in plain sight: to embrace both poles; to plunge in with full confidence, while staying open to later course correction. To keep an open mind in the midst of fervent belief.

Doesn’t that sound like Science? The genius of Science is to take all knowledge as provisional while working fervently to make it as solid as possible. We believe the theories that currently prevail — believe in them enough to build new theories atop them — but we are rigorously open to revising them in the light of new data and/or arguments.

You may be a skeptic about Science as it is practiced. I will join you in that skepticism: Science is practiced by imperfect human beings, imperfectly, sometimes falling onto one pole of the paradox or the other. The scientific consensus often changes its mind, seemingly arbitrarily (looking at you, purveyors of health and nutrition advice), and there is an arrogance that often comes in on the heels of such a spectacularly successful strategy, that believes that science is the only viable path to knowledge.

Still. 

Science never seems to get close to objective truth, or even to something we can really depend on. But Science is not after perfect knowledge, valid for all time. Science has given up that pipe dream, and admitted that it could be wrong. And therein lies its strength and its genius. Because not expecting to decide anything finally is exactly what allows science to get closer to the truth than any other method of extracting knowledge from the world.

This is a radical tradeoff that multitudes still struggle with. 

The Power of Certainty

The quest for certainty is, to put it mildly, an enduring aspect of the human experience. You can see it in the appeal of a God who has all the answers. 

You can see it in the dismissal of experts who are sometimes wrong, even if their advice is the best available. 

You see it in the attraction to authoritarians and ideologues who dangle comprehensive worldviews that Make Sense Of It All Despite What They Want You To Believe.

You see it in the hunt for abstractions and principals which explain everything.

You can see it in the power the converted feel in their certainty, the joy and relief on the faces of people plunging into “ism”s like libertarianism, racism, socialism, capitalism.

You can see it in the eyes of someone whose certainty is threatened, who is faced with relinquishing their certainty and going back to a state of ambivalence and a process of (again!) sorting things out.

But you see it most in the drive to finish investigating and questioning, and come to a conclusion which will make investigation and questioning a thing of the past.

Certainty and clarity are very serious matters, seriously pursued. The drive to acquire them, to cloak our deliberations in them, to rest our anxious souls in them, is universal, relentless, and largely unconscious. And they are so ubiquitous as to be invisible — until you start looking at humanity through that particular lens.

Life Without Certainty

The quest for clarity and certainty even at the price of correctness is so strong that it raises a question: What would it be like to let it go? What could we get in return?

Without such a powerful drive to reach a destination, we would be free to poke around the landscape of ideas, wandering onto a side road here, lingering for a while there, getting to know the territory in all its idiosyncracies.

Without the need to defend and justify our conclusions, we would be open to engaging openly with others and their ideas, exploring the landscape together in a process that’s less a wrestling match and more of a dance.

Without confusing our ideas with ourselves, and their viability with our self-worth, we could be more serious about questioning, clarifying, exploring and strengthening them.

Beliefs don’t need to be like coins we collect and guard jealously. They could be more like playthings. With a more jaunty attitude we might hold more than one incompatible idea at once, playing them off against one other, or no idea at all, browsing the possibilities. We could endure the silliness of taking an idea from one domain and using as a metaphor in another.

Without mistaking our beliefs for objective reality, we could get past the need to impose them on other people. We might even be able to glean some compassion, or even respect, for others in their own flawed quest for understanding.

…but none of this means we take ideas less seriously; they still are the gears in the machinery of democracy. It’s paradoxical but true: ideas matter, but they still need to be handled deftly. The mantra I like is “strong ideas, lightly held.”

This ceaseless quest for certainty reminds me of Al Pacino’s Satan character in The Devil’s Advocate, trying to get his son Keanu Reeves to stop feeling guilty:

You know, I’ll tell you, boy. Guilt…it’s like a bag of fucking bricks. All you got to do…is set it down.

Epistemic Humility

The whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts. — Bertrand Russell

In the interest of loosening the grip that the drive to certitude holds on humanity, I would like to propose that we start looking at it as a vice, one closely related to hubris: the vice of assuming that we are in any position to figure out The Way Things Are beyond the immediate need to stop reflecting and take action. The vice of believing that we have a uniquely privileged view of the world, such that everyone else must be misguided or delusional. This vice has always been with us, but isn’t it plain to see how catastrophic it has become?

But I prefer to look on the positive side. In contrast to this vice-without-a-name, I propose a new virtue. Because I suck at marketing, I call it epistemic humility.

What is a virtue? A virtue is a moral value, and a moral value exists to steer us in one direction when immediate circumstances want to send us another way.

A virtue is a hook for modeling. When we see someone of limited means making a sacrifice to help another, that would just be puzzling without understanding the virtue of selflessness. I’m not religious at all, but the Quaker faith does have a compelling tenet: teaching by example. Quakers believe that there’s no preaching virtue, no imposing it on others. It can only be modeled. You can’t make anyone else stop misbehaving; you can only show how to behave.

A virtue is something we teach our children and/or our students as an ideal to aspire to, and value that becomes part of our culture, if only aspirationally. We don’t expect all of our fellows to be kind, generous, chaste, etc. But we do admire those who are, and we at least aspire to be more like them.

Finally, a virtue sets up a standard of behavior, a default. Once a virtue takes root, the most bald-faced unvirtuous behavior becomes conspicuous and potentially shaming. Public standards of behavior cause people to feel obliged to keep up appearances, at least in public. It might become a matter of shame to go out into the world raving about voter fraud, kind of like taking a shit in the street. Wouldn’t it be nice if the worst actors on the public stage got a wee bit less shameless?

Epistemic humility is kind of like AA: it surrenders before the impossibility of true understanding given the hopeless position we are in, and to our credulity in the face of the influences from within and without: on the outside, the social pressures and information silos whose mission is to enlist our belief for any purpose other than real justification; on the inside, our limited senses and attention, our hardwired biases, our need to feel certainty.

I propose epistemic humility as a virtue — a public virtue — because humanity is fucked if we don’t get our brains around some basic ideas: that looking at the first three things that come up on a Google search constitutes “research”; that we are at the mercy of the impressions formed by a politically-motivated mono-diet; that the reality in which each of us lives is increasingly constructed by the attention economy; that certainty is untethered from correctness.

Life Under Uncertainty

Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is absurd — Voltaire

But how is this virtue to be pursued, by the pioneers who pursue it? I don’t have a code of ethics for this new world, but I do have a few modest suggestions.

Most general, and most diffuse, is eternal vigilance against signs of closing off in oneself. Adam Grant, in his new book Think Again, highlights three modes of thinking that reflect a closed mind: the preacher, the prosecutor and the politician. The preacher is working to make converts; the prosecutor’s job is to find flaws in the opposition and make a case by whatever means necessary; and the politician is trying to convince by schmoozing and charming, to make it easy to believe. It will be far easier to spot others operating in these modes than to self-identify, but it’s worth the practice, and that framework might eventually get recognized within.

I strongly recommend Grant’s book for anyone with an interest in lightening their grip on their beliefs and their thinking. He brings in clinical and social data and far longer case studies in what works and doesn’t work to change minds (including one’s own) than there is room for here. Instead, let me suggest Ten Commandments of Epistemic Humility.

Keep your Identity Small

Beware the sense of humor failure. A wise man once told me that the hallmark of a cult is losing their sense of humor, and in my subsequent experience it has turned out to be a surprisingly powerful test. When you lose the ability to find any humor in yourself or your ideas, it’s time to stop and take stock.

Don’t expect your intelligence to save you. Intelligence works just as well for rationalizing and defending as it does for exploring and solving. In my experience, one of the outstanding aspects of smart people is that they can talk themselves into anything.

Understand the opposition’s position better than your own. This is called steel manning. It not only makes your own ideas stronger, it’s uniquely disarming when you can articulate the opposition’s position better than they can.

What would it take to get you to change your mind? Asking this question, either of yourself or others, disrupts the confirmatory chain of thought and opens one’s conviction to pointed inspection.

Say things out loud. Talking to other people isn’t just a way of persuading those cretins on the other side. It’s a way of holding your own ideas up to scrutiny and seeing if you really know what you’re talking about. It’s amazing what happens when those moldy ideas from your mental attic get brought out and exposed to oxygen and sunlight.

Get others to say things out loud. I’m talking about listening without trying to persuade, and in so doing draw others into saying it out loud. Just by the act of listening, the limitations of their views may become obvious even to themselves. The opposite of defensiveness is openness, and you can get the latter just by inviting it.

Preface declarative statements with “I believe” or “It seems to me”. Even with no other changes to your conversational style, just those simple phrases are a devout expression of humility, and they introduce a context that turns any argument over facts into a discussion of why this thing is believed (which may or may not be a matter of fact). 

Learn the difference between having strong opinions and being opinionated. Paradox is one of my favorite things, and this is one of my favorite paradoxes: there is no contradiction between holding a strong belief and being open to changing it. 

Remember the purpose of confidence. The reason I’ve hammered on certainty as an epiphenomenon is that it does have a life of its own, almost independent of actual correctness. It was critical for survival when we evolved, and it’s critical for getting off the dime and taking action even now. But it’s always worth having the question lurking in the back of your mind: “Do I really need to be so sure?”

Cultivate comfort with not knowing. After spending enough time skeptically observing people and their thought processes, it’s hard not to be struck by their urge to state the case. I don’t know if it’s a personal inclination or learned skill, this state of not knowing, but I do know that a final determination, or just a working hypothesis — no matter how provisional — is definitely optional equipment going forward, in the absence of good data.

What I’m trying to describe is a world of the mind in which the craving to know finds its proper place (deciding and getting the hell on with things, and holding out for what must be believed, rather than what could be believed), but otherwise gets out the way and leaves us in a playground of the mind in which ideas are toys to be tried out, played with, banged together and taken as far as they can go but no further — not used as weapons, or as wedges to drive people, and countries, apart. It’s a positive vision for addressing the grim direction that our world seems to be headed, both online and off. I don’t know if this idea will make any difference, but I have a pretty scary idea of what will happen if we don’t manage to change direction somehow.

All views are bad views

Yes we have no choice but to proceed as if what we can make out of the world is accurate. What alternative do we have, really? And it’s part of the magic of consciousness that we can sometimes feel them in our bones as the right thing. But we should never forget that it is just a feeling, one which may or may not be accurate. And will never know about that any more than anything else.

item.title: Don’t Live Each Day As If It’s Your Last
item.description: There’s a better way to get your head screwed on straight.
item.content:encoded:
Don’t Live Each Day As If It’s Your Last

There’s a better way to get your head screwed on straight.

There are a lot of silly ideas floating around out there, and one of the silliest is the injunction to “live each day as if it’s your last.” I can’t be alone in imagining what it would actually be like to do that. If I had only a day to live, I promise I would be thrashing around in an unholy stew of feelings, mostly panic, both about the impending deadline and how to wind up my earthly affairs. Serene appreciation of my brief remaining time on earth? Not me.

Still, the thought behind the idea is a good one. We get so bogged down in the day-to-day that it’s hard to appreciate the life we have — and I mean really hard. The plain fact is that everyone likely to read this is living beyond the wildest dreams of the kings and cardinals of the past, and of most people living today. Simply having access to antibiotics, surgical anesthetic, dental care, adequate nutrition, air travel, personal automobiles, safe maternity, remarkable personal security, the supercomputer in our pockets — the list goes on — would be a laughable fantasy for 99% of the people who have ever lived — to say nothing of the ongoing wonder of nature, science, art and human relationships.

We should be hyperventilating with pleasure and astonishment at our lot. What’s wrong with us that we aren’t?

item.content:encoded:
Fighting Climate Change is Not That Hard

Conversation about climate change is rife with alarums and excursions. Typical of our modern political dialogue, the conversation is at a fever pitch. The urgency to take action is matched by an equally strident resistance, by concerns that the scenarios are uncertain and the cost of mitigation not worth it. With both sides banging heads, progress is uncertain at best and half-assed at worst.

I would like to suggest that most of this sturm und drang is wasted. The kind of real change that’s needed is not going to happen until everybody just calms. The Hell. Down. 

The dynamics at hand

My thesis here is simple: that both climate alarmists and skeptics are engaged in a tacit conspiracy to make action to mitigate climate catastrophe seem as hard as possible. 

Let’s put on our Manichean glasses and divide the contenders into the Crusaders and the Resisters. The Crusaders honestly perceive a world under threat; consequently, they are strident about it, and prepared to pay a concomitantly high price to head off that threat, including collapsing whole sectors of the economy, building new ones, disrupting careers by the millions, spending trillions of dollars along the way. The Resisters are less certain of the threat and alarmed about the cost of addressing it, and they get their traction from the costs and uncertainty involved.

So both sides are committed to a vision of great cost and effort, one side saying “Hell yeah!”, the other saying “Not worth it!” But as the issue rages on, the worse this dynamic gets. The more desperate and strident the Crusaders get, the more costly appears. And the Resisters have their own interest in making the costs seem excessive, the better to Resist undertaking them. Both sides have an interest in bidding up the cost of action.

Another way to look at it

leverage

pulling in the slack

Looking back in wonder

item.content:encoded:
In Defense of Reality

I hope that the above title conveys a little of how ludicrous our current predicament is. Like the battering that our norms and institutions have taken in the few short months of the second Trump presidency, it shouldn’t have to be said that paying due attention to the way things are, and acting in accord with that information, is just a better way to succeed than making things up as you go along. But here we are. It needs to be said.

…and yet, it’s surprisingly difficult to make the case that people who at least try to sail toward truth are better off than those who wander about steered this way and that by whatever pops into their heads or whom they last talked to. So I’ve attempted a little review of why realism is a good idea — generally speaking. 

A Note of Temperance

The Way Things Are isn’t always the most important thing. Sometimes, behaving as if something is true makes it so. (self-fulfilling prophecy) This is especially true in the social realm, in which the seemingly impossible comes to life simply because the right people become convinced it’s true. The classic case is a bank run: a financial institution may be perfectly sound, but if a critical mass of account holders decide that it’s not, their departure can trigger a confidence collapse that really does destroy the institution. Human affairs are rife with situations that are literally governed by beliefs: civil order depends crucially on the belief that civil life is orderly; functional interpersonal relationships thrive in an atmosphere of trust, and vice versa; even something as simple as showing up for a meeting depends on a mutual belief in the timeliness of others.

Conversely, great movements of people can be marshaled for astonishing achievements if word gets around that doing something about it is a) good and b) possible.

In cases like these, reality itself is built on a tissue of agreement and common perception. 

But we’re not here to talk about that.

So let me review what fealty to the truth actually brings to the party. But first, a philosophical sidebar: 

Following is a list of advantages that accrue when your perception matches reality.

God is in the Details

Truth exists at many levels of detail. Even if you have the right general idea, acting on that basis can be undone bu

Making change without detailed information makes you a bull in the china shop, heedlessly blundering around. Even supposing that border control and restricting immigration are indeed what you want doesn’t mean that the first, most obvious and appealing policy is the best way to achieve it. Some of us believe that there was no border “crisis” that couldn’t be addressed pragmatically and compassionately with Congressional mandates for clear yeah-or-nay criteria and enough court space to handle cases expeditiously.

Making Smart Bets 

As just one example, among many other things, government policy is a matter of placing bets on the future. Will we be better off if interest rates rise or fall? Will a get-tough policy or seeking cooperation make for a safer, more prosperous world? And so forth, endlessly on.

America is now making some of the biggest bets ever 

  • climate change, 
  • renewable energy vs. betting on fossil fuels, 
  • anti-immigration 
  • trade protectionism
  • vaccination 

Useability: 

“You can’t manage what you can’t measure” means that success is correlated with realism. 

Consistency 


Stability

Corollary to consistency: stability. oscillation is the enemy of progress. The truth is a source of stability; without such an anchor, impulse will drive you in one direction after another, at the very least a waste of energy. There are many sources of stability, of course, but seeking to anchor yourself to the truth helps a lot.

Composability

This is just a fancy term for the idea that you can build on reality. The more stable your view is, the more others can depend on it to take the next step. If there’s a single reason for the monstrous success of science and technology since the Enlightenment, it is this. Once orbital dynamics were understood, committees didn’t have to convene or leaders to dictate how to launch rockets; we could proceed directly to the exploration and exploitation of space. 

Reality is as reality does. If you believe that the vaccine is more dangerous than the disease, reality doesn’t care how strongly you believe it or how many people agree; you can kill millions with a misguided policy. If you believe that you have a “dead country” when in fact it is as robust as it has ever been and more robust than any other, then your desperation will drive risky policies to revive it, doing more harm than good. If you believe that climate change is a hoax, you’re gambling with the habitability of the environment.

There is a reason for keeping hands off of information-gathering functions: you not only want the best data you can get, you want that data to be trusted. We joke about shooting the messenger, but having the temerity to accept bad news is the only way to ensure the credibility of your position. 

Appeal to communality

item.title: Letter from the Future
item.description: Dear 2021,
item.content:encoded:
A Letter from the Future

Dear 2021,

This is your future calling — 2050 to be exact. We know it’s a bit disconcerting to hear from us like this, but we remember when you wrote to 1971. Do you? It seems like a long time ago, but it’s a good idea, every once in a while, to help our past selves buck up and face the future. 

Remember all the things you had to tell 1971? Institutions were in an uproar; young people were revolting (but aren’t they always, if you know what we mean…); women were marching in the streets to find their voice; America’s War On Drugs, The Counterculture And The Underclass was just gearing up; crime seemed like a never-ending plague; and on and on. It’s so important to have a little perspective, and we’re glad you were able to offer them yours. From 2021, violent crime as an overweening national concern is mainly a memory. Back in 1971, the odd woman who stuck out for doing anything outside home and hearth was really odd; but nowa(your)days, the prominence of women in leadership and achievement is, well, unremarkable. The word “smog” is enough to send young people to the dictionary. The Cold War is a distant memory. People of non-standard color and sexuality have come out from their cave into the daylight of your society. It’s dawning on your whole society that mind-altering substances are at least as viable an option as alcohol and potentially world-changing. The worst of world poverty and deprivation are vanishing at a miraculous pace. Even smoking cigarettes has gone from casual universality to weird quirk. (We notice you didn’t mention how quaint and naive their media and their political dialogue were, or let slip about the Internet or the supercomputers you have in your pockets. But we understand the sensitivities involved — hint hint.)

Most of those remarkable facts only arrived at the end of decades and tumult and tragedy, but they were all the stuff of fantasy for the people who received your letter. Which is why we’re writing this one to you now.

We can feel the pain throbbing in your era. But we want you to remember that the laurels of tomorrow are paid for with the struggles of today — even when those struggles seem to be driving you off a cliff.

Your year is just now coming to grips with a changing climate after decades of beating around the bush, and you are still looking at that challenge as a burdensome, costly effort to ward off disaster. It’s only now that we can see that the investment you put into rebuilding your world will actually pay for itself in terms of new economic activity and prosperity, especially lucrative jobs that must be done locally.

Your world, since 1971, has seen a bifurcation of wealth in which people living in tents and cashing in recyclables to eke out a daily meal live within sight of people who spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a painting just because they can. ’Twas ever thus, but ’tis moreso for you than ever. You cannot see the stress this puts on your social fabric, but we can tell you this: the tragedy of your situation is exactly what it takes to motivate a change, to define a level below which no one need fall, partly by trimming the excess that others have accrued beyond the needs of Croesus.

As with money, so with health care. Some of your countries have figured this one out, but America’s health “system” is so broken that this very brokenness birthed the will to fix it. By 2050, your people can concentrate on making themselves wealthy and wise rather than wondering if a medical emergency will bankrupt them — if they can get care at all.

Finally, and most importantly: you in America feel like you’re witnessing the final breakdown of civility, common purpose, even shared reality. Citizens by the millions trumpet beliefs about election integrity, the shape of the earth, vast conspiracies of child-eating politicians, tracking devices in vaccines — and more — that are strictly from Crazytown. Without giving away any spoilers, let’s just say that this kind of craziness is exactly what it takes to make change happen. Sitting here in 2050, we can recall the horrors of a population plunging into such madness, and for exactly that reason we are determined that it not happen here. We look at one another and nod knowingly, with a universal commitment to avoid these frailties that humans are prey to. We are hyper-vigilant for memes that tell us what we want to hear, or make us angry at the Other. We look warily at the Forward button, as though it has a little electric shock for us if we use it promiscuously. 

We do this not just to avoid re-enacting those days, but because we don’t want our fellows to take us for a buffoon. And we do it, frankly, because we’re better than you. But we only got that way because you were so lost. We know you can’t see that from where you are, but that’s pretty much what it means to be lost.

So we know that this letter will not have a material effect on you, any more than your letter did on 1971. But we do have one word of caution: the future from which you’re receiving this is only one future that the Multiverse has to offer. Finding your way to where we are is up to you. Choose wisely.

Regards,

2050

item.title: Life Among the Signposts

item.content:encoded:
Life Among the Signposts

One of the more sobering thoughts about being human is realizing how puny our mental faculties really are — how poorly equipped we are for comprehending the full scale of, well, pretty much anything outside our immediate experience. The universe, for example. Personally, I can’t get close at just the galaxy level: 100 billion stars just in our little corner of the universe — and something like a trillion more galaxies? Forget about it.

Same in the opposite direction. I can comprehend — barely — how small bacteria are in comparison to a human hair (roughly 100 times smaller, FYI), but an atom, 10,000 times smaller than that? Or a quark, millions and millions of times smaller still? The best we can do to appreciate such scales is to admit, sheepishly, how ill-equipped we are to appreciate such scales.

But forget the universe and just focus on the level of us humans. Can we even get our brains around the dynamic range of life on earth? Right now, there are people living in the darkest pits of despair and desperation, clinging to life by their fingernails, overwhelmed by natural disasters or just the everyday reality of their lives. People in prison by the millions, miserable at the hands of professional misery-makers. Children whose flesh is being shattered by wars they don’t even slightly comprehend. But there are still others for whom every moment is a radiant gift, who glow through life in a Valhalla of privilege and comfort.

We can name these situations just as we can reel off the billions and trillions in talking about the universe. But what would it take to really fit into our heads the full range of the reality of us humans? This grotesque poverty of our faculties is embarrassing, but also understandable: we evolved with brains whose sole purpose was to keep us alive long enough to reproduce, a very different charter than coping with anything like the full scope of reality. Upshot: we encode our experiences (in the moment) and our memories (in retrospect) with merciless frugality, eliding the non-essential and reducing everything to its essence. This is nowhere more evident than in the conceptualization embodied in language, wherein we: take a broad range of experiences; find their common essence, with special attention to what we care about; and associate that essence with a symbol — usually a word — that we can use to refer to any particular case. The word or symbol is a very useful — but limited — signpost pointing to a far richer experience. In general, the symbol is enough to get us through the day; recovering the richness of the source takes will and effort. Parsimony pays, bigly: in reduced cognitive effort, in saving attention for when it really matters, in defining symbols and abstractions that cover a vast range of reality.

This is one of the hallmarks of the human condition. It’s not just that we reduce stupefying realities to a vestige that will fit into our heads. We do that voluntarily as a matter of course, blithely unaware that we do it. But do we care about that? Does it really matter? Oh yes. Yes it does.

Signposts to God

There’s a great idea, attributed to Sufism, that “all religions are a signpost to God.” All the trappings of any given faith — assembly, ritual, practice, doctrine, iconography, hierarchy, culture, all of its earthly manifestations—are essentially just window dressing for The Real Thing. Behind and beyond that presentation lies what religion is really about: an experience of transcendence so powerful, so real, so true to those who have experienced it, that humanity can fairly be divided into those who have, and those who haven’t. Some people actually experience, in the most viscerally overwhelming way, the thread that connects them with the rest of humanity, with all life, with the cosmos. The difference between actually feeling that at a cellular level and holding those connections as an idealistic abstraction — words in a book — is like the difference between truly comprehending the scale of a galaxy and using the world “big”.

(Note: you may have an opinion about how “real” such experiences are—I know I do—but that’s beside the point: they’re real to the people who have them.)

Transcendence doesn’t necessarily play well with regular life, and so religions come laden with human hazards: reinterpreting the experience, bringing their own limitations and pathologies to it, trying to proselytize it, even just forgetting. But religion as expressed in the world can only be a signpost, a wan representation of…that other thing. Something vast. And it’s closely related to the data reduction of finding symbols for experience that will fit in our heads.

These kinds of data reduction are breathtaking, inevitable, and sad, but the real problem is that so many people never get past the signpost. They mistake the signpost for the thing it’s pointing to. They forget that church is not just about certain beliefs, or a community, or moral instruction; it’s supposed to be about experiencing the Divine, about transcending the mortal realm. They reduce the most profound experiences of human existence to their earthly representation, just as we reduce millions of starving children to the symbol “poverty”, or the prospective death of the planet to “climate change”.

Language can become a screen which stands between the thinker and reality. This is the reason why true creativity often starts where language ends.
 — Arthur Koestler

Life Among The Signposts

It makes perfect, practical sense to compress experience to fit into our heads. But having collected those signposts, why do we forget what they point to; forget, even, that the signpost represents anything else? We dismiss the wonder of the universe, both above and below. We satisfy ourselves that the symbols of language are all we need to know about our experience. We confuse the trappings of religion with its vast essence. 

Now here’s the point of all this:

We’re walking right by the opportunity to plumb the depths of our own, ordinary experience.

I live a pleasant ten-minute walk from my local hardware store. I can get there and back without my attention ever departing from what I’m going to buy and what I’ll do with it when I get home. But what would happen if I actually opened myself to the full experience of what’s around me on the way? The staggering variety of sights, sounds and feelings that journey offers: the endless variety of plants and homes; the texture of a leaf; the dense arrangement of leaves on a tree; the sometimes comical color schemes on display (What were these people thinking?); the flowers; the weeds; the undulating sidewalk uplifted by tree roots; the variegated humans passing by; the psychology of drivers as expressed in their driving; the extraordinary weathervanes on display; everything down to the colors and patinas of the cars in sight. I could be taking that walk several times a day for years and still be noticing things anew.

Or: I can go to the store, buy my screws, and go home.

Now consider human relationships, what we mean by symbols like “friends” and “family”, for example. Most of us know what such relationships are like during a crisis: when we’re brutalized by the death of a beloved, or a divorce, or a similar life-shaking event, we see each other in a very different light, painfully intimate in all our vulnerability and suffering. Is there some reason that it can’t always be like that? Why aren’t the humans always intimately connected? Conversely, why on earth do we count ourselves satisfied with the “connection” provided by social media? Or by a “community” of fellow churchgoers who are mainly about showing up and showing off?

But I don’t even need to get out of my chair to access rapture. Is the act of breathing just a bellows-like movement of air? Or is it a symphony of sensation from the tip of the nose to the depths of the belly, reminding us at every moment how intimately we are supported by our environment? Even that is just a sample of the vast range of bodily experience waiting for us, if we look at our bodies as more than just sporadically troublesome carrier vessels for our brains.

You see the difference, but what difference makes the difference? I submit that the bulk of it can be accounted for by a single variable: attention. Rather than treating everything in our path as a checklist item to be recognized and otherwise ignored, properly attending to what’s happening right now is the doorway to a limitless richness of experience.

What determines the quality of our lives, really? Our consumerist society certainly has its answer: More! More things, more experiences, more spending, more debt. More signposts that promise lasting satisfaction but turn out to be empty pointers leaving us grasping for the next thing. But have we truly experienced what we have already got? What if, instead, we traded breadth of experience for depth?

What if, having bought something, we set our minds on getting the absolute most value out of it — and only bought things that would reward such attention?

What if we decided to experience all of our relationships with the vulnerability and compassion we associate with falling in love?

What if we decided to marinate in gratitude, all day every day?

What if we decided to invest our attention, rather than our money, in living a richer life?

What, in other words, if we determined to recognize signposts for what they are, and to check out what they’re pointing to?

You might think that this is all a cynical exercise. It’s easy enough to ponder the poverty of our experience, to struggle to comprehend how vast the universe is, in all its facets, compared to our measly intellect, and realize that we can’t even comprehend that — and stop at “Too bad so sad.” But there’s another way to look at it. In truth, I’m trying to convey an opportunity. Here we are, stuck in our little meat packets, and there’s more out there than we can ever know! Isn’t that exciting? No matter where we look, we can gorge ourselves forever on richer and richer experience, to the very limits of our capacity. And all we have to do is: attend.

…but there’s a catch. I’ve established the sad inadequacy of our senses and our faculties in general, and our real need to reduce experience to signposts that we can deal with. Both things are manifestly, persistently true. Consequently, it’s critical to remember that “waking up” is an unnatural act. The option is and will remain invisible — unless and until we remember to pursue it. It just will remain effortful and relentlessly forgettable. It’s a permanent struggle and a matter of constant reminding (re-minding). 

I could go on, but why? Instead, I’ll sign off with a poem, from Wisława Szymborska, that other Polish Nobel-laureate poet. The title is Miracle Fair.

Commonplace miracle:
that so many commonplace miracles take place.

The usual miracle:
invisible dogs barking
in the dead of night.

One of many miracles:
a small and airy cloud
is able to upstage the massive moon.

Several miracles in one:
an alder is reflected in the water
and is reversed from left to right
and grows from crown to root
and never hits bottom
though the water isn’t deep.

A run-of-the-mill miracle:
winds mild to moderate
turning gusty in storms.

A miracle in the first place:
cows will be cows.

Next but not least:
just this cherry orchard
from just this cherry pit.

A miracle minus top hat and tails:
fluttering white doves.

A miracle (what else can you call it):
the sun rose today at three fourteen A.M.
and will set tonight at one past eight.

A miracle that’s lost on us:
the hand actually has fewer than six fingers
but still it’s got more than four.

A miracle, just take a look around:
the inescapable earth.

An extra miracle, extra and ordinary:
the unthinkable
can be thought.

People ask about the meaning of life. It’s a question that I’ve always spurned as meaningless (so to speak). But there’s an answer right here: life has an infinity of meanings, a literally infinite banquet, if we just go beneath the surface and look. With the right kind of eyes, we find all the meaning, all the richness, all the depth we’ll ever need, surrounding us, waiting for us to follow the signposts.

Speaking personally, that’s all the religion I need. I invite you to take this essay as a signpost. What is it pointing to?

Postscript: a few suggestions

There are two basic strategies for diving into meaning: 1) seek out high-impact experiences, or 2) open up to everyday experience by digging down and finding rapture in the everyday.

Going for high-impact experiences may sound like cheating (exactly what’s the signpost we’re getting past?), but opening our eyes does mean working upstream against past habits, and a powerful, arresting experience drags you there by force. That’s valuable if only as a demonstration of what it feels like to go beyond, so that you know what you’re aiming for, and recognize it when you get there.

So what are these “high-impact experiences”? I’ve written before (Why Everything Fades) about hedonic adaptation, by which any organism files the edges off and tamps its response down when re-experiencing the familiar. One key to overcoming that tendency is novelty. Travel does it, but so does anything that pushes at the boundaries of prior experience and/or your comfort zone: having a challenging conversation, developing a new skill, throwing yourself into a different social situation, even something as simple as checking out a new restaurant or taking a different route home.

But one kind of experience is especially fruitful: anything which induces awe, the sense of accessing something larger than oneself. The list of awesome experiences is long — for example, encounters with moral heroism, massive communal experiences, nature, wondrous music and art, encounters with mortality — and there’s no space here to do it justice, so I recommend Dacher Keltner’s book with the somewhat cheesy title Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life.

But how does one find rapture in the everyday, without overhauling our lives or becoming thrill seekers? There is a technology, practiced by millions, that’s been under development for thousands of years: mindfulness meditation. In its simplest essence, mindfulness is about foregrounding what’s happening right now by reducing how much we’re distracted by revisiting the past and rehearsing the future.

This is no mean feat, and it entails a consistent practice. But the difference between never practicing, and practicing even ten minutes a day, is not to be underestimated. I like Henry Shukman’s metaphor: if you have a container full of muddy water, but you habitually add a little clear water, eventually the whole container comes clear.

Speaking of Henry Shukman: there are countless approaches to mindfulness; without rejecting any of them, I recommend Shukman’s app The Way, which offers a training for accessing the full spectrum of experience, from simple mindfulness on up to full awakening. If that sounds boring, let me ask: have you ever experienced the simple act of breathing in all its detail?

(For a little inspiration on the mindfulness front, try Stop Ignoring All the Mundane Miracles in Your Life and/or read why A Single Small Map is Enough For a Lifetime. You can also find a little coaching on recovering attention here. Finally, consider looking closely.)

There is a way to bring meaning and depth to the things you’re already doing: find your way to flow. 

Beyond simple obliviousness, another block to fully accessing current experience is the distraction of emotions — not the emotions themselves, but the effort to supress them. We expend enormous energy shoving down and suppressing unpleasant feelings, which is both costly (it’s hard to numb one feeling without numbing them all) and fruitless: they’re still there, no matter how firmly they’re suppressed, hanging around like car hulks in your front yard. Bringing them to the surface and actually feeling them can recover that energy, increase the dynamic range of experience, and — this is the crazy part—work through them (the usual metaphor is metabolize them) so that they shrink to a manageable level or disappear altogether. Certainly, opening yourself to shattering trauma is a bad idea absent professional intervention, but below that level, many of us have feelings that we could deal with but just don’t want to.

For my money, the avatars of this idea are Tara Brach, with her book Radical Acceptance, and Michael Singer’s book The Untethered Soul. In both cases, integrating their lessons is the work of a lifetime, but they don’t require overhauling your life: every step along the way is its own reward.

Finally, let me just highlight something intriguing about this way of living fully: no conversion, no surrender to a guru, no woo, no ascetic discipline, no grand program or complicated theology, no imposed expectations or other setups for disappointment. It’s pretty much just us and our minds and remembering to pay attention, with modest amounts of acquired skill and practice — even 10 minutes a day. And every little bit helps: every deliberate pause to breathe and take stock; every choice to actually go through a feeling rather than run from it or clamp down on it; every time we just stop — for even a moment — ruminating about the past or rehearsing the future and take refuge in this moment; every bit of awe, even five minutes of going outside and staring at the sky. Really!

Footnote: obviously the suggestions above are just what I have personally found. How do you get past the signposts to The Thing Itself? And what are your favorite such experiences? Please, do use the comments to share your own.

item.content:encoded:
Playing the Odds With Your Life

We Americans, our minds are ruled by Horatio Alger.

It’s hard to grasp how important the Horatio Alger myth is to how Americans understand themselves. There’s something uniquely American about the idea that anyone can achieve anything with enough pluck and hard work. 

Traditional conservative politics were deeply rooted in that idea, and in the corollary that


What are the real odds of success — and does it matter?

  • making a living in movies/art
  • making a living in music
  • making a living writing books: even supposing you can climb the mountain of actually getting to the end of writing a readable book, getting an agent and finding a publisher, just 1% of books sell more than 5000 copies
  • having a successful startup
  • playing in the NFL/NBA/MLB
  • meeting the people that make it happen
  • playing the stock market
  • success in politics
  • funnels all over the place: where by definition only a few can succeed

The more you look, the more success looks like a lottery

The key paradox: anybody can become president, but not everybody

Takeaways:

  • Just because anybody can succeed doesn’t mean everybody can.
  • The odds are sometimes as bad as playing the lottery.
  • Luck plays an irreducible role in our success.
  • We should get out of the grip of Horatio Alger at least as far as appreciating that we can only take limited credit for success.

item.content:encoded:
Sanity Checks

One of the things that scares people off of mathematics, or any logical system, is the rigor. A logician really hasn’t done her job unless she’s dotted all the i’s and crossed all the t’s: you can’t build an airtight case if you leave anything out. And the idea of doing that, of building a complete, airtight case, is scary — especially as viewed from the outside because you’ve never done it. That’s why most folks are happy to cruise along on intuition and impression; logicians too, most of the time.

Despite my background in the rigors of computer science, my deep dark secret is that I share that aversion. So I really like the idea of a sanity check. Usually when we’re presented with a proposition or an idea, the goal is to decide definitively whether it’s true or false, which is a very high bar and not often worth the trouble of getting over it. A sanity check, on the other hand, doesn’t ask “Is it true?”, but rather “Is it sane? Does it make any kind of sense at all?” If it’s not sane, you can dismiss it out of hand. If it is sane, it may or may not be worth further consideration. But at least it’s not insane. A sanity check is a low-key way to get closer to the truth without going overboard.

An example:

“Believe all women” What if two women claim contradictory things?

“Character counts.” (Rush Limbaugh and others on Clinton, before getting behind Trump.)

“Fiscally conservative”

Does unfettered access to guns extend to POCs?

Was the War On Drugs ever about safety? See response to opioids.

Still awaiting test results

What if a bonafide study found that gay parenting couples had results somewhere between straight couples and absent-father households?

My lefty cohort is waging a pitched moral battle for voting rights, but it’s hard not to notice the political benefit, marginalized voters disproportionately coming down on the liberal side. But I wonder what would happen to that principle if it turned out that the voters thus graced weren’t quite the allies that one assumes. There are preliminary indications that Latino voters have a variety of interests and priorities…

item.description: This is a companion post to What’s Wrong With Horatio Alger?, which
item.content:encoded:
Spot That Turn!

This is a companion post to What’s Wrong With Horatio Alger?, which 

Trump supporters are a pack of deplorables

Hillary Clinton took withering flak during the 2016 presidential campaign for this statement:

You know, to just be grossly generalistic, you could put half of Trump’s supporters into what I call the basket of deplorables. Right? The racist, sexist, homophobic, xenophobic, Islamaphobic — you name it. And unfortunately there are people like that. And he has lifted them up.

It’s hard to argue with what she’s actually saying here, i.e., “who else are the racist, sexist, etc. people going to vote for?” Trump and his rhetoric give them a home.

The pattern under discussion thus has the features “Trump supporter” and “political deviant.” Political deviants are observable among Trump supporters. The Turn occurs with the reflex to tag all Trump supporters with the “political deviant” label — and basically everybody at the time fell all over themselves making that turn and blasting away that either Clinton was a horrible elitist or had made herself seem that way. 

But it’s absolutely untrue that Clinton herself had such a negative opinion of Trump supporters in general. Just read what she said immediately after that incendiary comment:

But the other basket — and I know this because I see friends from all over America here — I see friends from Florida and Georgia and South Carolina and Texas — as well as, you know, New York and California — but that other basket of people are people who feel that the government has let them down, the economy has let them down, nobody cares about them, nobody worries about what happens to their lives and their futures, and they’re just desperate for change. It doesn’t really even matter where it comes from. They don’t buy everything he says, but he seems to hold out some hope that their lives will be different. They won’t wake up and see their jobs disappear, lose a kid to heroin, feel like they’re in a dead-end. Those are people we have to understand and empathize with as well.

If The Turn didn’t actually cost Hillary Clinton the presidency, it certainly made a key contribution.

The police are a clear and present danger to Black men in America

The brutality of police killings of Black men in America is seared into the memory of anyone who’s seen the George Floyd video or tracked similar crimes in the news. The pattern associating Blackness (especially young, male Blackness) with atrocity is not to be denied.

As horrible as that reality is, and as much as it triggers justifiable fear and reanimates the sordid history of racism in America, nonetheless: you have to go through The Turn to reach the conclusion that police violence is an imminent threat to young Black males. Yes, absolutely, police violence is frequently visited upon them. But “threat” means a high risk that any given young Black man will be beaten down. Is the average Black man actually in danger of having it happen to them? Statistically, in a random group of 100,000 Black men, between 1.9 and 2.4 of them will be killed by police. (The corresponding figure non-Hispanic white males is between .6 and .7).

It’s important to put such figures into context. In a group of 100,000 Black men, how many will die of cancer? About 216— roughly 100 times more. In fact, the difference in cancer rate between white and Black men is more than 40 per 100,000. Black men are about 40 times more likely to die of cancer because they’re Black than to die at the hands of police because they’re Black.

More pertinently, what is the overall risk of dying by homicide, including all other contexts? According to DoJ figures, between 1980 and 2018, 27.8 Black people per 100,000 died of homicide. Only a fraction (1/10) of Black people are killed by police than by others.

So what is the point of stomping through this minefield of atrocity, feelings and triggers? If your sole focus is on protecting Black men from horrific death by focusing on official homicide, you’re being woefully distracted. The (much larger) race-based disparity in things like death from cancer and overall life expectancy is one thing. But even confining your attention to crime, the problem stretches far beyond police culpability. The truth is, law enforcement is grossly underserving the Black community, for reasons having to do with historical racism and an ongoing suspicion held by that community. We need to be working to heal the rift between the two, focusing on building trust in the community and, in general, moving police culture from a samurai-like Guardian model to a Servant model. It is possible to work in that direction if you’ve decided that the police are the enemy, but you might find it easier going if you back up and resist that Turn.


The media is dependably undependable? You’ve been snared by this bias.

A rare exception: COVID is observable, but not dependable

Medicine: The Dramatics dream of medical results does not mean predictable miracles

Stereotyping: the observation of group traits does not mean that you can depend on them.

Water is transparent. Does that mean you can’t tell an empty glass from a full one?

Marriage: can I love someone, versus can I dependably love someone?

“Drinking the kool-aid” as denoting the flip.

AI: special domains vs dependable gen. intel.

Patterns are at the heart of stereotyping. (young Black men wearing their pants low)

Love and marriage, love and marriage
Go together like a horse and carriage, horse and carriage

The difference between observability and predictability is at the heart of many a dispute or miscommunication. How many arguments have started with an interaction of the form:

It bothers me when you [action].
Oh, so you think I’m a [kind of person who does that all the time]!
