item.content:encoded:
Takeaways from 50 year of cooking

If you like to skim the cream from the experience of others, let me offer a few key gleanings from a life in the kitchen. Why should you care what I think? I’m not a professional cook, nor even a particularly distinguished amateur, but there’s one master lesson I’ve learned over time: Good cooking doesn’t have to mean tricky or difficult cooking. There are millions of recipes out there, and some of the simplest are some of the best. At the same time, there are a few cooking hacks that aren’t difficult at all but make a quantum difference in the outcome. It’s just a matter of paying attention. Skill and tricksiness are totally optional barriers to feeding yourself well.

  • Cooking for people and offering it to them is glue for bonding. Even (especially?) people who have no use for emotions and relationships expressed in any kind of overt fashion are touched by the act of sitting and eating together, and the offering of your makings. It’s been the foundation of my community (one that has no other obvious binding factors), and our kids have gone on to behave likewise just because the results were so obvious to them. So the meta-tip here is “Make a life for yourself by feeding people.”
  • It is a sin to waste meat carcasses. Instead of dumping them into the trash, dump them into a pot, cover generously with water, add a little salt (possibly some carrot, unpeeled garlic, bay leaf, etc. as well) and simmer for an hour. Then make soup! Almost any soup you make with a half-decent stock — no matter how simple — will blow the doors off almost any other soup that uses store-bought “broth”.
  • Keep an herb patch. Herbs are survivors: their hardiness is related to the volatile oils that provide the flavor. Many of them, like rosemary, parsley, mint, sage and thyme just keep going and going. There’s nothing more pleasurable than strolling outside and plucking a few leaves for your supper — unless it’s the pleasure of not paying multiple dollars for a small helping from the store. Even in pots, even just a parsley plant…
  • Get whole spices and grind them. I know, this sounds too twee for words, but again: volatile oils. They disappear fast from ground product. Using an old whirly coffee grinder takes seconds, and the smell that comes out when you open it…!
  • No recipe ever suffers from a third less sugar or twice as much garlic or vegetables.
  • Why, oh why, does anyone buy sugar syrup? A cup of water, a cup and a half of sugar, three minutes in the microwave, and a quick stir. Done.
  • …or salad dressing? Some oil, a little vinegar, salt and pepper and a quick whisk is all it takes. Elaborations (garlic, mustard, yogurt, chopped herbs, etc.) optional — and fun.
  • Do not disrespect the frozen pea, or corn, or canned tomato. These things are packaged near where they’re grown, so even when they’re seasonal I’ve rarely met a fresh pea to beat its frozen cousin.
  • Water is amazing…for thawing frozen foods. Its thermal mass gets heat into the frozen in a fraction of the time.
  • Measuring by volume and by weight are interchangeable, a lot of the time. The reason is that many foods are approximately as dense as water, and — what do you know? — 16 fl. oz. of water weighs…1 pound!
  • Sungold tomatoes rule. If you only grow one vegetable, let it be Sungold cherry tomatoes. Every year my wife plants tomato varieties by the dozens, and every year the most exciting moment is when the Sungolds start coming in.
  • Don’t be afraid of salting meat. 
  • The Maillard reaction is where the flavor is. From slowly browning onions to toasting nuts and roasting vegetables, to making gravy from the scratchy drippings in a roast pan, the magic that happens when surfaces are gently browned is the shortest, laziest path to richness and flavor across the board.

Invitation to Brave Space

Together we will create brave space.

Because there is no such thing as a “safe space” — 

We exist in the real world.

In this space

We amplify voices that fight to be heard elsewhere,

We have the right to start somewhere and continue to grow.

We have the responsibility to examine what we think we know.

We will not be perfect.

This space will not be perfect.

It will not always be what we wish it to be.

But

It will be our brave space together,

and

We will work on it side by side.

Micky ScottBey Jones

item.title: The Joy of Paradox
item.description: I love paradox. Isn’t that perverse? The word comes with discomfort, the tension between two ideas that take effort to reconcile: the Zen koans of everyday life. Yet there’s an energy there that becomes quite addictive. For those who love the feeling of Understanding The World, f…
item.content:encoded:
The Joy of Paradox

I love paradox. Isn’t that perverse? The word comes with discomfort, the tension between two ideas that take effort to reconcile: the Zen koans of everyday life. Yet there’s an energy there that becomes quite addictive. For those who love the feeling of Understanding The World, few things can compare.

Looking back (and around, today), the popular disdain for “intellectuals” was and is hilarious. The notion that there must be something wrong with anyone who would devote any attention at all to ideas when there is actual reality to engage with, was and is an evergreen source of contempt among the practical folk.

What’s hilarious about that, of course, is that it’s like fish dissing water. Ideas are the very coin of the realm for anyone dealing with the world or communicating with their fellows. They’re what we use to wrangle reality in our heads. It’s not that there are some who deal in ideas and others who have no use for them; it’s that everyone deals with them all day long. The only difference is whether they realize that, or turn their backs on it.

What happens when ideas or principles collide?

Spectra

Contradiction

Ambiguity vs. Ambivalence

As a good neoliberal, I hold two firm opinions about capitalism and the free market. It is the most efficient system for organizing economic activity ever devised, a relentless engine of prosperity. And also, it is a machine that discounts humanity and entrenches advantage, engendering cycles of both poverty and wealth to an extent that is simply oppressive in the absence of mitigating action. As my uncle, a staunch capitalist, used to say, “Them as has, gets.”

Yes, these two positions are paradoxical — but they’re not contradictory. Reasonable people can hold both of them at the same time; in fact, it seems obvious to me that reasonable people should hold both of them, and firmly, because both of them are true. But how much sound and fury comes directly and exclusively from the assumption that if one is true, the other can’t be? How much betrayal felt by those committed to one side when one of their own says anything sympathetic to the other? These are symptoms of one thing only: the instinct that says if two ideas are in tension, one of them must be wrong, i.e., you have to choose, to take sides. Politics arranges itself on a spectrum according to allegiance to these two positions, from libertarians firmly and exclusively planted at one end, all the way to utopian ideals of collective ownership at the other. The very idea of compromise becomes associated with dilution, of abandoning commitment.

The inability to tolerate paradox has another aspect: the image of the namby-pamby liberal who can’t make up his or her mind in the face of a difficult choice, who wants to have it both ways and so winds up with a kind of mental mush. But the error there is trying to resolve the paradox by combining the opposing poles rather than leaving them distinct and keeping them both vividly in mind. It’s the difference between ambiguity and ambivalence: the former denotes an unclear distinction; the latter, a strong commitment to both sides — literally, ambi-valent. The two couldn’t be more different (as it were).

What does this mean in practice when it comes to managing a market-based economy?

  • recognize market-distorting subsidies when you see them (ag, water)
  • make investments, not subsidies
  • remove competition over the public good, asserting a minimum standard of behavior for the market to work within (mileage standards for cars)
  • use the marketplace to force change: carbon taxes, realistic water prices, jump-starting “good” directions, e.g. renewables
  • act explicitly to mitigate the accumulation of wealth
  • resist the influence of money on politics
  • craft a firm social safety net, a minimum standard of living below which nobody need drop
  • Meditation can be quite paradoxical — sometimes we get what we want when we stop wanting it
  • We can’t predict the weather, but we can get a handle on the climate: https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-climate-change-paradox-20250915/

To the extent that political dialogue in the US is sincere, and centers around different people’s perspective on this basic issue,** polarization can be described as entrenchment at one side or the other of this paradox, with free-marketers ever more dismissive of social concerns, and vice versa. But I would like to suggest that embracing a paradox like this is actually the way out of the bind we find ourselves in.

** Yes, I realize that this may be a naive assumption. It assumes that American politics hasn’t devolved into a battle of power and naked self-interest. I suppose this is the namby-pamby liberal in me coming out.

Easy: freedom vs. responsibility.

The Mr. Rodgers Paradox: Did he truly cripple a generation of children? You’re Okay vs. unearned entitlement

“Unrestrained capitalism is anti-humanistic” vs. “Free-market economies are the most efficient mechanism known for allocating, optimizing and moving resources.”

In education, every child deserves an opportunity to be their best vs. the best and brightest need support

Tradeoffs: zero-sum games: indulgence now or cushy retirement later? Luxurious eating or manageable weight?

The pursuit of Awareness: in Zen, the pursuit of the goal creates a striving/craving that works against reaching the goal [Shukman]. Is this paradoxical or ironical?

Spectrums: one dimension covering two extremes

Both pertain: it’s possible to maintain both at once

Dialectic: two which inform, energize and lend meaning to the other.

The need for autonomy and the need for connection.

The relentless drive to achieve goals vs. the agility to change course as needed.

Pursuing goals is essential. Achieving goals is entirely optional.

Dialectic

Dialectic is paradox over time, in which contradictory patterns play out

Early childhood development: freedom or protection? Healthy attachment develops when the caregiver is available to a child in distress, which gives them freedom to explore, secure in the knowledge that they can come back for reassurance. The dialectic between distress and comfort builds resilience and ultimate sense of safety in the world.

Relationships: boundaries to maintain personal state vs. vulnerability and intimacy

Examples of High Paradox

Expertise vs. Humility: any healer needs to maintain scrupulous humility in the face of the complexity and intractability of reality, but at the same time sustain enough confidence to take action and/or to lead; otherwise: powerless.

item.title: The Last Word on Free Will
item.description: Do we have free will, are we the captains of our own fate? Is everything pre-ordained by brain chemistry? Are we just leaves blowing in the winds of circumstance?
item.content:encoded:
The Last Word on Free Will

Do we have free will, are we the captains of our own fate? Is everything pre-ordained by brain chemistry? Are we just leaves blowing in the winds of circumstance?

For most people, I reckon, the question is both trivial and persistently unsettling. Trivial, because the matter seems decided by a little introspection: I feel like I decide what I do, and I like feeling in control. Besides, what difference does it make whether I’m the original author of my own intentions or not? Don’t spoil my complacency by making me think about it too much. 

Fair enough.

But it’s unsettling because it leads directly to questions of personal responsibility. When someone behaves badly, either socially or criminally, then if that person was at the mercy of the universe, how fair is it to punish them? That’s just (re)action directed at the wrong target.

That tug of sympathy for the miscreant is one of the bigger differences between Right and Left, at least historically (modern-day political hysterics have different fish to fry), with one side focussing on a Biblical model of punishment for sins, while the other tends more to look for underlying causes (i.e., upbringing in poverty, childhood neglect and abuse, various personal psychiatric disorders, etc.).

While I’ve always been sympathetic to the addressing-underlying-causes side of things, I really didn’t want to give up on the idea of holding people accountable; wouldn’t accepting some flavor of determinism make that impossible to avoid, and set us on a slippery slope to anarchy?

Something I read a long time ago brought a lot of clarity to my thinking about this, and now I offer it forth to you. In a meeting in the California governor’s office with Herman Kahn, the question of free will came up and he remarked

What kind of people do you get? If you act as if there’s free will and people are responsible for their actions, you get one kind of person. If you act as if people and everything is determined and they’re not responsible for their acts, you get a very different kind of personality…And I don’t care what the real world has to do with this, because even if it’s a deterministic world you get a preferable kind of people by treating them as though they have free will.

From one perspective, it’s quite unsettling to think that everything we say and do is predetermined. If we as individuals are not in control, then who is?

Determinists ask, in the moment after you say or do anything, how could it have been otherwise? Perhaps you could have decided to do something different beforehand, but how could that have happened otherwise? And so on from there. Thus we are led to an infinite regress that to determinists sounds like a trump card, and to others (not naming names here) seems like the kind of cute philosophical argument that doesn’t mean anything.

For most of us, the matter is settled by simple experience, at least at the personal levelBut at the societal level, it becomes quite a sticking point. When someone else commits a crime (say), how harshly we judge them depends largely on how responsible we think they are for their actions

I think it’s fair to say that the question of free will lies just below the surface of arguments about crime and punishment. If a person has little control over their decisions, and thus their actions, there’s little to be said for a punitive attitude, vengeance aside. But if free will pertains, if the criminal was responsible for their actions, then punishment, while it may or not be a moral imperative, seems more like a reasonable option.

This argument shows no prospect of being resolved as long as the contenders bring their unspoken assumptions about personal responsibility. Even if they did lay their cards on the table, the argument would still rage on.

But I’ve always felt that there was a tension here, something looming unspoken over the whole debate. And I think I’ve finally put my finger on it:

Holding a person responsible for their actions is a reasonable course whether free will exists or not.

It’s obviously true when people do have free will. But if they don’t — if their actions are wholly determined by history and context — then an important part of that context is what will happen to them after they misbehave. In other words, determinism is no excuse for removing one of the factors that determines people’s choices.

In the immortal words of Herman Kahn, 

Whether free will exists or not, you get a better class of people if you assume that it does.

So, underlying a belief in punitive justice (again, setting aside motivations of vengeance) is an assumption that people are responsible for their actions. And behind much of the sentiment in favor of a more lenient approach is that they’re not. But if the question of free will is effectively moot, then where’s the beef?

Please, I don’t mean to imply that this realization would transform the debate. But it would help if everybody was barking up the right tree.

item.title: The Meaning of Life?!?
item.description: Is anyone else as annoyed as I am by the question “What is the meaning of life?”
item.content:encoded:
A Life of Meaning

Is anyone else as annoyed as I am by the question “What is the meaning of life?”

I’ve long been fascinated by the idea that our brains are in the business of reporting objective reality. The truth is that those brains are much more adept at making us believe they do that than they are at actually delivering veridicality. For decades, we’ve been awash in behavioral economics, data about cognitive bias and countless other streams bent on separating us from that impression, yet we remain unbowed. We don’t really know what to do with this information.

There are areas in thinking about thinking where meaning is found a legitimate and useful place (Buddhist psychology), but for the most part, what something is is all tangled up with what it means. And learning to tease the two apart turns out to be a surprisingly useful and productive endeavor.

Meaning in economics

Meaning-making in psychology

I recently had a very trying (to say the least) experience with meaning-making which permanently cemented its importance in my mind. In the course of working within a group, I committed some egregious errors. (Pardon the vagueness here; the details aren’t important, and the privacy of the parties involved is.) Nothing as bad as sexual assault or anything else sexual, and absolutely without malice or any ill intention, but still: bad enough to make me permanently ashamed to have failed so badly. And the reaction was cataclysmic. Two members of the group permanently wrote me off, and through a social process that I wasn’t privy to, I became a pariah and a scapegoat for the group at large.

Now, what to do with this? In some sense, what I did caused that reaction. Does that mean I have to take full responsibility for it? It seems that there’s a real disproportionality between the nature and intention of my actions and the ultimate impact, but how do I draw a boundary between the two? It seems like the other parties involved must have some role in the outcome but what could that be, when the spectre of “blaming the victim” is so real? The fact that I meant no harm doesn’t count for much. How can I not blame myself for everything that happened? How do I avoid the conclusion that I’m a horrible person? I want to take responsibility for what I did, but how to square that with the seeming disproportionality of the ultimate outcome?

The idea of meaning-making rescued me from this quandary. I did certain things, and those things had an effect. The actions and their direct effects were what is. But in the event, some of the others in the group chose to derive the absolute worst, most uncharitable meaning from those blunders, starting with the initial response and ending with ostracizing me. Other meanings could have been derived from the facts of the matter, and I can’t be responsible for which meanings prevailed.

Analyzing the meaning-making in situations like this doesn’t eliminate wiggle-room or judgment calls. All it does is establish a continuum, from inevitable, to reasonable, to unreasonable, to hostile and beyond. But it does provide the tools to think about the proportionality of response without either letting the perpetrator off the hook or making them responsible for everything that might result from a given action.

item.description: We’re stewing in the evidence, but we just won’t accept the simple fact: people are stupid and getting stupider with every passing year.
item.content:encoded:
The Phenomenology Crisis: Just how stupid are we, anyway?

We’re stewing in the evidence, but we just won’t accept the simple fact: people are stupid and getting stupider with every passing year.

I don’t mean “stupid” as in “blundering around bumping heads and breaking necks against reality”; Idiocracy stupid, Darwin Awards stupid. Our lives are generally arranged so that we can mostly avoid most fatal errors even with limited brainpower. I mean “stupid” as in “manifestly incapable of keeping up with the demands of modernity.”

The digital age has put humanity in a fatal bind: we are expected to know more and more at the same time that social media and the politicization of news have made it harder and harder to think coherently. If we keep going this way, democracy will fail and the only successful cultures will be ones where strong figures take over policy power and wrest control from contentious factions

A responsible thinker needs coherent beliefs far in excess of the human capacity for processing information. We have no choice but to use shortcuts/heuristics. There’s no getting around this fundamental limitation, regardless of education, dedication to truth.

We think the limitations on developing true beliefs have to do with intelligence, education and good faith. This implies that “some people” can dependably find their way to true beliefs, and enables the hope that we ourselves could be one of the epistemically virtuous. What we never stop to realize is that the real limiting factor is time, and none of us has much more time than anyone else. Some may use their time better than others, but no matter how well we use our time, it will never be enough. The time we have is no match for the time we need. Ultimately we’re all in the same boat, flailing against this limitation. We’re doomed to failure, and the only real difference between us is how dismally we fail.

item.title: The Problem with Commun(al)ism
item.description: It’s a crucial part of the divide between Left and Right, how much the state should provide resources on behalf of everyone. Even in America, despite its Everyone For Themselves ethic, most everyone agrees that it is the state’s business to provide for national defense, policing,…
item.content:encoded:
The Problem with Commun(al)ism

It’s a crucial part of the divide between Left and Right, how much the state should provide resources on behalf of everyone. Even in America, despite its Everyone For Themselves ethic, most everyone agrees that it is the state’s business to provide for national defense, policing, firefighting, roads and schools. But there are well-gnawed bones of contention over providing for the disadvantaged, climate-change mitigation, and “socialized” access to medical care. 

These seem like issues that begin and end with values like personal responsibility vs. compassion for those of straitened circumstances. People also differ on how seriously to take the free-rider problem of beneficiaries unfairly gaming the system. In such a battle of values, it’s hard to envision any productive dialogue and easy to despair of making any progress. But there’s a way to put such discussions on a much more practical footing. It goes back to a realization I had back in 9th Grade, when I assigned myself to write a paper for English class on The Communist Manifesto. 

This was back in the Sixties. The Red Scare of the Fifties was over, but with America embroiled in Vietnam — ostensibly to resist the hegemonious impulses of the USSR and Red China — Communism itself (as distinct from the dictatorial predilections of its nominal practitioners) was still the preeminent bête noire of the West. I wanted to figure out what the deal really was, so I picked up Karl Marx’s founding document.

Marx serves up plenty of socio-historical analysis, which 14-year-old me was eminently unqualified to judge and 69-year-old me can happily live without. Not so, though, the basic idea for a radical model of how a society should manage who gets what:

From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.

In other words, the production of labor should be pooled and then distributed among the population according to need.

The problems with that proposition may seem self-evident, because human nature. But looking underneath the obvious turns up a tool of thought that’s more than a little useful when considering many other policies for redistributing resources.

Consider the mathematics involved — or rather, simple arithmetic. 

Ideology and idealism aside, you can really learn a lot by looking closely at this proposition.

This is a manifesto for gaming the system. If I collectivize with three others, my contributions get me 1/4 back. With 10 people total, I get back only 10% of my production. Conversely, every unit I take out of the system only costs my share of the system a quarter or a tenth of that unit.

Under such a distribution scheme, it’s easier to get resources by milking the output than by contributing to the input. And the problem only gets worse as the pool of people increases. At the level of countries, the motivation to contribute to (or not to game) goes to zero, as does the cost to me of what I take out.

The only thing standing in the way of this insidious dynamic is the individual’s commitment to making it work — at the expense of his/her own interests. As an individual, you’re weighing your belief in sharing against the temptation for free-riding. And as the number of people in the system gets bigger, you have to get REALLY idealistic.

But it’s worse than that. Not only do you as an individual have to resist that temptation, in fealty to your fellow humans, you have to trust that everyone else is doing the same. Free riders and cheaters will be very conspicuous. How do you maintain your ideals when others are so richly rewarded for not doing so? This is exactly what happened in Soviet Russia, where party apparatchiks lorded over the commoners.

I should mention that such pooling of resources isn’t always a bad idea. This is exactly the idea behind insurance: people pool their money against some tragedy, paying out to the unlucky few it falls to. But insurance has systemic resistance to unchecked greed, so it’s harder to cheat. But even there, people do cheat: who resists the temptation to pad their insurance claims? It’s not just communist social organization that has this basic flaw.

item.content:encoded:
The Stupid Voter Problem

It’s sorely tempting for people like me to look at today’s electoral landscape and decide that a large fraction of Americans are just plain stupid. Personally, I’m grasping at straws trying to rationalize their behavior and avoid that conclusion, when I’m not doing handstands to avoid the question altogether. Ironically, that makes it harder to confront the question: what is wrong with the American voter?

 I know it’s hard to believe when we’re drowning in “information” and especially controversy, but there’s (at least) one question/topic that’s off-limits for serious discussion, addressed in only the most oblique way: what is wrong with the American voter?

I don’t mean that the word “stupid” isn’t slung around casually in online forums. I mean that the character and perspicacity of “the voter”, the ground-level participant in democracy, is an article of faith, and if you want to be taken seriously, then dropping any hint that some fraction of voters are letting the ball drop, is a good way to get yourself dismissed if not ostracized as elitist.

This crystallized for me recently when Jonathan V. Last of The Bulwark arguably stepped on that third rail in an episode of the Next Level podcast. In his frustration he made a few anodyne comments about that: 

Trust me, I understand why it’s such a hot topic. In America, any discussion that smacks of elitism — such as, oh, I don’t know, calling people stupid — is to be avoided at all cost, especially when the perception of elitism is such a hand grenade. Also, online “discussions” with or about one’s adversaries go first to anger and attacks on character. Finally, the spirit of “to everyone a vote” doesn’t play very well with the idea that some people thus enfranchised are idiots.

item.description: How fucked is America? It’s a question that haunts the days of Donald Trump’s presidency. Sooner or later he’ll be gone, but how much of the damage is recoverable? It’s always fun to speculate (How long to re-earn trust from the international community? To restore institutional n…
item.content:encoded:
We Are Not Serious People

How fucked is America? It’s a question that haunts the days of Donald Trump’s presidency. Sooner or later he’ll be gone, but how much of the damage is recoverable? It’s always fun to speculate (How long to re-earn trust from the international community? To restore institutional norms? To rein in future power grabs and corruption?), but I believe there’s one core truth that’s not speculative and it’s damning. Give me a few paragraphs to set it up.

[Spoiler Alert for the TV series Succession]

Succession is about the struggles of Logan Roy’s four children to become the successor to his vast media empire. After three seasons of teases and power plays in which one or another of them seem destined to win and/or struggle with the old man for control, the old man dismisses them all, delivering one of the most devastating put-downs ever to his privileged, delusional, narcissistic brood, making it clear that none of them is The One: “You’re not serious people.” He would rather cash out than entrust his empire to any of his offspring. It’s a killer stroke in the manner of many great dramatic reveals: it exposes, in the simplest possible sentence, a crucial truth that had been just below the surface all along.

My point is that there’s a similar, similarly cutting, observation about where we are just now: 

The United States of America is no longer a serious country in the charge of serious people. And that’s why we’re fucked.

That’s why we will keep thrashing around like a motorboat with no rudder. That’s why we’ll keep spending our energies attacking each other rather than tackling real issues. That’s why we’ll still be vulnerable to the siren song of authoritarianism. We’re no longer a nation of serious people.

How can we tell? How can we prove a negative like this? You can’t, of course: negatives are funny that way. Instead, I’m going to list out some qualities of serious people, and I think the differences between them and us will speak for themselves.

Serious people use reality to form their beliefs, not the other way round.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/17/opinion/inflation-affordability-prices-burrito.html

Economic perception vs. reality

Acceptance of claims of voter fraud

Vaccine skepticism

Serious people care about character and strive to embody it themselves.

Serious people factor in more than their own self-interest

There was a time when Americans took into account their national interest as well as their own. Think about the national response in World War II: widespread recuitment, dealing with privation rather than complaining about it, etc. 

Look at Canada in 2026, which has gone from an unserious nation in the US mold to a seriously serious one almost overnight:

[B]efore Trump started threatening to swallow Canada whole, Canadian politics was drifting toward the same lazy, vibes-based, punish-the-incumbent sleepwalk that infects every comfortable democracy on the planet. Then the human tariff schedule with a comb-over started ranting about annexation, and 40 million Canadians collectively sat bolt upright in bed and said righto, fuck this for a joke, no more mucking about, we are electing the most qualified adult on the continent.

Serious people heed wisdom over impulse

Serious people respect their own limitations 

Serious people know the difference between the serious and the frivolous, the real and the symbolic

Serious people accept the responsibility that comes with power.

Serious people prioritize the success of the enterprise over beating their rivals

How would we know that we were serious people? 

Serious people would take the national debt seriously.

Serious people would take the problem of housing supply head on.

Serious people would figure out a way to move forward on health care

Serious people would come to terms with immigration policy

Serious people take character seriously, even against their own self-interest

If you’d like to see a serious person in action, consider the Prime Minister of Canada. He is a member in good standing of the reality-based community. He will not cave to the whims of Donald Trump. He is a man of sober thought and thoughtful action

item.description: Six months in, cringing before the onslaught that is the second Trump presidency, we’re already asking ourselves “How much of this can even be undone by saner heads?” Such tides have reversed in the past, but this is feeling like a more fundamental change, in ways that are hard t…
item.content:encoded:
We’re Yahoo Nation Now

Six months in, cringing before the onslaught that is the second Trump presidency, we’re already asking ourselves “How much of this can even be undone by saner heads?” Such tides have reversed in the past, but this is feeling like a more fundamental change, in ways that are hard to put your finger on. Here’s one: it’s not just that the Yahoos are in charge. We’re a Yahoo nation now.

What do I mean by a Yahoo?

The US has always had its fair share of Yahoos.

Beginning with WWII and particularly its aftermath, the United States acquired a certain stature in the world. Science. Inter-relatedness. Trade. Institutional norms. 

Let me first make an important distinction. I grew up with some (white) people that others would dismiss as ignorant or otherwise uncouth by uppity standards, education being one of their issues, or being less rigorous about social graces. Growing up with people like that taught me that grace, compassion, reflectiveness and insight are only loosely correlated with level of education.

Yahoo == impulsive, entitled, empowered thoughtlessness. Sloppy of thought, impulsive of action. The opposite of careful, modest and rigorous. Yahoo thinking would turn on a dime given the least bit of thought.

Yahoo thinking is blind to simple distinctions: between Trump being prosecuted for crimes, on the one hand, and wholesale attacks on the independence of law enforcement and casualizing investigation and prosecution of political enemies. Between foreign criminals hiding out here and undocumented workers who are otherwise an innocent, productive presence.

Never mind better or worse policy, simple stupidity is acceptable: turning our backs on the future of energy. shooting ourselves in the foot with energy policy.

In embarking down the path of immigration enforcement defined by the BBB, America is blithely walking into deep, dark state apparatus. In ten years that will be retrospectively obvious, but it’s only the most casual observer who can’t see it coming even now. We’re giving ICE a blank check to sweep people off the street and hold them indefinitely without any due process. Why is approving of this a Yahoo stance? Failing to make a distinction between booting the worst of the worst and just rounding up people at Home Depot

Dismissal of professional journalism. “Doing my own research”. Failing to distinguish between pros who make mistakes and slapdash clickbait.

Never mind the constitutionality of giving ICE a blank check and default approval of masked officers hauling people off the street: detention centers and no courts with no purpose than giving a fearsome impression of an America bristling with hostility to the outsider

Acting like science is just another elite occupation bleeding the population dry for no purpose other than their own aggrandizement.

Idiocy in the ascendant: anti-vax, creationist, flat-earth, chem-trails, Jan 6 revisionism

America First vs. cooperation, trust and free commerce.

Let’s be frank: this strain has always been present in America. But two things kept a lid on it for the most part: representative democracy and institutional norms.

None of this is news. What we’re discovering is that 1) those values were our inheritance from the founding, and 2) the only reason we hung onto them was that we had always hung onto them; 3) Trump has blown them away like a castle made of tissue paper.

We ain’t getting that back.

item.content:encoded:
What Psychedelics Prove

Have you ever endured hearing about other people’s magical, transformative experiences with psychedelics? Whether you’ve had such experiences yourself or not, maybe you’ve learned to dread crackpot rants about alternative dimensions, mystical creatures and/or a drill down into the ultimate ground of being. What could be more tedious when received back here in quotidian reality?

As one who has had such experiences myself, I’m 

Under LSD, I have seen reality as we know it drop out altogether, “revealing” the cosmos as nothing but a flow of energy, with the people around me become pulsations of that energy.

Under MDMA, I have envisioned myself at the bottom of a swimming pool, swathed in tranquility and contentment, looking up at the surface with all the people churning and thrashing in their confusion, and thinking to myself “This is what it’s all about. This is what everyone’s trying to get to, whether they know it or not.”

But there’s always the voice in the back of my head that won’t shut up, saying “Yeah, well, that’s just the drugs talking”, or “What is there, really?” These experiences come laden with doubts that haunt serious people: mightn’t it all be a hallucination, a Coleridge revery with no intrinsic, material meaning?

Is any of that “real”? Is there any reason to think that these experiences have any more substance than a temporary shift in brain chemistry? Subjectively, absolutely. The sense of certainty that accompanies these flights is so complete as to be unquestionable — from the inside. From the outside, or even from the inside following the return to earth, can’t they all be filed away with dreams and delusions?

The “undeniable fact” in the title here is this:

Whatever the empirical validity of any psychedelic experience, one thing has to be true: the fact that my consciousness is capable of entering that state.

Just for one brief example: I have taken a group journey (MDMA) with seven other people. In the course of it, we did bonding exercises that, unsurprisingly, worked a treat. The group came out of the experience with a love that is palpable in their ordinary interactions today. 

That experience raises the question: is that love illusory? I’m here to tell you that it’s very real today. Is that current fact in any way diminished by its origin? 

Do you know what a catalyst is? In chemistry, a catalyst is a material that engenders a reaction among other substances, but the catalyst itself isn’t consumed. In the old tale of Stone Soup, the stone is unchanged at the end, but the village has been fed.

There’s an old joke that I keep coming back to again and again. It ends Woody Allen’s film Annie Hall (sorry), and even there it’s presented as an old joke:

[T]his guy goes to a psychiatrist and says, “Doc, my brother’s crazy. He 
 thinks he’s a chicken.” And the doctor says, “Well, why don’t you turn 
 him in?” And the guy says, “I would, but I need the eggs.”

item.description: The pre-eminent fact about American politics today is, not to mince words, the hard core Trump cult: the roughly 30% of voters who are unpersuadably loyal to Donald Trump. They are the basis of the reign of terror that Trump holds over the Republican majority in Congress, simply…
item.content:encoded:
What to do about the Trump Cultist?

The pre-eminent fact about American politics today is, not to mince words, the hard core Trump cult: the roughly 30% of voters who are unpersuadably loyal to Donald Trump. They are the basis of the reign of terror that Trump holds over the Republican majority in Congress, simply because they can be counted upon to primary any Republican deemed apostate by The Man. They are the number below which his approval ratings will never sink no matter how dismal his record in office. And they present a nigh-insurmountable barrier to any Presidential challenger: when you start with a third of the electorate in your pocket no matter what, then you can get to a majority of the votes with only one quarter of the remainder.

Let’s take a moment to ponder this phenomenon: how such a remarkable thing happened, why it’s so stubborn, how to cope with it now, and what it means for the future, after Trump is gone. All of these are interesting questions because they’re unprecedented in my fairly elderly experience, and because they’re key contributors to the stress test that American democracy seems to be undergoing.

How did we get here?

The unswerving attachment to Donald Trump by the millions is without equal or precedent in my (fairly long) lifetime. I speak as a former William Buckley conservative who grew up in the South among people who would now be considered canonical Trump voters: frequently middling- to low-education (and proud of it), grumpy about racial equality, with visions of the Welfare Queen and the Red Menace dancing in their heads. George Wallace voters, businessman conservatives, veterans who thought the way soldiers were supposed to think (stalwart, disciplined, America-first). I had disagreements all along the way, but I also had some sense of their perspective, and always intuitively felt that they were persuadable, or at least there was a certain amount of respect going both ways. That there was real racial progress in the Sixties, the shift toward environmental protection over business as usual, and the turn against Nixon and the Vietnam War, would seem to validate that impression.

This time is different. 

Let‘s count the ways:

  • While the Right has always tried to make “liberal” more of an epithet than a label, the tone has gotten uniquely contemptuous.
  • Fealty to Trump entails surrendering if not backhanding all sorts of values that always seemed core to conservative ideology: the rule of law; the value of truth, or at least appearing truthful, over overt bullshit; expectations of financial probity for public officeholders; understanding and defending freedom of speech; revulsion at hypocrisy; expressing and upholding immutable standards of personal morality; aversion to Presidential over-reach; alarm at even the appearance of corruption; deference to science; hair-trigger sensitivity to any whiff of a police state; rejection of socialism; respect for institutional norms in general and in particular the independence of institutions like the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve. Imagine Barry Goldwater rationalizing the January 6 invasion of Congress!
  • The US has become more geographically polarized, with rural areas becoming more red and urban areas more blue, with the effect of firming up siloes as it becomes more unlikely that anyone will meet/talk to their political others and, conversely, are surrounded by people who agree with them.
  • Similarly, on the education front the gap in level of education has turned into a gulf. David Brooks points out that “[T]he academic gap between the affluent and less affluent is greater today than the achievement gap between white Americans and Black Americans in the final days of Jim Crow.” This kind of segregation will of course tend to divide along partisan lines, but more important, the resentment it breeds will also be a major driver for attachment to anyone who capitalizes on it.
  • News has become more strained along ideological lines. When broadcast news came over the air there was a strict regulatory regimen (the FCC’s Fairness Doctrine) dictating at least the appearance of non-partisanship and attention to different sides of an issue. The advent of cable and online news
  • Starting with the appearance of Facebook and Twitter, various social networks have learned that the royal road to user engagement is outrage. 
  • Geographical and social siloing: 

There are many ways to describe their devotion and explain their loyalty; I prefer to look at direction of causality. 

Where does enthusiastic, joyfully committed loyalty come from

From the early days of the first Trump presidency, I actually thought that, shocking as it was that so many people had voted for such a creature, the truth on the ground as that Presidency played out would have a big impact on his level of support. In economic terms, I thought his support was elastic. I believe I said at the time that, soon enough, people would be begging for the crook

It didn’t take much polling experience before it became clear: about a third of the American electorate, the very core of Trump’s support, wasn’t going anywhere.

The most obvious consequence of that fact was electoral. When you’re running for President and you start with a third of the electorate in your pocket, the field is not just tilted, it’s nigh impossible: to get yourself over 50% of the votes, you only need a quarter of the remaining 2/3

item.description: It’s hard to exaggerate the hold of Horatio Alger on the American mind. If American culture has a foundational story, it’s that of America as the land of opportunity: with enough pluck, grit, hard work and sterling character, you’re bound to succeed. This story became popularized…
item.content:encoded:
What’s Wrong with Horatio Alger?

It’s hard to exaggerate the hold of Horatio Alger on the American mind. If American culture has a foundational story, it’s that of America as the land of opportunity: with enough pluck, grit, hard work and sterling character, you’re bound to succeed. This story became popularized in a long series of novels by Horatio Alger featuring stalwart boys rising above challenging circumstances to ascend to middle class respectability.

Some people take that story at face value, sorting others into the valiant and the poor. Other people take it as a historical artifact and a quaint bundle of naiveté. Still others see active evil in its implication that the unsuccessful have no one else to blame for their failures. But all these people should think again. The problem with the Horatio Alger narrative isn’t cultural, or moral, but logical. There’s a critical flaw in the logic at hand, a flaw that throws a cold light on a whole domain of human cognition. 

To spot that flaw, consider a lesser tenet of the American Ethos, the idea that “Anyone can become President”. While that’s strictly true (there’s theoretically nothing to stop any non-criminal of sufficient age from ascending to the White House), it’s kind of beside the point, because it obviously doesn’t follow that “Everyone can become President.”

That difference is so obvious that it hardly bears mentioning, but it’s that exact distinction that breaks the Horatio Alger paradigm. It’s “Anyone can succeed if…” vs. “Everyone will succeed if…” Pluck and hard work may be necessary for success, but they don’t necessarily ensure it.

To see this, consider a key feature of the actual books of Horatio Alger that gets short shrift in the ideal of the Self-Made Man(/Woman/Boy): the appearance of a “mysterious stranger” or a “worldly but warmhearted patron” who recognizes the hero’s potential and provides a timely boost to his prospects. In reality, pluck, hard work, etc. are rarely enough. They need to be met with some kind of assist from the outside world, whether it’s happening to hear about a job opportunity, a personal connection, someone who takes a person under their wing, or a host of other factors that are impossible to predict or control via personal choices — starting with choice of parents.

There’s an old saw that comes in handy here: “Luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.” Removing the irony connects it better with Horatio Alger: “Success is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.” Preparation is all well and good, and Horatio Alger is fine for such preparation. But what if that opportunity never arrives? What if it’s blocked by, for example, medical damage arising from straitened origins? What if you didn’t go to school with future titans of industry? What if opportunities are foreshortened by one’s skin color, or dragged down by culture gaps? Viewing people’s ongoing economic struggles through this other lens beyond personal character issues makes lack of success much more understandable.

The smaller point here — not small at all — is that a person’s character isn’t necessarily at fault for their lack of achievement, given the host of factors that go into the mysterious “opportunity”, including lucking into the requisite opportunity. But the larger point, what this essay is really about, is the logical flaw in Horatio Alger, one that undermines human thinking across the board. Another example will bring that into focus.

Islam and Terrorism

It’s a bit dated, but let’s go back to a syllogism guaranteed to raise hackles:

  1. Dangerous terrorists are generally Muslim.
  2. Therefore, Muslims are a suspect, if not hostile, population.

Politically, this is a pretty important syllogism, and the arguments against it usually boil down to two: 1) it’s factually incorrect, i.e., terrorism, properly defined, is more a function of white nationalism — at least in the US; and 2) even if a steady parade of terrorist actions are committed by Jihadists, it’s unfair, prejudicial, and xenophobic to tar all Muslims with that brush. Treated thus, the argument descends to arguing over the definition of terrorism, what period of time to attend to, pulling intolerant/aggressive quotes from the Q’uran, etc. Not very helpful.

But here again, there’s a logical flaw in the argument that trumps matters of fact and fairness. Assume for the sake of argument that all terrorists really are Muslim. Therefore one could, in theory, eliminate terrorism by eliminating contact with Muslims. But that’s all. It does not tell you that Muslims are in fact a dangerous population, for the simple reason that terrorists are so few in number. That is, even if all Jihadists are Muslim, they could be a vanishingly small exception in an overwhelmingly benign population. 

Muslim terrorists are observable. We have observed them, no doubt. Maybe even all terrorists are Muslim. But that doesn’t mean terrorism is predictable among Muslims. No matter how terrified you are, picking a Muslim at random and finding a terrorist is about as likely as winning the lottery. 

Horatio Alger may be right in that success is observable among people who work hard, etc. It may even be that everyone successful shares a certain set of character traits. But that doesn’t mean that everyone who shares that set of traits will be a success.

The Turn

This extra step in thinking, going from the observable to the predictable, is what I call “The Turn”. And it trips us up not only with regard to terrorism and success, but in a wide variety of situations across personal judgement and politics. It’s a deeply ingrained flaw in human thinking that’s insidious and commonplace.

The Turn happens because we have brains that use patterns to make sense of the world. For example, suppose you’re seeking a restroom in a commercial building. You find one near the elevator, but it’s for the wrong gender. Do you pass it by and start your search anew, as if you have learned nothing? Of course not. You start looking for the other gender in a similar position to the first one with respect to the elevator, perhaps on the other side of it, maybe even directly above it on the next floor. You can generally count on restrooms being found either together, or in some kind of symmetry.

We have a set of patterns for the way restrooms are organized in buildings, suggesting how they are arranged with respect to each other. We also have a meta-pattern of symmetry that’s useful as well.

Learning isn’t just a matter of memorizing facts; we notice and store patterns — for reasons tightly linked to survival. If eating this plant makes you sick, having that plant and the reaction associated in a pattern helps you avoid future harm. If you learn that baby bears are likely to be near a grumpy mama bear, you can avoid a deadly confrontation. And so on.

When, in the course of human events, elements of a pattern show up, we recall the pattern. If the pattern includes elements not in evidence, we infer that those elements are also present, perhaps hidden. In other words, we associate items that appear together in our patterns. If we see the back of someone’s head we recall the pattern for a human figure, and infer that there’s a face on the other side of it. We get into a car and know where to look for features like glove compartment, seat belt, turn signal, etc. We recognize a book by its general appearance (hand-holdable size, rectilinear shape, prominent title and cover matter) and know to expect a stack of pages with writing on them that flows from front to back, where each letter, each word, each sentence is a pattern defined by the language the book is written in. We know that speaking sharply to our boss is likely to come bundled with certain consequences sooner or later. 

One of the more important roles of patterns is the surprise reaction to having a pattern violated, because surprising circumstances are often where threats and opportunities lie. If your friend turns around and has a black eye, that becomes the most important thing in the room. If your boss responds to your criticism with warm equanimity, you’ll lose sleep that night wondering what that means.

Why Does Drug Use Seem Bad?

Sure enough, the wages of drug abuse are often visible, from crack babies to wasted meth heads to an epidemic of overdose deaths. Does that mean drug use predictably or dependably leads to such outcomes? Not at all. Not only are there more- and less-harmful drugs, but there are people who are more- and less-able to navigate those waters.

Nonetheless, a pattern took hold of the popular mind, beginning in the 70’s with Richard Nixon’s War On Drugs and continuing with Nancy Reagan’s Just Say No campaign and continuing today with the still-popular D.A.R.E. program.

The pattern in question associates two things: 1) the category “illegal drugs”, and 2) dire consequences, ranging from brain damage to addiction to social incompetence and family destruction. Those terms are resoundingly vague, but that doesn’t stop people from clutching that association with every ounce of their being. In fact, we have a meta-pattern that we overlay on the association: cause-and-effect: use of drugs causes these dire consequences.

The Drugs Are Bad pattern was never logically viable: The Turn goes from the obvious (some people have trouble handling mind-altering substances) to the unsupported (those things are dangerous in themselves) by passing right over the possible hordes who deal with them with no problem and in fact may derive great benefit. Fortunately, the hold on minds by this particular Turn is loosening rapidly: fatigue with the War On Drugs is finally setting in, and a number of the substances in the government’s Most Dire bin (in the US, the FDA’s schedule 1 for drugs with “no medical use and greatest potential for addiction”) are showing extraordinary promise, e.g. the use of MDMA (Ecstasy or Molly) to treat PTSD, or psilocybin (magic mushrooms) in treatment for addiction and end-of-life anxiety.

Science vs. Scientism

In recent centuries, Science has accumulated a glorious history of gleaning dependable (never say “true”) information about the world. Beginning with the Greeks and truly exploding with the Enlightenment, a torrent of knowledge has poured out of the scientific project: Pythagoras’s Theorem, Newton’s laws of motion and thermodynamics, Galileo’s cosmology, Maxwell’s equations, genetics, natural selection, epidemiology, electronics, etc., ad nauseum. The most prominent features of modern life — extended lifespan, technological magic, unprecedented material comforts — derive directly from knowledge accumulated scientifically. The pattern associating Science with knowledge seems irresistible.

But does that mean valid knowledge must be scientific? Will science help discern values? What does it tell about spiritual/mystical experience? Are there no other, complementary systems that provide, e.g., metaphorical understanding of life’s big questions? What about knowledge honed after generations without number by indigenous peoples? Sure, they can be empirically investigated, but, coming not from the lab but rather (often) other races or colors, they face an uphill battle to adoption.

There is a population of people to whom scientific knowledge, gained through a process of formulating hypotheses and putting them through rigorous testing, is the only kind of knowledge that matters. In other words, only knowledge that can be tested, and tested in the standard fashion, counts as knowledge at all. In making the leap from the breathtaking effectiveness of science for building knowledge, to the belief that no other kind of knowledge counts, such people are going from Science to Scientism.

What kinds of understanding does Scientism leave out? That question deserves a whole essay of its own, but just think about how the scientific method would work on:

  • spirituality: the sense that we are connected to something larger;
  • wisdom: defined as an inchoate belief, derived from experience, that has no means of proof;
  • values: the sense people have of what matters to them;
  • meaning: every response we have to a situation beyond cold hard facts;
  • metaphor: our gift for using knowledge about one thing to shed light on another. How unscientific can you get?

To dismiss everything that can’t be put under the reductionist, empirical microscope of science is Scientism. And the root of Scientism is starting with the pattern associating Science with firm knowledge, then taking The Turn, associating firm knowledge only with Science.

Interestingly, the belief that all knowledge proceeds from science is itself 100% unscientific: untestable, unfalsifiable, it’s nothing but a judgment derived — illogically — from experience. Moreover, scientism is itself refuted, for the quintessentially scientific domain of mathematics, by Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorem, which showed that no system built from a set of axioms that is internally consistent can be used to prove all true theorems in that system. In other words, if a (mathematical) system is consistent, then it cannot be complete (represent all truths). It must leave something out.

The scientistic mind has been hijacked by The Turn.

Free-market Economics

Ever since Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations, the North Star of American economic policy has been free enterprise: the ideal that when people are rational actors, and when they each pursue their own self-interest in a fair marketplace, the “invisible hand” of competition optimizes productivity and wealth.

This clear and clean story is, of course, muddied by issues like the licentious extraction of resources, failure to assign the cost of externalities, colonialist and racist exploitation, and the way that money and power just seem to go together so that, in my uncle’s immortal phrase, “them as has, gets.” Still, America has done very well for itself these last few centuries. So let’s assume for the sake of argument that free-market economics strongly support an economically vigorous nation.

Thus, the pattern at hand associates free-market economics with prosperity, however loosely. In this case, one aspect of The Turn is the idea that “the freer the market the better it works”: every impediment removed from the market’s machinery tunes its performance higher. That’s the libertarian ideal, and it has gotten plenty of pushback. But I want to highlight another aspect of The Turn here: the implication that a free market is all you need for a healthy society.

Put it like that and you’ll hardly find anyone to disagree; everyone has their own pet feature(s) of a “just” society, whether it’s religion, healthy communities, family, patriotism, equal opportunity or any other ancillary value. It’s a tenet of liberalism that these elements need to be nurtured directly, often with state support, because they’re orthogonal if not contradictory to the general materialistic impetus of the market.

But, optional extras aside, there’s still another issue that gets left behind in The Turn: does freedom alone even do what it’s meant to do? Are there important elements of this Social Success pattern that are being left to take care of themselves, and thus they wither on the vine as the system becomes more and more “pure”?

I ask this because the free market — at least in America, which is among its purest test cases — seems to be serving its purpose less and less well the “purer” it gets.

Take, for example, the financial crisis that started in 2008. It’s hard to recall how that happened and not see an example of the free market running amok — but rather than having me explain it, why don’t I take this opportunity to share this classic, laugh-out-loud funny yet robustly educational slideshow using cartoon stick figures to explain it on my behalf? 

The sheer, evil innovation here is free-market economics through and through.

There also used to be a kind of socio-economic contract between large businesses and workers, in which the workers devoted their careers to one entity, which showed something like loyalty to them by treating layoffs as an act of desperation, and providing health coverage and pension benefits. There’s nothing in free-market economics that dictates or even implies any of that, and it has all evaporated in recent decades, with companies shipping jobs abroad, eliminating pension plans, shifting to temporary workers, and engaging in leveraged buyouts whose payoffs dictate draconian cost-cutting, to name just a few. 

Why does modern-day capitalism seem so strained, so abstract, so “pure”? Because it used to be embedded in a society that knew not to take it too seriously: one where business leaders had outside values like community and patriotism to temper their acquisitive impulses; one where the notion of fiduciary responsibility, which nominally requires companies to consider only the interests of their shareholders, was tempered by the notion of companies as participants in their society as well; . But present-day business behavior seems to be shedding all of those distractions, and rushing headlong to execute the Free-Market pattern ever more purely. Result: stratospheric executive compensation, relentless short-term focus, obsession with stock price, consolidation into larger and larger entities, etc.

Where is The Turn in all this? It takes a plausible pattern associating an ecology of competition with congenial economic outcomes (especially compared to, say, feudal, aristocratic or authoritarian systems), infers that all congenial economic outcomes must arise from the free market, and then concludes that The More Free The Market The Better.

We’re all familiar with people and institutions that Take It Too Far: take a good idea and run with it so far that it breaks from the strain. I think The Turn is behind a great many of those.

A Few Challenges

Let me leave you with some challenges: diagnose The Turn working behind these propositions: (analyses available by clicking the links)

  • Trump supporters are a pack of deplorables. (Yes, I know that’s not what she said, but that’s how it was heard.)
  • The police are a clear and present danger to Black men in America.
  • Driving after drinking kills.
  • If you smoke, you’ll get cancer.
  • Gun deaths are a public health crisis in America.
  • Gay men are so promiscuous!
  • Rich people are suspect.
  • The Right and the Left in the US couldn’t be further apart.
  • If you say something offensive to the Left, you will be cancelled.
  • Sex education is behind teenage promiscuity.

item.content:encoded:
When Rationality Became Irrational

So much of what’s right about modern life owes its presence in the world to Science. The legacy of rigorous, skeptical, empirical inquiry bequeathed to us by the Enlightenment has rendered a world unrecognizable compared to what came before — for good and ill. The good news is overwhelmingly good, but so is the bad, and we tend to take that as a take-it-or-leave-it proposition. The thing is, the two can be teased apart. It is possible to identify where Rationalism went wrong, and that would go a long way to getting humanity back on track.

The Enlightenment’s Original Sin

In the early 1700’s, an earthquake shook the world. If there is a turn of events that shifted the history of the world more quickly or comprehensively than the Enlightenment, I’d like to hear about it.

If you’re reading this, I doubt you need much convincing about Enlightenment values. But just so we go into this with an appreciation of the scale of change they represent, let me just hit some highlights:

Medicine

Chemistry

Mechanics

Electronics

Biology

Religion

The great discovery of the Enlightenment, the truly earth-shattering revelation, was that the Universe didn’t have to be an inscrutable mystery that could only be (partially) explained by resorting to gods and prophets. People could, themselves, find truth in a process of proposal and experimentation.

At the heart of Enlightenment values is skeptical enquiry, and at the heart of skeptical enquiry is this stunningly brilliant move: let’s give up the quest for final, unquestionable Truth, for immovable ground on which to stand. Instead, let’s leave every proposition, no matter how solid it seems, up to questioning and revision or replacement.

This model of skeptical enquiry is the finest engine ever devised for getting closer to The Truth, exactly because it gives up on the idea of ever getting there.

The Enlightenment model of skeptical enquiry is truly one of the most cunning schemes ever invented. It said that the hunt for solid epistemological ground to stand on begins by giving up the idea of ever having permanent such ground.

And yet, today, ironically enough, there is a tidal wave of skepticism about the fruits of the Enlightenment, and even its core values of “Reason, Science, Humanism, and Progress”, as enumerated in the title of Steven Pinker’s defense of same, Enlightenment Now.

Depredations of capitalism

Discounting of soft values: community, spirituality, 

Rational jurisprudence vs. justice

Mistaking the rational human for the whole human: history of psychotherapy

Medicine: organism vs. whole human

There is a case to be made (and Pinker makes it, vociferously) that rational enquiry is itself revealing the blind spots of the rational worldview, i.e. the cure for irrational rationality is more rationality. For example, medicine just is revealing the importance of bedside manner and placebos. Modern physics itself identified the shortcomings of Newton’s mechanistic universe. 

But it is also true that rationality enquiry is uncovering the limitations of rationality itself. Godel’s Incompleteness Theorem says it outright: no system of logic that is internally consistent can include all true propositions. In other words, no matter what logical system you choose, if it is consistent then there will be truths that lie outside it.

Blind spots about the limits of rationality: part/whole discrimination

[1] What Is Scientism?

item.content:encoded:
Why Donald Trump Should Lose

One of the worst people ever to run for President of the USA stands a good chance of winning. I don’t know any undecided voters, but I assume they are dazzled because Trump has successfully “flooded the zone with shit” to where they can’t fit it all in their heads. So I suggest focusing on just enough to close the deal. So here is the minimalist case against Donald Trump. Please share with anyone who 

  • George Washington is turning in his grave. Starting with the Founding Fathers and for over 250 years, patriotism was defined by loyalty to the Constitution, especially the peaceful transfer of power and the sacredness of elections. And now we have a man who is just fine with an assault on Congress, calling the assailants ‘heroes’, ‘hostages’, and ‘patriots’, and intending to pardon them if elected — and still insisting that he won without a shred of evidence.
  • Reality Matters: Trump may be lying, or he may not actually know that violent crime has been dropping for 40 years, or that the American economy leads the world, or that California does not have an electricity crisis, or that there isn’t a bird cemetery under every windmill. Either way, we have to have a leader who is in touch with reality, otherwise you might as well have a lunatic at the helm. 
  • Time was when nations literally devoted half their budgets to national defense to avoid being conquered by their neighbors. Today that figure is a tenth of that. Why? Because the world has agreed that wars of conquest are out of bounds, and they back each other up on that. If Putin is allowed to annex Ukraine, that pact is shattered. If he gets away with it, then what?
  • Look at the man, and ask yourself if this is who you want representing America. The rest of the world is already somewhere between hilarity and horror that a country with the stature of the USA would choose such a dangerous buffoon — twice! And over half of the Trump cabinet (“the best”, in his words), including his own vice president, have broken with their party to object.

There’s much more to be said, of course. But what else do you need?

item.content:encoded:
Actually, You ARE Living In A Simulation

Did The Matrix blow your mind? Even if you were familiar with the dorm-room idea that we’re living in a simulation, that movie really slammed it home. What if our whole life, the world we think we live in, is nothing but a carefully crafted, impenetrable illusion? How could we tell? What if there isn’t any solid ground under our feet, but only what we think is true?

The genius of The Matrix was to take an old thread of philosophy and mysticism (i.e., brains in a vat, the illusion of samsara) and transmogrify it into a propulsive, epic sci-fi plot, complete with gunplay, martial-arts spectacle and brain-melting special effects. But beneath the spectacle lurked an existential nightmare: embedded in a system that gives you no hint of its actual nature — or even its very existence: being fed a stream of artificial information that seems unshakably, undeniably real. You live out your days completely immersed in this construction, in serene ignorance of your actual circumstances. What more perfect bondage could there be?

But here’s the thing: this is the life we lead. Right here, right now. And it doesn’t take a red pill to expose it, just a little thought.

In short, the only difference between the Matrix and reality

If you doubt the ability of a brain-bound simulation to convince you of its reality, consider dreams. Within a dream, it generally doesn’t even occur to the dreamer that what they’re seeing isn’t 100% real — this in the face of physical inconsistencies, gaping holes and fantastical elements. Sometimes you can realize that you’re having a nightmare and pop out of it, but keep in mind that in dreaming, we have another reality to go back to.
