item.content:encoded:
Why Donald Trump Should Lose

I sent this out in email, but in case you know any voters who are still undecided(!), ask them to read it. It’s as short as I could possibly make it.

Why Donald Trump Should Lose

It’s easy to understand how undecided voters could be confused, uncertain and/or cynical: when we’re engulfed by noise, it’s mind-boggling. So lets clear the air with the simplest, most clear-cut reasons why Donald Trump should be kept out of the White House.

  • George Washington is turning in his grave. It’s hard to grasp the danger to our democracy of someone for whom the Constitution is just so much toilet paper if it crosses his own political interests and his ego. Here we have a man who is just fine with an assault on Congress even if it meant hanging the Vice President, calling the assailants ‘heroes’, ‘hostages’, and ‘patriots’, intending to pardon them if elected — and still insisting that he won. From the Founding Fathers forward, patriotism has been defined by loyalty to the Constitution, especially the peaceful transfer of power and the sanctity of elections. By that standard, Donald Trump is the opposite of a patriot.
  • Disconnection from reality: Trump may be lying, or he may not actually know, that the US is not a crime-ridden hellhole, or that the American economy leads the world, or that California does not have an electricity crisis, or that climate change is real, or that there isn’t a bird cemetery under every windmill. Either way, the line between fact and fiction means nothing to him. But if you don’t have a leader who is in touch with reality, you might as well have a lunatic in charge. You wouldn’t hire a babysitter who is lost in their own head; why a President?
  • Agent of chaos: This country is losing its mind with disinformation and division. (Eating pets in Ohio?!? Death threats to election workers and hurricane recovery crews?!?) Call politicians unreliable, but Donald Trump is special: fomenting contempt and distrust among Americans is what he is about, the foundation of his appeal. Is this what leadership looks like? Is this who you are and what you hope for your country?
  • Everything else: The threat to the world order if Putin is allowed to annex Ukraine; the trail of fraud convictions (for his businesses, his charity, his University and his campaign), with worse in the future; his hapless first Presidency, when he couldn’t even build his wall with a compliant Congress, and let 130,000 people die unnecessarily of COVID-19; his obvious mental decline. What does it tell you that these things are just footnotes?

In the partisan, tribal swamp we live in today, consider how hard it is to get anyone to break with their party. But over half of Trump’s hand-picked cabinet (“the best people”), including his own vice president, have been driven to do just that, because Donald Trump is an unprecedented threat to who we are as a country. If these people are risking their own necks to save us from him, maybe we should listen.

item.title: The 2024 Election Is Over
item.description: [update, December 2024: Obviously I couldn’t have been more wrong. But I’m not taking this down because, you know, humility?]
item.content:encoded:
The 2024 Election Is Over

[update, December 2024: Obviously I couldn’t have been more wrong. But I’m not taking this down because, you know, humility?]

You can judge an election by how dramatically it changes minds in the aftermath, from uncertainty and speculation beforehand, to forehead-slapping and eye-rolling amazement that anyone thought it could have turned out otherwise. I’m putting my money down that 2024 will be one of those elections: this will be a historic defeat for the Republican Party, possibly enough to trigger a re-organization of America’s two-party configuration, in which bonafide conservatives and Republicans who haven’t fallen under the spell of Trump — Republicans without a home, in other words — finally tire enough of being captive to his cult to break ranks and form a new party.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. Why will this election be such a surprise? Because it will unveil any number of should-be-obvious realities:

  • Donald Trump is increasingly incoherent and enfeebled, which will become undeniable when he proves too arrogant to avoid getting on a debate stage with Joe Biden.
  • Onrushing dementia aside, Trump 2024 is a downgrade from previous versions in so many respects: more caustic, more aggrieved, more openly authoritarian, more cruel, more flagrantly himself. The closer we get to the election, the clearer it will become that he’s a rotting albatross around the neck of the Republican Party.
  • Dementia and toxicity aside, Trump’s trials will increasingly weigh on his viability even without verdicts in the most important ones.
  • Joe Biden has a story to tell, and if his State Of The Union speech is any indicator, he’s ready to tell it. It’s one thing for voters to signal disgruntlement in polls more than half a year from voting, but what is the trend going to be as they actually start focusing on the fact that the country is, well, in the hands of adults?
  • Speaking of polling, what question do people think they’re answering when asked about their satisfaction with Biden, or their preferences in the upcoming election? How much are those answers infiltrated by concern about the general state of the country? The Presidency is a focus for popular discontent. But in the voting booth, the question is different: Whom do you want running the country? Could the choice be any clearer?
  • There is actual affection in this country for democracy and the institutions thereof, lingering though it may be. For anyone who holds such values close, the choice is clear — and, again, will only become clearer in the minds of voters as the election looms.
  • People — not just women — care about reproductive rights. Arizona has just come alive, and abortion will be on the ballot in Florida in the starkest terms: a six-week ban vs. a constitutional amendment securing reproductive freedom. How many other states will be voting too? And how many MAGA officeholders will be turned out over the issue?
  • I have a rule about impending disasters, derived from long experience, including Y2K: onrushing disasters that are anticipated in enough force and detail fall flat when the time comes. There is enough alarm in the nation over the prospect of a second Trump term to get people by the millions moving to forestall it.
  • Just on the simple matter of campaign management, Trump has jettisoned a wide swath of the Republican Party organization — and the work they have done to date — in favor of his loyalists. And, as David French has pointed out, Trump can’t help making the election all about himself — a strategic blunder when running against an incumbent.

What does Trump have to counterweight these realities? His inflamed sense of grievance strikes a chord with some segments of the population, to be sure, but it seems increasingly clear that his manner of keeping them onboard is a boat anchor dragging on the the task of reaching others. He has cast the spell of the Strong Leader over a wide swath of the electorate. But how is that segment supposed to grow?

I’m sure that these and many other factors will be obvious in retrospect — so obvious, in fact, that there will much hand-wringing over a very interesting question: what is wrong with our information systems that we could miss something so obvious? Why is polling so poor at providing relevant data? Why did the ongoing monsoon of “news” about the antics of Trump so thoroughly drown the through-line, the high-order bit, the thing we actually care about?

It’s an interesting question to ponder about our information systems as a whole, but it assumes practical importance when you ponder its effect on the state of our politics: the remaking of the Republican Party in Trump’s image — in particular its running roughshod over conservatives of principle and integrity — gets its juice from his perceived invincibility. When that illusion burns up like a magician’s flame effect, leaving a hollowed-out Republican Party behind, and a generation of pols blinking their eyes in the daylight, what then?

item.content:encoded:
Are Elon Musks Necessary?

What a source of raging ambivalence is Elon Musk. This is the guy who made electric cars cool, thereby taking a bigger bite out of climate change than pretty much any individual, ever. This is the guy who reawakened space travel and will, it seems, bring high-speed Internet to the remotest places on Earth. BUT…he is also the bull in the china shop at Twitter, dismissing key employees by the thousands, impulsively suspending accounts for personal reasons and generally thrashing around, all knees and elbows, in a situation that calls for a cool head in charge. A history-making figure who has more than a whiff of the sociopath about him.

It’s tempting to believe that those poles can’t be separated, the genius and the sociopath. Indeed, it’s part of the Great Man archetype, the manly man who rides roughshod over any and all obstacles. (This is distinct from a normal leader who can inspire others to follow their lead without being an asshole about it.) Certainly the movers and shakers of Silicon Valley agree, whether publicly or privately, per the New York Times:

They admire him for ruling Twitter with an iron fist and making the kinds of moves that tech executives have resisted for fear of alienating workers — cutting jobs, stripping away perks, punishing internal dissenters, resisting diversity and inclusion efforts, and forcing employees back to the office.

Of course Elon Musk is only the current exemplar. History is strewn with such figures, from Steve Jobs to Robert Moses to Ronald Reagan to Donald Trump to Winston Churchill, and on and on. So you’ve got to wonder: if you want earth-moving change, does it take an asshole? In other words, are Elon Musks necessary?

This is a serious question for a place as seemingly stuck as the present-day US, struggling to effectively address its many generational challenges when its last collective achievement was the moon landing half a century ago. It recalls Richard Nixon’s image of America as a pitiful, helpless giant in the face of Communism, only this time the enemy is us.

So will it take an asshole to fix us? Do we have to choose between continuing to languish or putting an asshole in charge and giving him or her free rein?

Assholes Don’t Mind Breaking a Few Eggs

One of the reasons it’s tempting to say Yes is that there is an aspect of destruction in pretty much any progress. As they say, you can’t make an omelet without breaking some eggs. For example, real progress on carbon emissions is essentially incompatible with continuing to burn coal, which just is seriously bad news for the coal miners.

Anyone who makes tough choices will bear a heavy burden of responsibility, their only comfort the fairly abstract idea that the net outcome is positive, all things considered. It takes a certain kind of person to cope with those impacts…but does it take an asshole? It does seem at least possible to compartmentalize without sacrificing your humanity, and the person who taught me that was Barack Obama.

Here was a man who bore the weight of the Presidency, whose every moment in office had real impact on ordinary lives across the globe. You would think that a person in such a position would devote every waking moment to optimizing that impact. And yet, here was a guy who could, every evening, put down that burden to focus on his family. I don’t know how anyone’s ego can avoid being crushed by such responsibilities, but it doesn’t seem to require a sociopath — though they do have a natural advantage.

But there is another class of situations where assholes have a distinct advantage, situations condensed nicely in the Trolley Problem.

Of Trolleys and Assholes

The Trolley Problem is a thought experiment in ethics. A trolley is rolling down the tracks, its brakes failed. A group of five people are on the tracks, about to be killed. But wait! There is a siding to which the trolley can be diverted, and you have the switch in hand to do that. The problem is that there is one person standing on the siding, and that person will die if you pull the switch. What do you do?

Human response to the Trolley Problem has been studied in experiments without number; results are mixed and hotly debated by both psychologists and ethicists, but one thing is clear: people are powerfully troubled by pulling that switch. They have a deep aversion to taking any action that might cause harm even when the costs of inaction are greater.

How reluctant are we to take action that might cause harm? This question goes directly to the heart of the Asshole Problem if you assume that the key trait of an asshole is willingness to plunge in anyway, consequences be damned. So let’s look a little closer, with some more experimental results, graciously provided by Daniel Kahneman in his classic Thinking, Fast and Slow. Consider your response to the following two scenarios:

1: You have been exposed to a disease which if contracted leads to a quick and painless death within a week. The probability that you have the disease is 1/1,000. There is a vaccine that is effective only before any symptoms appear. How much would you would be willing to pay for the vaccine?

2: Volunteers are needed for research on the above disease. All that is required is that you expose yourself to a 1/1,000 chance of contracting the disease. (No vaccine exists in this scenario.) How much would they need to pay you to volunteer for this program?

The two scenarios probe the difference between undertaking a positive action vs. simply mitigating an existing issue. In theory, you should be willing to pay the same amount of money to relieve an existing risk as you would ask to take on the same risk voluntarily. But people expect a lot more money to take on a risk than they would pay to eliminate it — and I do mean a lot: Richard Thaler’s experiments found it was typically fifty times as much.

What’s going on here? The main thing seems to be the potential for regret. If Scenario 2 turns out badly, the one who took on that risk is far more regretful than the actor in Scenario 1 who simply failed to take action. This is why it’s such a struggle to get people to wear masks and get vaccinated: they’d much rather deal with the consequences of inaction than take positive steps toward prevention.

Thaler’s colleague Cass Sunstein calls this the Precautionary Principle, which rules our personal decision-making but also plays out at grand scale in all kinds of governance. It ensures that the risks of taking action loom large — massively, critically large — overwhelming any prospective positive outcome. Sunstein lists all sorts of innovations that exist only because someone overcame precaution: “airplanes, air conditioning, antibiotics, automobiles, chlorine, the measles vaccine, open-heart surgery, radio, refrigeration, smallpox vaccine, and X-rays.” Those someones had to stick their necks out, swimming upstream against precaution, to make those things happen. And who but the asshole is better suited to do so? “Damn the torpedoes, full steam ahead!” is the cry of one who is invulnerable to regret.

The Precautionary Principle dictates the conservatism of bureaucracies of all kinds. Remember “Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM”? Or “It’s easier to get forgiveness than permission”? There’s a thunderous truth behind those sayings. When you go for a permit for a home project, or take out a loan, that requires someone to sign on — give their permission — for a positive action. It puts them in a scary and vulnerable position full of potential for regret, compared to letting it slide in retrospect. No wonder bureaucracies often feel like they’re hard-wired to thwart invention and innovation.

Progress is Risky

The Trolley Problem and the Precautionary Principle are compounded by the fact that novelty and innovation come bundled with uncertainty and risk. It’s not obvious that bold initiatives will work out; in fact, they may leave us worse off than before.

There were many reasons, good and bad, to object to Obamacare, but the stark reality is that it was presented as a way to solve the problem of 45 million Americans without healthcare, when far more people already had healthcare that by and large they were happy with. Those numbers were laden with risk to the status quo for an uncertain gain. Of course there was resistance! The potential losses loomed too large over the potential gains, and the resulting package was significantly compromised.

Assholes have no such problems, since they can narrow their vision to potential gains, dismissing potential losses and dismal odds of success.

So yes, we resist taking positive action, and we also, reasonably, worry about uncertainty and risk; the Elon Musks of the world are tailor-made to power through both. But there is another reason such figures are so appealing just now, and that reason is most clear when you look at the case of Donald Trump.

Frustration and the Appeal of the Asshole

Donald Trump offered his supporters many things, but high up on the list was his function as a wrecking ball. His deepest support came from people who felt passed over, ignored by the powers that be on matters ranging from immigration to globalization to cultural change. They truly felt the need for an asshole, to the point of missing that he was too wrapped up in his own self-glorification to actually do anything more than channel that frustration and own the libs. That that was enough is a powerful statement of the appeal of the asshole.

But the MAGA movement was just the canary in the coal mine for a stark fact: America doesn’t feel like it can do anything anymore, and such a vacuum seems designed to be filled by an asshole. But it gets worse. Why is America stuck? Because, in the absence of forceful leadership, positive action requires public support, and that in turn is hard to come by without a certain level of trust in public institutions: trust that they will have your interests at heart, trust that they will keep their promises, and trust that they can deliver the goods.

If that seems abstract or obscure, consider the response in this country to the COVID pandemic. In The Atlantic magazine, Derek Thompson compares that recent experience with the invention of vaccines and the total eradication of smallpox from the world. It’s a pretty stark contrast, and he makes a convincing case that the crux of the matter in the case of COVID was failure of trust and the spirit of cooperation, rejecting the counsel of scientific institutions and government, and raging at the blandest public health measures. Common sense measures with plenty of precedent that might have been taken up easily became incendiary.

Nothing is more inimical to the success of positive community action than lack of public trust. And when people don’t trust their institutions because they have failed to deliver, it sets up a doom loop: lack of trust begets institutional failure, which begets frustration, deeper distrust and suspicion of institutions, further undermining trust. And on it goes, spiraling down. Does that sound familiar?

Will America ever be able to voluntarily achieve anything as a nation again? Not if it’s stuck in such a doom loop. Go far enough down that spiral, and the allure of the strongman, the authoritarian, the asshole blossoms. Unless America can recover a semblance of public trust and faith in institutions, the writing is on the wall: some version of Elon Musk, or Donald Trump, or Ron DeSantis, or Jai Bolsonaro, will become inevitable.

Necessary? Or Inevitable?

Are Elon Musks necessary? At the very least, they have intrinsic advantages over normal human beings. On the one side you have leaders like Barack Obama who seem hampered by their very reasonableness and by their inclination to build a big tent. On the other, we have the assholes, who don’t have their egos crushed by the consequences of their actions, who don’t let the fear of regret inhibit them from taking action, who can pull the switch on the trolley. Are those advantages decisive? Should we give up hope that normal leaders might overcome their limitations, and instead just buckle up for a turbulent ride?

The real question might be: are Elon Musks inevitable? Here the prospects are pretty grim. As prosperity makes societies more risk-averse (because they have more to lose), and as public trust in institutions and one another frays, the wheels of progress get more and more bogged down. And as the missed opportunities pile up, as crying needs go unanswered, as elites and institutions seem increasingly unresponsive, frustration builds…and builds…until it seems like putting an asshole in charge is the only choice.

I wish there were an easy, obvious way to prevent such a dire outcome, but the best we can hope for is to twig to the slippery slope and be alert for the many temptations offered by the asshole. If things keep going the way they seem, we’ll be setting ourselves up more and more for the assholes of the future. But if we can recognize the temptation and where it’s coming from, maybe we can resist just a bit more.

item.description: I don’t know about your world, but in mine, success counts for a lot. Especially in America, defining goals and running your life in their direction loom large if you expect to feel like a complete human being. From the platoons of self-help books on the shelf to the whole of sta…
item.content:encoded:
Dare to Suck!

I don’t know about your world, but in mine, success counts for a lot. Especially in America, defining goals and running your life in their direction loom large if you expect to feel like a complete human being. From the platoons of self-help books on the shelf to the whole of startup culture, if you’re not on the road to somewhere then there must be something wrong with you.

Coming behind, at a distant second, is a competing ideal: the notion that the journey is the reward, that getting across the finish line may be less important than having a goal and working on it, opening to whatever adventures happen along the way. Even in startup culture, failure is much prized as a learning cycle — toward ultimately prevailing. Either way, success is still the dominant frame.

Let’s not minimize achievement, but what about the complementary space? You know, a space where drive doesn’t suck all the oxygen out of the room? To be maximally provocative about it: What if it’s okay to suck, and maybe even a good thing to suck? If you can’t imagine such a space, or recoil in horror at the very idea, we should talk.

How hard would you work to avoid failing in public? About something you care about? Among people whose esteem you prize? Personally, I would walk barefoot over broken glass to escape such a situation. But any time I feel so averse, it’s a hint to check if something interesting is going on, and this is no exception — as I learned long ago from an article in Keyboard Magazine entitled (I think; it seems to be beyond the reach of even the Internet Archive) Dare to Suck.

A sad tale

It was a rueful piece. The writer — let’s call him Floyd — recounted a night out in a jazz club in New York. In the wee hours, after the scheduled sets were finished, it was time for the musicians in the audience to take the stage. Some pretty notable musicians headed hence; one of them looked at Floyd and gestured for him to join in. Floyd resists in all politeness and humility (justified humility, from the sound of it), but the dude persists: “Come on man, we’re just messing around. Come have some fun!” But Floyd just wouldn’t have it; paralyzed with fear of embarrassing himself, he stayed rooted at his table, looking on.

Floyd spent most of the piece musing sadly about what a mistake that was. He had been invited not to play, but to play. Without being paralyzed by fear of failure, he might have surprised himself. Even if not, he might have found that the others responded with the support and grace of the community they gave every indication of being. But worst case, at least he’d have tried. He would have become part of a group experience from the inside, whatever it turned out to be, participating. Joining the dance.

Instead, none of that happened. None of it could happen, because he was so wrapped up with succeeding that he had foreclosed all such potentialities.

It’s easy to read this fable as a carpe deim message to knuckle down and be better/braver than you are. Just get more character, dammit! But we have plenty of Hallmark™ cards and affirmations to that effect. There’s another, less obvious, lesson in there: that sucking — I’m talking about flailing failure and hilarious misperformance — is key to any number of endeavors, and you’re going to lock yourself out of a wide range of achievement if you can’t, that’s right, Dare To Suck.

Learn without Sucking? Not happening

First, consider the stark fact that sucking is how we learn.

Remember the “10,000 hour rule” that a person needs to put in that much time to master a non-trivial skill? It’s questionable in the details, but there’s no doubt that you have to spend a LOT of time sucking at something before you’re any good. I’ve been told to plan on making 1,000 bad drawings before you produce something you’d ever show. If all you care about is getting to the point of mastery — unless you’re comfortable with sucking for a really, really long time — you’ve set yourself up for misery and failure.

You have to find some other way to get you through all those hours. Maybe this week you get a little better at this one fingering technique. Perhaps you make a faulty woodworking joint fifty times before it fits right. Or you keep your ass in the chair writing for endless hours of miserable frustration, but then this one turn of phrase comes from nowhere, and that keeps you going. The point is: getting to be good isn’t a good enough reason to stick with it. If you can’t Dare To Suck at it, you’re done before you start.

Creating without Sucking? Not happening

How many creative endeavors die in infancy (or conception!) because the creator couldn’t face an extended period of floundering frustration? It’s the focus on the end result, and unwillingness to engage with the prerequisite period of sucking, that bears a lot of the blame.

There’s a great thought that might be helpful with this quandary. (Unfortunately I can’t track down the source, but I’ve seen it attributed to Picasso.) It goes like this:

Those of you who are making something new need to forget about making it beautiful, or right, or perfect. You are making something that didn’t exist before, and you should be satisfied with that. Those who follow in your footsteps can worry about perfecting it. Giving birth to it in the first place is such an achievement that simply bringing it into existence should be enough.

Samuel Beckett, one of the more despairing writers of the 20th Century, was a bit more pithy:

Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better.

To make this uncomfortable reality a bit less abstract, let me opine about the only creative endeavor I know anything about: writing.

Even the most accomplished writers will never get anywhere without a willingness to suck. Notoriously, the first draft of anything is terrible. Anne Lamott is a renowned novelist and memoirist, but what will make her name shine down the ages is naming and teaching the principle of the “shitty first draft”.

For anyone who cares about their writing, the temptation is always there to perfect each sentence, each paragraph before moving on to the next. But that temptation is a trap, because it becomes an endless process of tweaking at ever finer levels. If any progress actually accrues, the result pales compared to the enormous amount of effort/time/frustration invested. Demotivation, thy name is tweaking.

By contrast, the shitty first draft points in the opposite direction: getting anything down, no matter how bad. The operative idea is “getting it down” and out of your head. See what she’s doing there? She takes a prospect full of fear and loathing (failure, and the dread thereof), and just sets it aside, specifically embracing suckage in the interest of getting somewhere, anywhere. And make no mistake: having a shitty first draft that expresses all your ideas badly, replete with unreadable spelling, mystifying usage and second-grade grammar, is a wonderful achievement — especially compared to all the perfect manuscripts that don’t exist.

What happens then? Well, let’s hear from Chris Abani:

People think that writing is writing, but actually writing is editing.

A shitty first draft is just a compost pile for editing. And that ain’t nothin’.

I’m not a painter, or a composer, or an architect, or a filmmaker, but I have to believe there’s an analogy to be made with such other endeavors: even if there isn’t an analogue to the shitty first draft, having the Devil Of Public Regard whispering in your ear at every stage of the game — especially when your work is at its most tentative and tender — can only gum up the works.

Growing without Sucking? Not happening

However you define your own personal growth, the prescription is the same: work your edges. There will always be a territory that you’ve mastered, that you feel comfortable navigating, your home base. Venture much beyond that and you enter the wilderness of insuperable challenge, beyond the pale. But in between, there’s land that you may visit, tentatively, before ducking back to safety, until you next venture forth, again and again, until it too becomes comfortable and you realize that your comfort zone has grown.

How would you expect to expand your territory without ever failing? Just as the definition of safe is “risk-free”, the less-safe — the growth zone — must come with an element of risk and/or discomfort — by definition. Unless you Dare To Suck by moving into those areas of risk as boldly as possible, they never will become part of your home. And the “success” of staying safe will haunt you.

It’s simple, really. If you’re going to grow, you have to work your edges, and if you work your edges, you’re going to fail, at least part of the time. To put it the other way round: if you’re not failing at least part of the time — because you don’t Dare To Suck — you’re not getting anywhere interesting, and/or repeating yourself.

The Inescapable Necessity of Failure

Success is the ability to go from one failure to another without any loss of enthusiasm. — Winston Churchill

Failure and ongoing suckage are not just a way-station to success. Sometimes failure is the only item on the menu — and yet it’s still necessary to proceed.

Changing the world is like that. No matter how impeccable the goal, no action by an individual will ever move the earth. Even those with their hands fully on the levers of power — the effectiveness of which is always more apparent than real — find themselves thwarted routinely. For the rest of us, it is only collectively that we make any difference at all, but even if there is a mass movement, one person more or less doesn’t make the slightest difference. As individuals we are utterly powerless, yet only if we move forward together — only if we all proceed as if we have the power — can anything happen. And success is not guaranteed even then. But without the attempt — without proceeding in the face of near-certain failure — failure is guaranteed.

Once again, Gandhi:

It’s the action, not the fruit of the action, that’s important. You have to do the right thing. It may not be in your power, may not be in your time, that there’ll be any fruit. But that doesn’t mean you stop doing the right thing. You may never know what results come from your actions. But if you do nothing, there will be no result.

George Clooney and his wife Amal, the international human-rights attorney, have a certain history of activism, both individually and together. Clooney, who is in a better position than most to make a difference, summarizes his experience nicely: “You fail and you fail and you fail and you fail, until you don’t.”

It’s not Disneyland

The relationship between success and sucking is like a world with a shiny surface, under which is a churning mass of chaos where the real work gets done. Kind of like Disneyland: step through the bushes and you’re in a nondescript warehouse district. It takes a lot of hidden activity — messy and not much fun — to maintain that gleaming surface. It’s fun to focus on the surface and convince yourself that this is the way things are. But we know better, don’t we?

Even as a kid, I never found Disneyland to be all that alluring, much less The Happiest Place On Earth. I’m much more interested in the underneath. That’s where the real stuff happens — but only if you Dare To Suck.

item.title: A Little Hope for the New Year
item.description: Many of us are struggling to maintain hope for humanity. The reluctance to get serious about a warming planet. The fiercely divided response to COVID. The global groundswell of naked authoritarianism. The culture of contempt, oozing from cable news and social media, that poisons…
item.content:encoded:
A Little Hope for the New Year

Many of us are struggling to maintain hope for humanity. The reluctance to get serious about a warming planet. The fiercely divided response to COVID. The global groundswell of naked authoritarianism. The culture of contempt, oozing from cable news and social media, that poisons our politics and makes it seem like we’ll never again accomplish anything good, noble or even competent. To name just a few.

And yet, I have hope. Without making any predictions, there is a hopeful scenario available. And that gives me a little dollop of cheer, which is what we want at the year’s outset, right?

I start from two premises: first, that human beings are fundamentally decent; and second, that modern life — at least modern political life — is an appalling carnival of humanity at its worst.

At first, these two tenets seem contradictory: if people are decent, why are they acting this way? And even if both are true, why would anything change? That’s a lot to unpack. In fact, unpacking it is where my argument lies.

Simple decency has not vanished

If you only attend to the public square, it’s hard to muster much belief in the decency of human beings. We see tribes at war, selfishness if not outright criminality as the standard in economic behavior, and politicians rigorously trained in venality and short-sightedness.

But look up from your phone and you get a very different picture. In my personal life, I don’t know anyone like that, and I suspect you don’t either. The people in my life distinguish themselves with their humanity, concern, engagement and basic decency. And this isn’t just a sampling error: I have met rage monkeys online who turned out to be perfectly decent souls when engaged with one-on-one. A little fraught, perhaps, but everything we know about how mammals engage with each other teaches us that behavior in public, especially behavior in competing groups, is no indicator of the core, private character of the individual, as expressed in the flesh. People have evolved to relate one-on-one and within small groups, using not slogans and abstractions but evolving relationships mediated by a vast system of cues and responses, from facial expressions, to body language, to apparent levels of arousal, to verbal and non-verbal communication at all levels of intimacy. We respond to the people near us in a way that is nowhere in evidence at the societal level.

I don’t mean to imply that people are uniformly excellent to each other one-on-one or that venality has no private expression. But when I consider the difference between what I experience with the people around me, vs. strangers in the public square, it’s pretty stunning.

Changing the way we are in public isn’t a matter of changing who people are. It’s about aligning public behavior with who we are (by default) in private.

A dire present

I confess that I take it as a hopeful sign that people treat each other with such scorn and derision online and in the political arena. It is a hopeful sign that people are embracing, distributing and promoting the most blatant nonsense. It is a hopeful sign that the news has become an outrage factory pitched at those already primed for high dudgeon. It is a hopeful sign that the algorithms in news feeds drive people insane.

What makes these things hopeful? There’s an old saying that it’s always darkest just before the dawn. I thought that was completely ludicrous when I was a child, and it hasn’t improved much since, but it turns out to actually express something true and important.

Darkness is hopeful because that’s what drives change. Mediocrity is the enemy of improvement.

It’s only when matters devolve into the darkest darkness that the choice between muddling through with the status quo, and risking the uncertainties of change, tips toward the latter. In fact, and ironically, it is our very despair at the status quo that motivates deliberate change.

Are you despairing enough yet?

What would change look like?

If people are actually better than they seem in public, and if life as we know it is desperate enough to trigger a reaction, what might a reaction look like? Let’s take a quick trip down Fantasy Lane:

  • An understanding emerges that questioning everything is only the first step toward a free mind.
  • Cable news and social media become recognized as a toxic disease vector for alienation and contempt. Perhaps one network declares it their mission to be different, and they actually win viewership?
  • Some politician or politicians put a stake in the ground that their bailiwick is finding solutions, not rubbishing their opponents; that re-establishing effective governance is Job One. And they attract support from an exhausted, circumspect majority.
  • Posting disinformation online becomes Not Okay. Individuals who knowingly mislead others become treated as parasites feeding on the social fabric.
  • A recognition dawns that righteous wrath online doesn’t denote actual rightness, but is rather the self-declaration of a dopamine junkie. Word gets around that the feeling of certainty is a function of neurophysiology, not true belief.
  • Public figures like Alex Jones, peddling nonsense for profit, and Tucker Carlson, trading in outrage on the cheap, become social pariahs, alongside Big Pharma executives and people defrauding the elderly.
  • People start taking individual responsibility for the spread of toxic memes, pausing to think twice about forwarding that link that gave them a little dopamine hit of righteousness.
  • The practice of building and hardening information silos becomes identified as deeply unpatriotic, and honest engagement with the Other ascends as a prized value. We learn to appreciate good-faith information when we see it, and become averse to naked appeals to vitriol and cognitive bias. Shamelessness attracts shaming and shunning. Calling out bad actors —especially in one’s own camp — becomes an act of virtue.
  • Participating in a “discussion” that devolves into contempt and ad hominem attacks becomes seen as a failure, and online discussions become a competition for the moral high ground. The first person to bring up Hitler loses.
  • Attention becomes recognized as a private resource; respecting and managing this limited resource becomes a matter of personal hygiene and responsibility.
  • People develop a resistance to clickbait headlines. If we can learn to outwit Nigerian royalty scams we can learn to recognize appeals to impulse when we see them.

Didn’t that feel good? Can we just linger for a moment and savor the feeling from this round of Wouldn’t It Be Nice?

Now, back in reality, we can see how far we are from that world…or are we?

The story we make

Without a doubt, the reality above would be a momentous change, and it’s natural to associate momentous changes with hard work, moving heaven and earth to make something happen, winning elections and passing legislation and building new systems and breaking up Facebook and fixing human nature, and…and...and…

But this is not like that.

Every item on the laundry list above is a matter of headspace. Specifically, they’re about mores, ethics, standards of behavior. They don’t require changing minds, but changing attitudes. People easily become identified with their ideas; but the way they behave when they look at the world? As far as I know, no one has ever sworn allegiance to a poisonous information system. Seduced by it, for sure, but how much loyalty does it command? The question hardly even makes sense.

What drives such shifts of attitude? The best answer I know is: a good story.

Maybe a story about a desperate situation (the impending collapse of civility and democracy), with good guys (honest brokers) and bad guys (bad-faith demagogues).

Or, there’s the story of The Matrix: the idea that our reality is only a computer simulation, and while we think we’re walking around in the sunshine, that’s only an illusion: our brains are fed a comprehensive but false reality as our bodies are harvested for energy. The act in the movie of taking the red pill and learning the truth is already used as a metaphor by a wide swath of conspiracy theorists. Could we be just a meme away (“That’s what they want you to believe!”) from the wariness of information sources that’s called for?

Another meme might be aimed at exporting the standards of decorum that we use one-on-one and in small gatherings for personal and family issues, to political issues and discussions with strangers in the strange channels of the Internet and social media. It could be as simple as raising a persistent background question: Would I talk this way to my mother? Do I really want the world to see me as a fulminating blowhard?

And history has shown that there’s nothing like a common enemy to bring people together. Perhaps a story that tells the tale of humanity itself as a tribe with a shared interest in getting at the truth, where the enemy is the fog of tribal warfare, bad-faith argument and active deceit.

Why? Why not?

Anyone can think of countless reasons why this is all fantastical thinking at an embarrassing level of naiveté. But, at the same time, few things are as powerful in the world as a good story. The civil rights struggle began as a story of unfairness and oppression that was plain for all to see (on the evening news — which everybody watched!). It didn’t take over all at once; sufficient it was and is for a few people to take up the story and infect others with it. If it’s a good enough story, and minds are primed for it, the snowball rolls on until it’s hard to remember how things were ever so bad in the past.

All that has changed is minds, and only by taking a single story to heart.

How does that happen? How does a story take over? Since we are social creatures, minds change in large part when they perceive other minds changing. (Note that it doesn’t really matter whether they are in fact changing; only that others sense that change is afoot.) It is possible, but not predictable, to envision a wave of sensibleness that transforms the way we look at information and its bearers. The tragedy of our modern crisis is that it’s built on nothing more tangible than brain cells intercommunicating. The magic is, that’s also its solution.

All it takes is a Population 0 having a change of mind, and a further population primed to being infected with the idea that this is how it should be.

But no one, no matter how naive, should expect anything more than an incremental change. Even well-established standards that everyone agrees on get violated all the time. Men still beat their wives, thievery abounds, and people can still be appalling when no one is looking. Still, the fact that we do agree that these things are Not Okay improves the lay of the land: think how much worse off we would be without such principles. And that’s exactly where we stand now vis-a-vis the anarchy — and worse — of online behavior. Even a burgeoning ethic that misinformation is uncool would be a radical improvement in the back alley that is our Internet. Some people will always act out in public just as they do in person. But a little shame would go a long way.

To summarize:

  • People are better than we give them credit for, at least in private. We don’t need people to change qua people so much as we need private standards to go public.
  • The situation as it stands is primed for change just by how awful it is; our disgust at it represents a latent demand for a better information ecosystem.
  • Radical changes in standards can occur for the wispiest of reasons: it is not necessary for an individual’s attitude to actually change as it is for them to perceive that the attitude of others has changed.
  • Cultural shifts can happen like the end of a game of Janga, i.e., everything goes on as usual until one small difference makes all the difference.
  • Predicting such events in a chaotic world is a fool’s errand. Who knows which will be the last block, when the whole system comes tumbling down? But hope is not the same thing as prediction.

This is a good place to mention the End of History Illusion. When asked how they will change in the next ten years, people have a very hard time imagining being any different — whereas they have no trouble recognizing how much they’ve changed in the last ten years.

As with individual destinies, so with cultural norms. Slavery, child labor and spousal rape used to be part of The Way Of The World…until they weren’t. They haven’t vanished, but the tide has turned against them. Bigly.

One of my favorite lines from Lily Tomlin/Jane Wagner is “Reality is nothing but a collective hunch.” Some people love the idea that the world is a mental phenomenon and, as such, is malleable under mentation, i.e., we can get what we want if we just wish hard enough. Others like me consider that the most ludicrous hogwash if the goal is physical, material change. But what if the mental activity is the reality? What if the goal is just a change of mind? If the reality is cultural, then no matter how oppressive, no matter how pervasive, that reality can be transformed just by a shift in mental activity. The wonderful thing about our epistemic crisis is that it is pure mentation, stem to stern. Therefore, all it takes is a transformation in thinking.

How does such a change happen? It’s a capital-M Mystery, and it’s irreducibly unpredictable.

But we can have hope, can’t we?

item.content:encoded:
The Power of Us: A Book Tribute

We hear a lot about “tribalism” in politics these days, especially in the US. It does seem like a useful idea for thinking about the miserable state of our discourse, invoking as it does warring factions that aren’t quite sure what they’re fighting over. But as it stands, “tribe” is mainly used as an epithet, a mob of those other people that renders them immune to reason, but is otherwise not very interesting. There must be more to it than that.

So it was with great relish that I heard Jay van Bavel on a recent episode of one of my favorite podcasts, You Are Not So Smart. It turns out that social psychology has a lot to say about tribes and tribalism, and he gave me that lovely scales-from-the-eyes feeling of “Oh my god, where has this information been all my life?” So I read his book (written with Dominic Packer), The Power of Us, and I must say: we’re overdue for a reckoning with group identity and group behavior.

What is a group?

First, let’s swap out the pejorative vocabulary: instead of “tribe” or “cult”, let’s talk about “groups” of people; that sounds bland enough. But now consider a question: why has humanity succeeded so spectacularly, dominating to the point of destruction all the other species in the world that are so much stronger and more numerous? Intelligence doesn’t hurt, of course, and language is also key. But even equipped thus, where would we be without the ability to cooperate? Acting in concert, we can gang up on any adversary. We can care for each other as the need arises. We can build larger and more sophisticated things than any set of individuals. In truth, the ability to aggregate into groups is one of the great enabling features of humankind.

As with other species, so with other humans. When humans contend for resources, who is in a position to win? Random, unfocused collections of individuals, or people who could gang up and perform as one, who help each other out? Those who could cooperate, who operated with superior group cohesion, simply must win the battle for future genes in very short order. So today we have a population whose inbuilt programming for group identity is so universally compelling, and cohesion so strong, that it runs our lives almost invisibly.

[Incidentally, the need for group coherence provides an excellent answer to an enduring question: Where does morality come from? Why is human interaction not just a matter of naked power and dominance, both within and between groups? The answer lies with the need for group cohesion. A group that’s not tightly bound is hardly a group at all; you can’t have members at each others’ throats. There have to be rules for how to treat one another, even if the group is run by a top-dog power structure. Interpersonal morals, as enforced by the group, are just as important for success as group-level logistics. Groups with strong interpersonal standards of behavior — who don’t waste energy battling each other — just will dominate those without. Guess whose genes we got?]

The grouping instinct

Fast forward a hundred thousand years or so. Civilization has commenced, government has become the norm, and people are still forming groups and tribes. We seem to have inherited something like a grouping instinct.

Do you doubt that? Do you think we’re innately driven to form and work in groups, or are our tribes just about what they’re about, e.g. race, political loyalty, class, etc, with their power derived solely from attachment to those concepts?

Enter Henri Tajfel at the University of Bristol. His team set out to explore what factors make for stronger groups, starting with a meaningless grouping condition so that other factors could be added in to study their effect. But, to their great surprise, they could not find such a condition, an organizing abstraction so trivial that it didn’t trigger group behavior.

For example, they assigned subjects a meaningless task: estimating the number of dots on a page, then told the subjects that they were one of the “under-estimators” or the “over-estimators”. Group dynamics were kept pristine: members of the groups never interacted in any way. Even the labels were not just trivial but actually fictitious: the results of the tests were ignored and group assignments were random. And yet, when subjects were assigned to allocate resources between a member of their “group” and a member of the other “group”, they consistently gave more money (say) to their anonymous fellows than to anonymous others.

The principle social scientists use for this phenomenon is “social identity”.

With membership in a group, each member’s sense of who they are becomes entangled with the group identity (literally, individuals become identified with the group). The criteria for qualifying as “us” gets left behind and social identity takes on a life of its own. In other words, there may or may not be good reasons for forming or joining a group, but once formed, groupiness takes over.

Social death is worse than physical death

Tajfel, et al, showed how groups form for the most trivial of reasons, but does group behavior per se really have much effect out in the real world?

Consider the case of the flat-Earther. If you really want to explain how people can go so wrong, you can point to all kinds of cognitive biases, together with an uncharitable assessment of the flat-Earther’s intelligence, to cobble together a rather unconvincing explanation for such demented “reasoning”. Or, you can think about the role of group dynamics. If flat-Earthers are a group (as they most definitely are, complete with internet forums, conventions, books, meetings, T-shirts, bumperstickers and all the rest), and their individual identities are bound up with the group, can’t we easily understand the cognitive backflips and extraordinary mental gymnastics that they undertake to keep their identity secure? To change one’s mind about the shape of the planet would be to ostracize oneself from a group that supplies a great deal of the community and meaning in one’s life.

There are so many modern movements so far removed from reality — think QAnon, 9–11 Truthers, COVID skeptics, election-fraud zealots — that they’re easy to see as a sign of humanity off the rails. Instead, I look at the depth and power of the beliefs they command, and I see a group exercising its power, through entirely understandable means, right down into the neocortex.

It’s incredible but true: group identity can even trump the imperative for personal survival. That is, people will extinguish themselves in service to their group. Why else do young men by the millions march off to war, except in service to “the greater good” of the country with which they identify? I like the maxim “Social death is worse than physical death” because 1) it sounds like an exaggeration, and 2) it totally isn’t. Why suicide bombers? Because their group offers prospective (if post-mortem) glory. People will even die at the behest of their group when their death terminates the group itself. Need I say more than “Jonestown”? And today, we have COVID patients on their deathbeds refusing to acknowledge that they were wrong about the virus, or about the vaccines.

Social death is worse than physical death.

The Intertubes hum with astonishment whenever political identity blinds people to obvious facts and bland reason. But the fact that anyone is shocked only shows how poorly they understand the nature and power of groups at work. If people are willing to lay down their lives for a group, should we really be surprised that they’re willing to surrender their brains?

Invisible tribes

Another myth about groups is that groupiness is for other people. If you’re an American, the Lone Wolf archetype is strong within you. But where does that Rugged Individualist value come from? It’s part of our group identity as Americans!

If you’re reading this, my bet is that you are interested in ideas. You’d like to figure out how the world works, whether to be more effective personally or out of simple curiosity. Thus, you also hold values for truth, inquiry, rigor. You want to sort out true ideas from false ideas. You believe in evidence, and science, and overcoming cognitive bias, and deploying the skills of discernment in service to realism.

Welcome to the tribe of Rationalists.

Consider the hallmarks of group identity on display in that group. Rationalists have a glorious history of success since the Enlightenment; we have the rituals of higher education (“learning how to think”) and inquiry, from business memos up to peer-reviewed publications and books; shared values like Truth, Reason, Empiricism, Materialism, Skepticism; norms of what counts as rational (Out with the supernatural. If you must be spiritual, do it on your own time.); common experiences of education, reading, and even choices of entertainment; pride in the headlong success of science; and clear boundaries distinguishing the Ins from the Outs, starting with a language of discourse that spotlights members of the group like a badge of honor and leaves the less fluent out of the conversation.

Don’t get me wrong. I am a proud and practicing member of this tribe. I am convinced that the world is a better place, and gets better over time, when people value the truth over their own prejudices and do their best to rigorously investigate how reality functions. I firmly believe that people of our ilk should be in charge. But just because a tribe is formed for good reasons doesn’t mean it’s not a tribe, and that fact definitely has implications.

My point is not just to show how invisible groupiness is, or to tweak my fellows. I want to highlight two aspects of tribal behavior in the rationalist group. One is ironic; the other is rather critical to modern-day America.

Tribal behavior among the Rationalists

There is one aspect of groups that the authors don’t mention. If a tribe is defined by a certain quality in its members, there’s a natural tendency to overestimate the prevalence of that quality in that group. Part of the function of the tribe is to emphasize the qualities that distinguish the tribe from “the others”. Haven’t we all noticed church-goers who so identify and probably strive to be better Christians, but also overestimate the true extent of how their faith actually affects their attitudes and their conduct? Groups often include an element of wishful thinking.

To call such people hypocrites misses the point. To an outsider, they just are going to look like people who are falling short of their ideals, because their group identity makes up the difference — for them.

To be blunt, rationalists are borderline delusional about their actual dependence on collecting, verifying and analyzing primary data. Nobody can rigorously derive even a small fraction of what they believe. I personally have no qualifications or time to evaluate climate change or COVID vaccines, but I know whom I trust to do it for me: my fellow rationalists. Such a dependence on in-group trust seems and is reasonable, but it looks to people on the outside just like the behavior of any other clique, especially when it seems to flout such a core value.

Consider how the rationalist tribe looks from the outside:

  • Preferentially trusting in-group members as above.
  • Looking down on members of the out-group. Deserving or not, the devotion of Rationalists to Enlightenment values does inferiorize others.
  • Limiting their access to resources. Is there any questioning the prosperity of the educated?
  • Wielding power over them. Let’s face it: by and large, rationalists (aka wonks) are in charge around here.

I invite my fellow rationalists to take a sober look at group effects working on us, not just in the spirit of inquiry, but because it goes a long way to explaining how a certain ex-President got such astonishing power.

A masterclass in group manipulation

The story of Donald Trump on the national political stage is a masterclass in fomenting and exploiting group behavior. In a matter of weeks, it turned an indifferent businessman and blowhard into the avatar of a movement numbering something like a third of US adults, leaving pundits, politicians and historians alike dumfounded. No matter the narcissism, the lies, the impeachable behavior, the disinterest in actually governing; loyalty to Trump seemed immune to the news in a way utterly without precedent.

Donald Trump recognized the dominance in America of a group much like the Rationalist tribe I just described: the meritocrats, the media, the educated elites that had been running things for decades; the ones who had the qualifications and the inclination to take control; who benefitted from globalization and were unconcerned about immigration. This may not seem like a very pointed group, but the actual coherence of this “group” matters not at all, nor does it matter how sinister or exclusionary it really was. For Trump’s purposes, it only needed to have an outside.

The genius of Donald Trump (and yes, I can’t believe I just typed that) was to form a new group based on exclusion from “the elite”: an in-group defined by being an out-group. The invisible. The non-college-educated. The people in the middle of the country. Those for whom globalization (specifically, the export of working-class jobs) was a net loss. Anyone annoyed with the way things were going and felt isolated from the process.

From the day he rode that golden elevator down into the lobby of Trump Tower, Trump’s rhetoric was aimed like a laser at fomenting this group of “outs”, with him as its focus and leader. He drew in an inchoate population grumbling on right-wing talk radio and Fox News, and turned their simmering disquiet into a raging flame of grievance against those who had left them out. He defined a rallying, MAGA-hat-wearing, “I’d rather be Russian than Democrat”-T-shirt garbed team, defined by the idea of taking vengeance on those who had given them the backhand.

Ever wonder why “owning the libs” seems more important than anything else to the Trump supporter — every other concern or matter of policy or even decency? Now you know. It’s the core, defining value of Team Trump, the identity to which Trump’s legions have hitched their own.

Heads were scratched naked and raw trying to puzzle out why Trump’s supporters seemed to be acting in contravention of their own interests, supporting a massive tax cut largely targeting the wealthy, cheering for dismantling Obamacare, and opposing many issues that even Republicans support when polled on an issue-by-issue basis. But isn’t the very definition of group identification that it suppresses self-interest in favor of the group’s?

Once Team Trump had coalesced, Trump found that he could strengthen that group bond with tests of loyalty. When you’re strongly identified as one of the righteous crowd, and Trump asks you to swallow a piece of patent nonsense like the numbers at his inauguration, you have two options: you can abandon the group, surrender your identity and find another membership to sustain you — or you can swallow. And with every swallow, every surrender of your credulity and your own good sense, you’re bought in more, evermore committed to the group. This is what was most puzzling and enraging to those looking on appalled from outside of Trumpistan: why did the constant avalanche of bad news, that would have sunk any other presidency straightaway, not just bounce off of Trump but have the opposite effect, like some comic-book villain who absorbs the energy directed against him and turns it around to become stronger?

If your goal is to cement someone’s identification with your group, there’s no better way than such nonstop, meaningful tests of loyalty. This is why the fortunes of Donald Trump not only survived, but thrived under:

  • the lies and delusions
  • the hypocrisy of proclaimed vs. practiced values
  • the malfeasance to the point of criminality
  • the indifference to actually governing
  • the flouting of institutions and norms
  • the obviously fictitious healthcare and infrastructure plans

But here’s the beauty part: while all of this was making the loyalists more loyal, it was driving the opposition into a frenzy directed at Trump and his crowd, which only reinforced the group’s sense of embattlement and outsiderness bonding the group together!

To paraphrase a thought from evolutionary biology:

Without an appreciation and understanding of group dynamics, nothing about Trumpism makes sense. With it, everything makes sense.

A note of hope

There’s more to The Power of Us than I have space for here. Group dynamics and group identity make an illuminating and productive framework for thinking about race and racism, suggesting that racism might not be as inexorable as it is tragic, in that racist tendencies apparently can be overridden by other group identities. When it comes to teaming up in groups, race is not the only game in town.

Whether group identity can actually be marshaled as a weapon against prejudice in general is still an open question. But if racism, as expressed by implicit bias, can be manipulated out of mind in the lab, then maybe it isn’t quite the pox on the face of humanity that it seems. Someday we may look back and see that it was more like cholera: a plague that actually did have a solution.

Conclusion

This is entitled a “book tribute” rather than a “book review” because I wanted to communicate the substance of The Power of Us, and why what it tells us matters. If you’re not going to pick it up, I hope you can now see how:

  • Group identity is an instinct that exists for good reasons.
  • Social death is worse than physical death; renouncing the beliefs of your group is a social death sentence.
  • My fellows in the rationalist/skeptic community should realize how tribal they really are.

Some of the biggest, hardest problems we face today (e.g., climate change) get stuck at the level of getting individuals to act in the collective interest. Others (e.g., racism) are deeply enmeshed with group dynamics. And American politics feels like it’s broken over the knee of group identity. The Power of Us supplies a most welcome toolbox for thinking about and deploying a hitherto obscure human reality. You’ll learn a great deal.
