item.content:encoded:
Uncontrollable Rage For the Win!

Irrational anger must be a bug in the software, right? The spouse who crashes their life partnership with an outburst. The driver who lashes out at a policeman and winds up in jail. The worker who tells his boss to take that job and shove it. When people fly off the handle in the heat of the moment, you have to wonder: why are we like that? What’s the advantage of building a species that can cut off its nose to spite its face? Wouldn’t this be a fatal bug for a social species?

Surprisingly, there is a perfectly rational reason for irrational anger, under certain circumstances. Can you guess how that works?

First, define “irrational anger” as an emotional reaction that costs the perpetrator more than they gain. Now, consider the case of the schoolyard bully. Every day, he shakes down his victim for their lunch money, and the victim hands it over because, well, what else are they to do? It’s not worth a beatdown to keep a few coins, is it? The rational thing is to just go along.

But suppose the bully picks the wrong victim. Suppose one victim is so outraged by the unfairness of the situation that they decide to do something about it. They’re so irrationally angry that they strike back, even knowing what it’s going to cost them.

Now consider it from the bully’s side. They can deliver the expected beating, but an enraged victim is going to do some amount of damage in return. Is it worth it? There’s a good chance that, faced with someone who doesn’t care that they’re getting worse than they give, the bully will retire from the field — or at least move on to another victim.

Chalk up a win for irrational anger. The victim’s willingness, thanks to their anger, to bear a cost greater than the immediate benefit to them, shifts the bully’s equation decisively.

Even the most primitive societies have an innate respect for the insane. — Motorcycle Boy, Rumblefish

There’s a certain advantage in being willing to pay more for power than it’s strictly worth — a payment that may never have to be made, once the willingness is established. But isn’t this why psychopaths so often prevail in struggles for power? They’re the only ones willing to take the losing risks and pay the excessive prices. The rest of us are too rational.

Ironic, isn’t it?

item.title: Why Everything Fades
item.description: Look at you. You’re swimming in miracles, and they barely register:
item.content:encoded:
Why Everything Fades

Look at you. You’re swimming in miracles, and they barely register:

  • You carry an all-knowing supercomputer in your pocket that connects you instantly across the world.
  • You have an unlimited selection of foods and goods from everywhere, and you have the means to buy them.
  • Your odds of dying from any disease that responds to vaccines, antiseptics or antibiotics are vanishingly small, and if you have a toothache, you don’t resign yourself to debilitating torture for weeks or months; you can make it vanish in an afternoon.
  • You have a car that will take you further in an hour than anyone could travel in a week just a few centuries ago, and if you want to go further you will, as Louis C.K. has pointed out, “sit in a chair and fly through the air, like a god!” The last time you flew, did you even look out the window?

Your plans and goals were all-consuming — when they were in the future. That next job, that big raise, that nice new car, that college admission, that big project, that exotic locale beckoning, that romantic partner who would make it all good. They loomed over your life and consumed your attention — then. And when you crossed the finish line, they were exciting…for a while. A very brief while. Now that you’ve tossed them on your pile of achievements, what is left of them?

And it’s not just you; the same is true for everyone, all the time. What’s wrong with us?

There is a key to this mystery. It’s rooted in basic sensory physiology, the wiring by which we take in the world. And there’s no better place to get insight into perception than looking in the eye, the human visual system.

How does anything register, visually?

How do you think vision works? The obvious, default model is that light gets projected on the back of the eyeball, where some neural circuitry picks it up and transfers the image to the brain, much like a digital camera. But the truth is far more interesting.

Consider the individual photoreceptor, one of the rods and cones at the back of the eye. When photons hit a receptor, it converts the light into a neural signal headed for the brain. If those signals were scaled to the force of the light (bright lights producing strong signals, dim lights weak ones) then you would have something akin to a video signal. But that’s not how it works.

Converting light into an electric charge involves chemistry: each cell has a stockpile of ions which give up their charge to fire the signal when struck by light. Once an ion discharges, it is depleted and needs to be restored, and that process can only go so fast. When the retina is being bombarded by bright light, more ions get depleted and the cell loses its sensitivity. Conversely, under low-light conditions there are plenty of ions available and the cell becomes more sensitive.

Middle-school biology teaches us that opening and closing the pupil is the whole story about dealing with different levels of illumination, and it is — within very strict limits. But this neurochemical accommodation is far more important in enabling our eyes to respond to a mind-boggling range of conditions. From a moonlit cave at midnight to a ski slope at noon, our visual system accommodates a range of brightnesses well into the billions. We do notice the difference between the worst extremes, if we have to put on sunglasses or wait to “get used to the dark”. However, there is a vast middle range over which are blissfully unaware of differences in overall brightness as they range wildly.

We are far more sensitive to changing conditions than to the steady state: remember blinking when stepping out into the sunlight. When a change hits, we become vividly aware, but then adaptation sets in and we head back toward a middling response. When I shave my beard off, I can feel air currents convecting up from my chest. Every little breeze announces itself with voluptuous clarity. But before long, my face is no more sensitive to such changes than my forearm. My baseline level of response is restored.

The importance of change to our perception cannot be overstated. Why do you think emergency signals blink and alarms modulate in sound? If we cared about absolute value, wouldn’t we just set them as bright/loud as possible and be done with it? Instead, we exploit sensitivity to change.

This is why movies which are just one heart-pounding scene after another, and music that’s relentlessly loud/aggressive, seem so dull: they’re literally monotonous (“one tone”).

And this is why the most salient thing about most flights is not the miracle of flight, but the traffic to and from the airport; why the joy of that new car fades in short order; why lottery winners and paraplegics find their way back to their prior level of contentment after a year or so. It’s the change that counts; before long, perception returns to normal

But why on earth would we work that way, emphasizing newness over the way things are? After all, the objects in the world out there are defined by their continuity. Shouldn’t our reactions track that? But preferential sensitivity to change makes evolutionary sense. If you’re a defenseless hairy ape, and you’ve survived until this moment, where are threats and opportunities more likely to come from: the environment as it is, or from moment-to-moment developments? From all the boulders piled up on the hillside, or the one that’s come loose and rolling toward you? From the placid pool of water, or from the glint of motion underneath? From the thousands of cars that pass without incident, or the standout who is veering into your lane?

Once you put on these conceptual glasses, you can see human life as a struggle against the fact that our perceptions, our attention, our reactions, are based less on any fixed, objective reality, than on moment-to-moment change. Modulation.

But then there’s contrast…

There’s a second part of the story, also relating to visual physiology. When a photoreceptor fires, a signal heads for the visual cortex. But the signals passed thereby do not proceed in isolation from one another. Each “wire” is not an independent reporter. The retina also contains a lateral inhibitory network of interconnections among nearby cells, such that when a given cell fires, its signal inhibits the responsiveness of its neighbors.

This mechanism has two major effects. When nearby cells have a similar stimulation, they all inhibit each other. That reduces the visual response to flat fields like a uniformly painted wall. The second effect occurs near the boundaries of such fields. If the boundary between a brightly lit region and a dimmer region falls between two cells, the highly stimulated cell will inhibit its neighbor, making what’s darker appear darker still. Conversely, the dimly-lit cell will not be inhibiting the brightly-lit cell the way the latter’s other neighbors are, so its responsiveness is enhanced.

If this sounds confusing, you can see the effect for yourself:

By Aliwiki at French Wikipedia.

You’ll never convince yourself, but each bar in this image is precisely the same shade throughout. The righthand side of each band appears darker than its left because of inhibition across the boundary (and the left side is brightened by the absence of inhibition coming from its neighbors on the other side of the boundary). In other words, the visual system is biassed toward the contrast at each boundary.

Again, perfect evolutionary sense. Just as adaptation factors out absolute values of illumination and emphasizes temporal change, contrast sensitivity looks for spatial change, at edges and boundaries. If you’re trying to make out objects by their shape or texture, the boundaries are where the action is.

Now you can see why your left hand stuck into cold water will feel colder if the right hand is in warm water rather than the same cold water; why people who are poor relative to their surroundings feel poor, when they objectively have more infinitely more access to technology, nutrition, information and other resources than the kings of centuries past; why, in the memorable words of Gore Vidal, “It is not enough to win. Others must lose.”

What does this understanding buy?

You may question the connection between retinal physiology and, say, ongoing levels of happiness. Is this really how our minds process our larger experiences? What I’m proposing here is visual processing as a metaphor for how we deal with the world in general. Specifically, I’m offering the concrete facts of visual processing as a way of throwing light on the more abstract philosophical concerns of happiness, satisfaction, motivation, etc.

I’m inviting you to take this leap with me because 1) it helps to release the grip of the idea that we deal with things the way they are, rather than how they’re changing or how they compare to their neighbors; 2) from the standpoint of survival, we really are more interested in new threats and opportunities than in the steady state; and 3) minds really do seem to behave this way, heeding contrast and modulation over fixed facts. For example, the phenomenon of hedonic adaptation is well known: the pleasure of an ongoing stimulation diminishes over time, such that it requires increased levels of stimulation to achieve the same effect. So let’s go with the metaphor and see where it takes us, shall we?

With any such metaphor, it’s a reasonable question how far it goes. Adaptation reaches very far indeed, but there are exceptions. A very few phenomena fail to adapt out; it appears that animals of all kinds never get used to stress, for example. And there is such a thing as acquired sensitivity, in which the response to a stimulus increases with exposure. Some allergies develop over time — especially allergies to particular people.

Certainly absolute values do matter absolutely…sometimes. But change and contrast matter much more than we think, suggesting a number of lessons to keep handy in the adept thinker’s mental toolkit.

Don’t be surprised when things fade

Novelty is a force of nature in our perceptions and reactions, and nothing is ever as effective as when it is new. The failure to factor in that reality is responsible for a staggering amount of human disappointment.

How many lives are consumed with making more money, looking for that next step up that will finally let you relax? For paupers as for billionaires, the answer to the question “How much is enough?” is always “More”. Maybe 10, 20 percent more. That’ll be enough to stop striving. But when that day arrives — or not long after — the answer is still the same. It’s like the joke with the fool and the shampoo bottle: Lather, rinse, repeat, ad infinitum. If the phrase hedonic treadmill sounds like something hamsters get stuck on, there’s a reason.

When it comes to picking and prioritizing future achievements (goals), our forethought pictures them on first encounter, in all their novelty, without thinking about how they will look and feel when they are no longer new. This is why “the next shiny thing” is so seductive: it can’t help but stand out against the existing things that are no longer new.

Exploiting novelty

But the unique value of novelty can be exploited for good, too. You may be lusting after some new thing, juicing your imagination with visions of how it will transform your life. Instead of diving into a prolonged battle of acquisition, or piling up your credit card debt even further, why not figure out a way to enjoy the novelty of it without a long-term cost? Is there a way to borrow, rent or otherwise use that thing, and see how long the allure lasts?

If you are looking at the dessert menu, but calories are an issue, you can remember what novelty (and experience) tells you: the first bite of that dessert will be eye-rollingly awesome, but by the time you finish the whole thing you’ll barely be paying attention. For me, the first two or three bites is half the net effect of the whole thing, but with a fraction of the calorie load. Maybe share dessert? Or take a teensy serving in the first place? Then give it your full, rapt attention. Just don’t fall out of your chair in a swoon.

Variety is the spice of life

There’s an excellent word for any stimulation that remains constant over time: “monotonous” (literally, “one-tone”). Gratuitous variety can be a low-cost way of enhancing experience.

I attended university on a fairly large campus, with far-flung classrooms. Walking among them, I made a conscious decision to vary my route, not because one was intrinsically more scenic than another, but because it kept my attention engaged more brightly.

Sometimes we think we need an improvement or a replacement, when we really only need a change (modulation) that makes us appreciate anew what we’ve got. To pick one coarse example, a couple who are bored in their relationship could try taking separate vacations. The simple act of parting and then reuniting may be all it takes to get back on track. And how many people have derailed their lives in a midlife crisis out of a sense of monotony, when a smart application of contrast or modulation could have made everything better?

The moment of change is the hard part

When facing a major change in life — breaking up with a partner, changing careers, moving away, etc. — it’s the moment of change that gets all the attention: the disruption, the chaos, the uncertainty, the unadapted rawness of it. But that focus distracts from where you’re going to spend the vast bulk of your time: in the rest of your life after the change has settled and you have adapted to it. I find it reassuring to realize that if I just hold my nose and get through the transition, the rest will take care of itself.

The faster the change, the greater the impact

There’s an urban legend that you can boil a frog alive if you put it into a pot of cold water, then raise the temperature gradually. While that’s not true in reality, it does illustrate an important point: the faster the onset of a change, the more noticeable it will be — and vice versa.

If you’re going to make a change happen, and you want it to get the maximum attention, make it quickly. Conversely, gradual change is much more likely to sneak in unnoticed. Human relationships of all kinds often fall apart due to changes that no one would tolerate if they occurred suddenly. From lovers taking each other for granted, to toxic personalities revealing themselves gradually, dramatic changes can accrue one baby step at a time, finally reaching levels that seem intolerable to any bystander.

Conversely, you can introduce a big positive change in small increments. In his book Atomic Habits, James Clear suggests that it’s a mistake to just jump into a new habit in hopes of holding on until it takes root. His strategy is to start with the smallest possible version of the habit (e.g., driving to the gym without even getting out of your car), and increase the level of engagement gradually.

Notice contrast at work

When we look around, we see the world as a collection of objects. They persist through time, and you can move them from place to place without changing them. But the ideas with which we deal with the world are a different matter. The importance which we assign to any phenomenon thoroughly depends on the context in which we view it.

This is not the place for a treatise on duality and relativism. But for now, it’s enough to point out that we often think we’re dealing with some fixed, absolute fact of the world, when we’re willfully ignoring its need for a contrasting Other to give it meaning. There is no yin without yang. There is no figure without ground. There is no up without down. There is no evil without good. There is no long without short. There is no rich without poor. There is no smart without stupid. Keeping in mind the importance of contrast helps to remember that.

Find grounds for comparison

If adaptation makes the steady state invisible, we may become aware again by consciously comparing it against some other context. This is part of why an explicit practice of gratitude is so rewarding: it brings into mind (re-minds us) the ways in which things might be different. So does a recent memory of being sick; there’s nothing like sickness to make you appreciate health. And Sam Harris suggests a worthwhile exercise: recall the worst part of your day, and think about all the people in the world who would consider their prayers answered if they could trade places with you in that moment.

When our daughters were teenagers, the challenges of sex, drugs and alcohol suddenly loomed. The default track for parents is to push on abstinence as hard as possible, in hopes of holding off the inevitable as long as possible. Instead, we told them “Look, these things are real, but your brains and your emotions are still developing, so the smart move is to wait until you’re 18. After that, go nuts.” Framing the issue in terms of a contrast between now and later worked surprisingly well, at least in these two anecdotal cases.

In trying to communicate some state, it’s tempting to bring out strong, hyperbolic images in hopes of getting the point across (“You made me feel so so so so so bad”). But unless the communicatee has a similar experience to refer to, establishing some grounds for comparison helps to get the point across. This is one (not the only) reason why criticism is more effective when prefaced by noting some positive things a person has done.

Diversity pays

The movement for social justice in the US promotes diversity as a way to increase opportunities and participation for marginalized populations. That’s a laudable goal on its own, but there’s a more selfish reason to promote diversity of all kinds: keeping things fresh, vital, alive. Not only do we learn from different others, there’s no better way to understand who we are than by contrast with others of different origins, education, history, interests — quite apart from the simple fact that we can’t learn from people who are the same as us.

There’s no denying the very human tendency to sequester in tribes of all kinds, defined by what the members have in common. In fact, social cooperation goes a long way to explaining what made our species so spectacularly successful. And God knows how social media have weaponized tribes and tribalism in this century. So it’s especially important to keep in mind the associated hazards. In a landscape of sameness, not only does the lack of contrast make you unaware of where you’re at, but people become so sensitive to any difference that the smallest infraction can send whole populations off the rails. Sound familiar?

Coping with difference may feel like an onerous burden, but it’s good, and good for you.

Adopt an Alien Perspective

A.J. Jacobs has a post on Substack, The Benefits of Thinking Like An Alien which I think pertains here. The idea is simple: describe an aspect of your life as though you were an alien with no knowledge of life on earth. For example “I used a sharp metal object to remove some protein strands on my face but left those over my eyes untouched” to describe himself shaving.

I don’t expect anything in this essay to come as a great surprise. All of us are vaguely aware that change and contrast matter in our lives, that novelty has its own value, that it’s not what something is that matters so much as how it relates to its surroundings both temporally and spatially. But I doubt that most of us realize how important, yet invisible, these matters are as we go about making our plans, assessing our situations, navigating in the world — an importance that’s obscured by the seeming persistence of the things we deal with directly.

Anais Nin said “We don’t see things as they are. We see things as we are.” Using the visual system as a metaphor for how we deal with things goes a long way to explaining the astonishing realities listed up top. It also makes suggestions for a few life strategies:

  • Understanding that it’s not what you have that matters, it’s how you feel about what you have, especially in relation to its surroundings.
  • Redirecting attention away from things whose impact is going to fade with time and towards things of persistent value. For example, does it ever grow old having friends over for dinner?
  • Remembering that maintaining the gratification you get from things in your life is actually a problem worth paying attention to, and cultivating ways of refreshing your appreciation of them. Don’t marriages need attention in and of themselves?

Examining our lives with these tools in hand can be quite an eye-opening exercise. I’ve found the visual model to be a rich and entertaining way to cast a new light on life strategies and priorities — as well as to make better sense of these crazy humans (myself included) and their ways in the world. I hope it can do the same for you.

Either You’re For Nuance or Against It

What a miserable word “nuance” is. Unlike words like “philosophy” or “psychopath”, its etymology is obscure, so it seems a little disingenuous. It even sounds sneaky: its hardest phoneme is that sibilant ‘c’, as in “snake” and “sneak”. Could it be French? Yikes! So it’s easy to be leery of any calls for nuance in a heated discussion. Isn’t that the wishy-washy liberal’s call to sit around dissecting detail instead of plunging boldly and forthrightly forward?

Or is it? I want to question that implicit divide between the forthright and the nuanced — because there’s nothing wimpy about restraining impulse long enough to acquire some clarity and get priorities sorted, and then move forward with more assurance once you know what you’re actually about. In fact, once you start looking around from that perspective, you find a history littered with disasters directly tied to failures of nuance.

What it Is

The definition of “nuance” that Google offers is

a subtle difference in or shade of meaning, expression, or sound.

There are two problems with that definition: it talks about subtlety (never a good quality for popular discussion), and it rides on a gradation — from more subtle to less subtle — rather than laying down a clear boundary. So, both vague and subjective. But there’s a more useful definition available, as suggested by some very public failures of nuance.

When the gay rights movement came to advocate legalizing marriage between same-sex partners, the prospect brought religious feelings about “the homosexual lifestyle” together with “the sanctity of marriage” in a gasoline-and-matches kind of way. But after a while, there appeared what seemed like a brilliant solution: civil unions, which would explicitly take religion out of the equation while still providing legal recognition for committed romantic partners regardless of their respective genitalia. But no, the religious right wouldn’t have it, calling it “marriage by another name,” and resisting civil unions with all the vitriol it did gay marriage.

The ultimate result? One of the great own goals of our time: the US has full-on same-sex marriage because the “defendants” of marriage refused to make a simple distinction, between the religious and secular aspects of that institution. This was a dismal failure of nuance.

The opponents of gay marriage could have stopped to think about what really mattered to them about the issue. They might have then decided that the religious aspects could be separated from the pragmatic ones for a secular society. They could have decided to focus on the aspects that really mattered to them (i.e., not seeming to give same-sex couples religious sanction) and focused their efforts on defending that. In other words, the issue could have come to a mutually uncomfortable compromise. Instead, the evangelicals devoted all their energy to pushing in a single direction, committing full-bore to an uninflected “principle”.

There is a choice here that comes up so often as to seem fundamental: are we going to commit all our energies to pushing in a particular direction no matter what, or do we stop to look for useful distinctions? Do we declare a generality and charge forward with that as an unwavering standard, or separate the situation out into various components that can be addressed separately and, ultimately, more effectively?

Think about the issue of legal abortion in the US. The ruling in Roe v. Wade was a triumph of nuance. Rather than rule on the simple question “Is abortion always and everywhere wrong?”, it laid out a distinction between 1) a period (the first trimester) when a fetus is still unconscious and inviable; 2) a period (the last) in which it is both conscious and viable; and 3) a gray area in between. But since then, public discussion has degenerated into increasingly extreme unitary views: on the one hand, that a fertilized egg is a human being, subject to the protection of homicide law from the moment of conception; on the other, that the mother’s interests are all that matter, right up until full term. (Notice the correlation between vanishing nuance and the temperature of the issue.)

Nuance, properly considered, is not about getting lost in detail; it’s about getting past a hard, either/or choice in which combatants line up on either side and shout at each other. Perhaps a better word is distinction, the drawing of boundaries and the search for meaningful difference. That is,

The process of examining a problematic situation for distinct elements and treating those elements distinctly, as opposed to seizing and defending an over-arching principle.

That definition sounds so bland and obvious as to hardly be worth mentioning. What’s difficult or interesting about that? Apparently, what’s difficult is to actually put it into practice, and what’s interesting is the carnival of flubbed opportunities for a nuanced approach that makes up so much of life both public and private.

Guns: I’ve lived a number of years in New Zealand, where anyone can own a gun who needs one, if they pass a police review and adhere to a management protocol. Gun ownership is a widespread, unremarkable feature of life, but gun owners are held to a high standard of responsibility and accountability, both by the government and by gun owners as a group.

In the US, as we know, the issue is a nuance desert, a battle pitching those for whom the “right to bear arms” is all that matters, against those who view guns with suspicion or outright hostility, across the board. Today, it’s hard to believe that the NRA used to be an outspoken advocate for gun policy.[1] The hardening of the issue in the last half-century is the tale of a flight from nuance and a willing blindness to distinctions— the distinction between responsible and irresponsible gun owners, for one — with predictable results.

Consider how easy it is to demolish nuance, and what a challenge it is to get it back. It was easy for the Nixon Administration to sell the War On Drugs: drugs represent Vice, full stop, and the only job of Virtue is to stomp it out. Similarly with Nancy Reagan’s Just Say No campaign. It’s taken half a century to recover a more nuanced perspective, relaxing cannabis laws and looking seriously at psychedelics for treating serious psychological conditions, even when the harms of the former and the potential of the latter were plain to see. Portugal has gone so far as to remove criminal strictures in favor of treatment, with great success, but the US still has a long road to re-establish nuance.

In political dialogue in the age of social media and tribalism, nuance and distinction are the first to go. How often do you hear that either: 1) the police are a pack of militarized racists whose role is to secure racial dominance and suppression; and 2) the police are civic heroes who deserve our full support, to the exclusion of talking about their crimes, much less acting on them? How much oxygen is left in the room after those two camps have their say?

In general, the surge of impulse and collapse of nuance is a red flashing warning sign of a degenerating discussion if not a breakdown in civility. The only mystery is how a shift so dramatic, commonplace and harmful happens in plain sight yet unremarked and basically invisible. How hard is it to fit into your head that the police have a vital, heroic role to play in society, AND that misuse of their power needs to be dealt with forcefully? Really hard, apparently — so much so that the question hardly comes up. Shame on us.

Why is nuance so hard?

Failures of nuance are so painful to ponder in retrospect, why do we keep plunging into them, then waking up later with an intellectual hangover? Why is it so hard to take a nuanced stance in the heat of the moment? And what forces predicate against those who try?

First, we have an instinctive attachment to rules and generalities: much of civilization rests on rules, which do provide generality and consistency, from commandments to constitutional articles and amendments to legislative fiat. Justice is blind (to nuance) — at least in principle. And hard-and-fast rules do serve us well much of the time; life really is easier if we can just pull up a rule when faced with a problematic situation.

The very foundation of our cognition, in fact, is the gleaning of patterns, and pulling up the right pattern in any given situation. Once you’ve got a good set of patterns to call on, it’s efficient to just use them, rather than open them up for inspection all the time.

There’s also a popular perception, not entirely unwarranted, that a call for nuance is just a cover for doing nothing. Indeed, there is a certain kind of soul who is content to noodle endlessly, getting caught up in detail and never reaching a useful endpoint or taking action.

There is also a complementary figure looming large: the manly man of action, the Clint Eastwood/John Wayne archetype who stakes his claim, takes no prisoners, and stops at nothing to win the day. Sober reflection is not on the menu for such as they. Figures who present themselves in those terms, straight-arming nuance in favor of clarity and thrust, have obvious advantages in the battleground of ideas.

When social pressure pertains, how much easier is it to coalesce a group head around a clear-cut message and simple principles? Conversely, what kind of group gets all fired up about dissecting a situation and teasing out its most relevant bits, then marching forth, enlightenment in hand? Nerds, that’s who!

Someone who hit the nail on the head about that point was Adolf Hitler. In an excerpt from Mein Kampf published in the New York Times, he spelled out what nuance is up against:

The task of propaganda lies not in the scientific training of the individual, but rather in directing the masses toward certain facts, events, necessities, etc., … so skillfully that a general conviction is created of the reality of a fact, the necessity of an event…
All propaganda should be popular…its intellectual level must be screwed the lower, the greater the mass of people which one wants to attract….The more modest…its scientific ballast is…the more striking will be its success…It is wrong to give propaganda the many-sidedness of scientific thinking…As soon as one’s own propaganda admits even a glimpse of right on the other side, the ground for doubting one’s own cause is laid.
The people…are motivated less by sober consideration than by feeling and sentiment. This sentiment…does not differentiate very much, but it is either a positive or negative; love or hate, right or wrong, truth or lie; but never half this and half that, or partially, etc.

Hitler understood very well that any move toward nuance will be fighting an uphill battle against propaganda. In light of contemporary “discussion”, he seems almost prophetic.

What does decisiveness look like in a world of nuance?

The “standard” choice is between 1) taking forthright action based on a simplified kind of understanding, and 2) dithering around looking for nuance. But this is a false choice. There’s nothing necessarily wishy-washy about nuance. The willingness to insist on good reasons for acting, and then moving forward smartly, is a special expression of intellectual integrity.

A real commitment to nuance is a commitment to figuring out what really matters, and then fully committing to the distinctions that turn up, pushing hard on the elements that matter and letting go the ones that don’t.

Scott Turow, the author of best-selling legal thrillers like Presumed Innocent, illustrates in Ultimate Punishment how this plays out in capital cases. When, say, a child is beaten and murdered, prosecutors and police face a tornado of public outrage; justice predictably takes a back seat to the need to quell those voices. It may not always come down to doctoring evidence and foreshortening investigations, but there is a rush to justice that is inimical to justice itself — a cost made outrageously clear by the DNA evidence that has exonerated hundreds of people wrongly convicted by just such storms: the urge to do something, anything, nuance (if that’s what you can call sorting out the innocent from the guilty) be damned.

In such a situation, who is more respectable/heroic: the prosecutor whose only goal is to get anyone plausible into the court docket, letting the guilty party go free? Or the one who withstands the political storms until the right person stands indicted? Who has better served justice — and the public safety?

I do respect people of principle who stake out their territory and stand pat against every shift in the wind. There’s good reason to prefer them over the school of liberalism which views all boundaries and distinctions with suspicion if not hostility. But the people I really respect who are just as steely-eyed about pursuing nuance and fully committing to the distinctions that turn up. Those are true intellectual heroes.

Being a Hero of Nuance

It’s a cliché to say “Think for yourself.” I don’t know what that means, really, but an excellent first step toward thinking for yourself is to develop a nuance reflex. Do you take on board the bundle of ideas that’s handed to you by convention and/or those who mean to use you, or do you look further into them to tease out distinctions that otherwise get short shrift? In the immortal words of American Beauty:

Look closer.

Resisting the floodwaters of propaganda — especially from your tribe — to stand up for nuance is heroic. It means standing up for a singular principle, a principle that begs to be dismissed and/or ignored. It doesn’t lend itself to bumperstickers and banners. (Trust me, I’ve tried; the headline of this article was the best I could do.) It will never be a meme.

One way to be a hero of nuance is to recognize heroic nuance when you see it. Sometimes it comes in the form of standing athwart an impulsive rush to judgment, so its very presentation can seem frustrating. Sometimes it arrives sounding just like waffling and indecisiveness, or split-the-difference centrism. But genuinely looking for distinction and nuance is none of those things. The differences aren’t always obvious, but they’re generally there to be found.

Another feature of heroic nuance is appropriate depth of discovery. When you divide an issue into its factors, each of those factors can be further divided, and so on, ad infinitum. An intellectual hero knows when to quit, and also knows that just the first distinction, the simplest analysis, is often enough — and almost always better than no distinction at all.

Third, once an issue has been studied and appropriate distinctions made, the hero has the courage to act on the convictions thus acquired. In short, real heroes have confidence: the confidence to pause to look more closely, and the confidence to move forward on the basis of those findings. Dithering around poking into meaningless detail is the opposite of confidence.

Another good practice is to notice when you as a citizen are being asked to discard nuance in favor of a harder, clearer, simpler message; to ignore distinctions and throw out information you already have. Nowadays, I want to throttle anyone — whether I agree with them or not — who has the temerity to say “Well what’s the difference between…?” Democratic policy and socialism. Homosexuality and pedophilia. Mask mandates and dictatorship. Handguns and AK-47s. Taxes and theft. Tightened voting restrictions and Jim Crow, or even slavery.

As Herr Hitler tells us, propaganda works by simplifying issues; so do persuasive messages and recruitment memes of all kinds. Not just online but out in public dialogue, you can observe the history of an issue in terms of the ebb and flow of nuance. Anyone who expects you to ignore worthwhile distinctions is not your friend.

Nuance is the dead opposite of propaganda: it’s the essence of critical thinking.

Heroes needed: Apply here

There are a few issues of moment just now which are desperate for an infusion of nuance:

In thinking about racism, instead of locating ourselves on a continuum from “everybody is racist” to “nobody is”, wouldn’t it be useful to distinguish between explicit hostility, blindness to privilege, the ways that history plays out in the present, etc.? For that matter, maybe we could give the very word “racism” a rest: it’s a third rail of a word that repels nuance.

On climate change, instead of dividing into the camps of “do nothing” vs. “do whatever it takes, cost be damned”, how about if we looked for revenue-neutral possibilities like cap-and-trade, and for moonshot opportunities to turn the costs of climate mitigation into investments in future infrastructure, technology and employment, focused on restoring domestic jobs?

On policing, how about instead of having to choose between “defund the police” and “what’s the problem?”, how about if we take a sober look at the effects of militarization of the police, the appalling lack of training in de-escalation techniques, and ways to make police more a part of the communities that need them the most?

On health care, with a divide between “socialized medicine is bad” and “healthcare is broken and needs a radical solution”, doesn’t it make sense to provide a public option which ensures care for those who fall through the cracks and tests the viability of a government alternative to private insurance?

The first level of nuance in many situations like this is to notice that we react as though they’re political problems, when they’re actually problems of management.

Extreme Nuance

When I look around at what passes for “dialogue” on the Internet, the most scorching nuance desert in sight isn’t over any issue in particular, it’s in the way that we look at each other — the way each of us looks at the Other, I mean. Whether online or around the living room, the pattern plays out again and again: each person starts grossly simplified view of the other, and the argument becomes less and less nuanced as time goes on; the air becomes full of straw men, ad hominems and non sequiturs. We all know where that ends up, neatly summed up by Godwin’s Law: the longer an online discussion goes on, the probability of a comparison with Nazis and/or Hitler approaches 1.

(Sorry about that.)

What would an alternative look like? In my circles, I hear talk about “steel manning”, the practice of understanding and articulating another’s position at least as well as they do themselves. That idea has all kinds of critical defects, starting with the assumption that everyone has good reasons for their positions (best not to look too closely at that one, especially about oneself), but again, an excellent first step would be to look for some kind of nuance, any kind of nuance in your view of the other, and to maintain a hair-trigger alarm for any move that lowers the ambient level of nuance. Will this statement/claim add more nuance to the discussion, or make it continue to spiral down?

Here’s one idea that’s rich in nuance: resist the urge to take the opposition as an undifferentiated group, en masse. One dubious move is to charge The Opposition with hypocrisy, saying different, contradictory things. In reality, it’s easy for a group as a whole to be inconsistent even when the vast majority of its members are consistent. (See the Addendum if you’re wondering how that works.) Any charges of hypocrisy need to be leveled at the individual, not the group to which they belong.

If you want to find balm for troubled waters, make it your job to identify some aspect of nuance in the position of another, or, better still, in them, the person as an individual.

Consider the Trump supporter. To wind up in thrall to one such as he, something powerful must be at work. Feeling at the mercy of people who “know better” (with or without the air quotes), feeling alienated in their own country, caught up in change that seems to happen to them rather than for them, the sinking sense that their children will be less well-off. Is the anger, the intemperance, the slavish acceptance of every word from his mouth really the whole story? How did a bona fide human being, who may well be loving to their family, active in their community and adores kittens, get to such a state? There must also be useful distinctions among Trump supporters. They can’t all be slavering racists and goons.

And if you want to be a saint of nuance, consider Trump himself. I know how hard it is to find any sympathy for this arch-nemesis of nuance in word and deed. But really, is it that hard to get past his toxic effect on everything he touches, and locate the sad, wounded soul who will never, ever feel the pulse of a genuine friendship, or raise his head to look past his own self interest? Could asking such questions possibly be more productive than a mono-diet of ceaseless, uninflected rage?

I don’t know what it will take to unwind the partisan divide in the US, and I don’t know whether the lack of nuance with which we view each other is more symptom or cause. But doesn’t it seem obvious that nothing will change without more nuance in our dialogue and our politics?

In some ways, our culture has become so much more sophisticated in recent decades: morality, attitudes toward those of non-standard sexuality, recreational drugs, etc. That progress is a shift toward more nuance. Conversely, so many of the challenges still at hand are distinguished by the drying up of nuance as time goes on.

In our time, we spend so much attention righteously (and rightly) focusing on how misinformation and disinformation degrade public discourse, and on the caustic effects of social media and tribalization on the quality of democratic deliberation (if you can call that). What we don’t seem to think so much about is the unknowing unwillingness to draw distinctions that need to be drawn, to look into matters at a level beyond rules and impulse and the simple slogans of propaganda. But we would do well to do so; to notice when someone says “Well what’s the difference between…?”; to notice when someone starts using a principle or ideal as a battering ram; to notice when the nuance with which we view one another starts to dry up. It’s time to start making nuance a thing.

There is a tendency to associate commitment — no matter how blind — with clear-eyed purpose and ruthless drive. But in truth, understanding and committing to nuance is 100% as mature, demanding and heroic as swearing allegiance to a principle, because it is swearing allegiance to a principle, viz, that there are valuable distinctions to be made in the world, and the urge to seize on passion and impulse, while it has its place in forthright action, needs to be managed skeptically. Taking the time and effort to seek those distinctions out isn’t generally the easiest thing, but it’s the respectable thing, and, ultimately, the honorable thing. Let’s get to it.

[1] Gunfight: The Battle Over the Right to Bear Arms in America

Addendum: Hypocritical Groups, not Hypocritical Members

It’s entirely possible for a group as a whole to express inconsistent views even when the vast majority of the group’s members are consistent in themselves.

Let’s say that the group of 100 people face competing views: Higher Spending vs. Lower Taxes. If a majority is for Higher Spending AND a majority is for Lower Taxes, you might call the group out for being hypocritical. But consider the case where 49 of the people choose Higher Spending but not both, 49 choose Lower Taxes but not both. Only two opt for both — and that means 51 people are for Higher Spending AND 51 are for Lower Taxes. Just like magic: an inconsistent group where the vast majority of the members are consistent.

The moral of the story is that, once again, we shouldn’t confuse individuals with any group to which they belong. But you already knew that.

item.title: Taking Refuge in the Present
item.description: “Live in the Present!”
item.content:encoded:
Taking Refuge in the Present

“Live in the Present!”

“All you have is Now.”

“Today is a gift. That’s why they call it The Present.”

“No matter where you go, there you are.”

I wonder if everyone is as weary and leery of these dictums (dictae?) as I am, their meaning dulled from sheer repetition. Mindfulness — living in the present moment — is a paradigmatic mantra of new-age thinking, the premiere virtue of a certain kind of secularism, and we all pay it some kind of credence. It makes sense, doesn’t it? To be where you are rather than be distracted by revisiting memories or rehearsing future disasters in your mind? Give me more of that, please!

But it also has something shared by many other virtues: an aspirational, ideal quality, a wouldn’t-it-be-nice right up there with “Live every day as if it’s your last”: the domain of an elect, setting themselves apart with character beyond the grasp of us poor distracted souls. Surely it must be a special kind of person who can stick with where they are, when they are, rather than be dragged hither and yon by turbulence of mind.

Finally, mindfulness seems a little like spinach: good for you in some indistinct, take-your-vitamins, get-enough-sleep kind of way that lumps it in with all those things we could be doing for ourselves, and would be doing if we knew what’s good for us. So what else is new?

I’ve been regularly meditating on a very low-key basis (ten minutes a day, using the Waking Up meditation app) for a couple of years now, and I’m still just a floundering amateur. But I have put my finger on something about it:

Mindfulness — actually being absorbed by what is happening now — is not an act of discipline and denial — a virtue, in other words —for humans to aspire to. It is actually a comfort, an indulgence — a refuge.

Let me explain — with full caveats not to mistake my voice as authoritative.

What Is Mindfulness?

There are many ways to approach meditation/mindfulness, but the common essence is this: observing the mind at work and developing a full awareness of what it’s up to as it goes about its business. In broad strokes, there are two facets to that: seeing cogitation for what it is; and finding out what conscious experience is like when cogitation and rumination subside.

The first facet is finding a way to look at thoughts from the outside, as opposed to being swept away in identification with them — to view them as something you do, as opposed to letting them define who you are. With a glimpse of this stance, you are shocked to realize how few thoughts are really necessary, how goddamn long they go on, how repetitive they are, so that the bulk of the time and effort you spend thinking is a wholly gratuitous waste.

By default, present experience is dominated (to put it mildly) by the past and the future: loops endlessly reviewing what has happened, or rehearsing/worrying about what the future might hold, or — my specialty — critically evaluating every move, from driving to crossing the room to folding toilet paper. Certainly, you can’t do without those kinds of thoughts altogether — just try to live without learning from the past or planning for the future — but if you learn one thing in meditation, it’s how useless the overwhelming majority of those thoughts are, from even this pragmatic perspective. And I do mean overwhelming, because they literally overwhelm what’s going on now, usurping all but a tiny fraction of conscious attention that could be spent attending to the moment, whether it’s pleasant or challenging.

What Practice Is For

There’s a reason meditation is called “practice”: unwinding these rumination loops, getting to where they fall away of their own weight, is devilishly tricky. Monkey mind is always clamoring to take over: just try to spend 30 seconds — or even 10 — without a thought popping up. But what happens when present experience is no longer all about the past or the future? You gain access to a whole landscape, facets of present experience that you’ve only known in theory, or in the grossest of detail: the sensations of your body; the sights, sounds and smells of the world outside; an intimate, responsive connection to the people nearby; the wispy breezes of emotion that float into view, then drift away; ideas and inspirations that are too ephemeral to stand up to the gales of thought that are normally blowing through your mind; showing up for challenges and facing them with your full self; being absorbed and fully committed to whatever you happen to be doing (in flow); and, finally, just an abiding sense of being, in which simply existing and paying attention is such a rich experience that it becomes all you need.

This is what I mean by taking refuge in the present. Achieving an attentive state of mind erects an almost literal barrier that keeps the past and the future where they belong — and gives you the space to be where you belong: right here right now. This is what the title is about: the present as refuge from all those ghosts of the past and speculations about the future.

It’s paradoxical to think of real mindfulness as a profound pleasure — the sensation of pleasure being just another thought — but the gratification is real. The relief is real. It’s like putting down a bag of bricks you’ve been carrying for as long as you’ve been sentient.

A Road Worth Traveling

Again, nobody will mistake me for any kind of adept. Anyone who knows me will attest that what I’m describing is 90% aspiration. So I’m not here to proselytize about some brave new world I’ve found, only to submit that I can see what lies down the road, and have tasted it, however sporadically. It’s not what I thought (as it were).

When it comes to a life well-lived, quality of attention is the coin of the realm — literally the stuff of life. Everything in the past has passed, and the future is imaginary. Why would you spend any more attention on them than you need to? What else is there, really, but this moment? Why wouldn’t you milk it for all it’s worth? How much are you giving up otherwise?

Carpe diem, indeed.

Photo by S Migaj on Unsplash

item.title: What I learned from a housefly

item.content:encoded:
What I learned from a housefly

One sunny afternoon, I was in my bedroom and I noticed a fly trying to get out through a window. The window itself was a large fixed pane, with open panels on each side, but the fly was trying to fly out through the unyielding middle.

This was not an intelligent critter, but it did have room in its head for a really smart strategy. You might think that such a simple organism might just pick a spot to fly through and keep banging into it there, over and over. But no. Instead, it would try one place, then divert randomly left or right and try again…and again…and again. Such a random walk (or fly) doesn’t seem much shrewder than just banging away in the same place (indeed, it doesn’t take much more brain power), except for one important difference: trying the same thing over and over without variation is doomed to failure, but introduce a random variation and you’re actually doomed to succeed — as the fly showed when it eventually wandered into one of the open panels and flew away. It didn’t have to know about the openings. It didn’t need some grand plan for reconnoitering the situation. It just used almost the simplest possible strategy.

This fly didn’t exactly teach me about stochastic perturbation (!), but it did leave me with a superb metaphor for navigating through life. We all have a fairly clear idea, reinforced by self-help tomes beyond numbering, about how to pursue a goal: 1) decide where you want to go, 2) suss out a sensible route from here to there, 3) drive forward along that path until you get there. What separates the adults from the children, the successful from the strivers, is that word “drive”: the determination to let nothing stand in the way, overcoming all obstacles. You may have to build habits, overcome self-doubt, learn to self-promote, sacrifice other priorities, consult the stars, buy nutritional supplements, whatever. But it all comes down to: push, push, push.

The mythos of the self-made man is just that simple: if you only try hard enough (push through your own laziness, overcome all resistance, make it happen no matter what), you will eventually succeed. But it’s not just this masculine ethic of overpowering the world, and it’s not just the American pioneer/Horatio Alger vision of conquering the land with your own blood, sweat, toil, tears and gumption: the basic idea behind The Secret is that you can bend the universe to your will by using only…your will. But no matter what form this principle takes, your reality and your achievements are just a test of character: succeed, and the credit is yours alone; if you fail in tailoring the world to your liking, it’s your fault.

It’s an alluring strategy. It makes sense, lends clarity, appeals to our Puritan work ethic, gives people a way to separate themselves from the competition, and generally seems to work. It’s an all-purpose recipe for success, insofar as it applies to anything you might want, from riches and fame, to community, to love. But like so many alluring ideas, it matters for what it leaves out as much as what it includes. As the fly will tell you, what it leaves out is randomness. Chance. Serendipity. Luck.

Grace.

Luck and Success

Looking back, I’m in awe of the role that chance has played in my life. I didn’t choose to go into computing because I knew that tech was becoming a thing; I set out to do computers because one fine day I came home from school to find in my mailbox a magazine with an article about long-haired freaks spending their working days developing and playing videogames. (This was 1972.) I didn’t set out to do computer graphics at a time when a dozen people in the world, at most, were making a living at it; I happened to be walking across campus with a friend when he casually mentioned an upcoming course being given by people from George Lucas’s company; if I hadn’t heard about it then, I’d have missed out. (This was 1979.) I didn’t set out to meet my wife in New York City when I was first in university; I just happened to see a notice for an off-campus project to spend a term living and working in NYC, which is where I met her.

In all those cases, two things happened: 1) something unexpected occurred, and then 2) I changed course to accommodate it. I could have kept plowing toward my initial EE degree. I could have decided to finish my first year of school before tearing off to New York. I could have carried on with my MS for a generic career in tech, rather than ultimately joining Pixar on its first day. And that’s what a relentless focus on goals and control leaves out.

Conversely, my experience is also dotted with incidents of risky behavior, where I got away clean from a bad decision that could have wrecked my life, and the difference was 100% luck. Surely I’m not the only one.

It’s worth noting that Steve Jobs was one of the most outspoken advocates for “following your dreams” no matter what — yet, as Cal Newport has said,

If a young Steve Jobs had taken his own advice and decided to only pursue work he loved, we would probably find him today as one of the Los Altos Zen Center’s most popular teachers.

Jobs didn’t follow his dreams. He followed the opportunities that fortune brought his way. His drive was peerless, but he had the good sense to know when to loosen his control.

You may be thinking that this interplay between drive and luck is obvious, but if you ask successful people what they attribute their success to, more often than not you’ll get an earful about how hard they worked and how determined they were; you won’t hear much about luck and happenstance — and this skewed perception has all sorts of unhappy consequences, from an unwarranted sense of entitlement to diminished empathy to, that’s right, conservative politics, which view any action to redistribute wealth from the more fortunate to the less so as theft from the deserving to the losers. As Robert Frank points out in his book Success and Luck[1], high achievers will argue that they worked hard for their achievements, and that’s often true. But other, equally talented, hardworking people did not succeed. What separates the two? Did they earn the genes for the aptitudes that got them there, the place in the world they were raised? Was their history really devoid of happy accident, of opportunities that came from nowhere, of mentors and other supportive souls who came along at the right time?

Luck Looking Forward

If the role of good fortune and happenstance is easy to miss in retrospect, it’s even harder to see it looking forward, if all you’ve got in mind is drive, purpose and overcoming obstacles. Fortune doesn’t always take the form of opportunities popping up in the road, and grace doesn’t always arrive as a chauffeur from the future. Sometimes they show up disguised as obstacles and interruptions. And sometimes, you can be surprised by what happens if you just loosen the grip that control has on your thinking.

At one point in my life, my wife and I hosted weekly Movie Nights: a potluck dinner party with a dozen or so guests, followed by a movie in our good-sized movie room — the wrinkle being that I picked the movie. (I didn’t even tell anyone what was coming up until it was all cued up and ready to go.) I only promised to show them something they would be glad they saw, even if they wouldn’t have picked it themselves. I like to think that they gave themselves the gift of letting go, and got the reward of serendipitous discovery. Maybe it was the food or the company that kept them coming back, but they did keep coming back — for more than a decade. Remarkably, of all the people that were invited to Movie Night over the years, only one steadfastly declined, refused to relinquish control. He wanted his cinematic diet to consist only of what he thought he would like. Isn’t that sad?

That’s a superficial example, but there’s one phenomenon, far, far out in the wilderness, that throws a stark light on any assumption that more autonomy and control is always, always better than less: arranged marriages, the practice of life partners being chosen for the betrothed by parents and extended family. In my culture, arranged marriages seem like a barbaric artifact of an unenlightened past. It must be a disaster to give up that much control, right? But in point of actual fact, arranged marriages generally work out quite well [2].

The institution of arranged marriage is fraught with obvious moral hazards. But it’s also a case study in how much we’re capable of accommodating, if we can loosen the grip of control-above-all on our thinking. Even a situation as out of control as an arranged marriage can have a happy ending. It may take a strong culture to make that happen, and a commitment to making it work, but someone who has the issue settled for them just might be better off than those who have to deal with the nightmare of dating and romantic uncertainty. It turns out that control and ultimate freedom of choice aren’t always the Platonic virtues we take them for.

Off-track is where the wins are

There are even goals where interruptions and digressions are not just a good idea, but a necessity. One of those is thinking — that is, navigating the landscape of ideas and trying to make sense of the world. If your goal is to refine your current thinking, to improve your internal map of the world outside, where are those improvements going to come from, if not from outside your current thinking? To put it starkly, every new thing you might be thinking will seem absolutely irrational — until it’s not. As Paul Graham points out in his essay How to Think for Yourself, new ideas are literally those which a population isn’t already thinking; the only way to get to them is to confront the (currently, seemingly) irrational. (He elaborates this point more explicitly in New Ideas.)

As with individual minds, so with cultures and civilizations. Is the way to build a civilization to figure out the best way to be, and then be that, to the exclusion of all else? I doubt that stagnant sameness should be our highest aspiration as a society no matter how well it’s honed and optimized, even if history weren’t roiling about us — but it is. Are culture and civilization even meant to be fixed and finalized, sooner or later? It might be that the peak of civilization is like the top of a mountain where no more climbing is necessary and matters may rest there forevermore. But isn’t it equally likely that progress is less a forward thrust than it is a ferment, a process of experimentation and accommodation? And that the mark of a robust civilization is its capacity to flex and divert in the face of the new?

If that’s true, then you’re not allowed to reject ideas just because they’re off the reservation as currently defined. We don’t have to either accept or believe them; we just have to recognize that the good ideas of the future are likely to be found among the bad ideas of today, and it’s the very process of working through bad ideas that keeps us on our toes, both as individuals and as whole societies.

Not only can we not know which of today’s bad ideas will be the good ideas of tomorrow, but calling bad ideas out into the open — as opposed to censoring or otherwise suppressing them — can teach us lessons that are seemingly unrelated. This is why the appalling parade of delusional nonsense in today’s public sphere (QAnon, Flat Earth, election fraud, etc.), as well as the off-the-rails history of the Trump presidency, just might be useful, i.e. if they shock and alarm the culture into growing more sophisticated about dealing with information bubbles, tribalism, confirmation bias and malignant narcissism in positions of power. If it does, that will be precisely because the current situation is so heinous.

Diversity reconsidered

To me, cultural ferment by actively engaging with the “abnormal” (as currently understood) is the single greatest argument for cultural diversity. In a way, our present-day culture wars come down to a battle between the model that says that “our” society is as good as it’s going to get, and those who believe in their heart of hearts that difference and diversity are valuable just because they’re different, because they plant seeds of change that make the society more robust — and this is true even if they’re wrong! The only way to sort out the valuable ideas from the inimical is to throw them against the wall and see which stick. The best case scenario is that diversity provides the impetus for useful change; at worst, it makes us appreciate how good we’ve got it. In any event, sorting through such issues at the edge of our collective comfort zone is good exercise for a culture.

But never mind change over time. Even in the present, no group can do without rich internal variation. Most of us are intuitively leery of groupthink and the “madness of crowds”, but James Surowiecki, in his book The Wisdom of Crowds, put his finger on what distinguishes a smart crowd (which, for example, can guess the weight of a bull at a county fair within a few pounds) from a dumb one (which thought it was a great idea to storm the US Capitol building). When the members of a decision-making body are uncorrelated with one another in their thoughts (meaning, essentially, that diversity of thought is actively promoted), and they provide their input outside a context where groupthink can prevail, then their chances of success are vastly improved. Do I even need to paint a picture of echo chambers as cesspools of correlation?

The Joy of Randomness

Of course, my fly had none of these lofty ideas in whatever it had for a mind. It reached its goal of getting away just by incorporating randomness into its strategy, even while maintaining its unrelenting purpose. And this is the purest, scariest form of relaxing control. Can we actually roll the dice with our lives, throw ourselves entirely on the mercy of Fate?

That’s a scary prospect — until we start to notice processes where success depends on a certain amount of randomness. Consider evolution by natural selection. Selection is meaningless without a diverse set of variations to be selected among. The source of the variation driving evolution on Earth is a matter of hot debate, but one aspect of it is not: nobody is in charge of deciding how to steer the process or which variations to try and which not. The fact that the system is literally out of control is its beauty and its strength.

The Leap of Faith

The development of life on Earth is all well and good, but don’t we want matters in our individual lives to feel a little more regular? You would think so, but the fact is that our lives already abound with situations where you have to commit to a path before you know what the outcome will be — and there’s no going back once you start. The outcome may not be random, but it is deeply uncertain; such situations come with an irreducible element of risk, which is to say they are fundamentally, definitionally out of control.

Parenthood is one example. Every first-time parent learns one thing right off the bat: they had no idea what they were getting themselves in for. Many parents thrive under the circumstances and others are crushed by it, but they all took the leap without having a clue how it would turn out — because how could they know?

I have done a little single-track off-road mountain biking, and one lesson comes rushing in straightaway: timidity is not your friend. Slowing down enough to pick your careful way over the next tree root or to ensure that you can make that hairpin curve is a challenge to your balance and a disaster for your ability to control the bike. The only thing for it is to fling yourself forward, giving up the idea of being safely in control and having faith in your skills to manage what comes up. And what’s exhilarating is: it works!

Human relationships are often like that. How many times have you been in a situation where there was something to say to another person that could either take the relationship to the next level or send it off the rails? There was no way to tell in advance how it was going to go, and you couldn’t un-say that thing once you said it, nor could they un-hear it. Confronted with that choice, you either stayed silent and let matters stagnate, or took the leap, counting on the ability of you and the relationship to get through the crisis even without knowing the outcome.

I like to call the decision to move forward with no assurance of success the leap of faith. It reminds me of jumping off a cliff into a fog bank. There may be a safe landing on the other side, but so might broken bones or a funeral. Either way, there’s no getting around the need to take the leap — if you want to live a full life. Such situations generally include the option of standing pat and doing nothing, in the name of keeping certainty and control. And how sad is that?

Seize the Distraction; Embrace the Obstacle

In pursuing goals with single-minded determination, when interruptions, distractions and obstacles present themselves, the automatic reaction is to see them as threats. But that reflex is at least questionable, because opportunities sometimes arrive disguised as obstacles, and recognizing them for what they are only takes a little thought. Blessed are the times that obstacles arise spontaneously, for that is when we get our blinders knocked off, and we have an implicit choice whether to get annoyed (because our purpose was violated), or to take it as an opportunity for exploration.

Brian Eno has described his creative process in a way that captures this interplay beautifully. He’ll set out on a project with a goal in mind, and work toward that goal until he encounters a problem. Then he sets out in a new direction suggested by the obstacle — until another obstacle presents itself. In this way he takes a path through the space he’s working in that weaves together intention and serendipity. Eno even developed (with Peter Schmidt) a set of dictums, dubbed Oblique Strategies, for breaking the creative blocks that occur when drive meets blockage, employing such seemingly Dada-esque instructions as “Ask your body” or “Gardening not Architecture”: anything to throw a spanner into the works of single-minded pursuit. And the finished work isn’t some construction that sprang whole from the forehead of the creator. It is informed and inspired in large part by the interruptions, and the process of working with them.

Randomness and Intentionality: a Dialectic

There are also ways to dip your toe safely and playfully in the waters of chance without really leaving that safe shore, and that can really be a refreshing exercise. Think about choosing music to listen to. Do you always go back to the music of your youth, or do you look for newer tunes that might be just as compelling. And how exactly does one do that?

Unsolicited plug: Spotify presents as the answer to this prayer, with its options for helping a person step knowingly outside the familiar. Starting with a familiar, beloved song or artist, you can ask for “more like this” and get just enough difference to be interesting. Once you establish your own listening patterns, the service produces daily and weekly Discover playlists, and a Release Radar playlist for new material by people you like. Even better, if you stumble on a new genre of music you like, as typified by a particular artist, you can launch a “… Radio” that presents you with a panorama of adjacent music. The exhilaration of finding something new that slots right into your brain is difficult to convey.

Parties are surprisingly similar, both in the strategy and the opportunity they present. One can spend a whole evening bantering and catching up with people you know — but you can also make it your purpose to engage with strangers. They won’t be that strange (after all, they are also connected to the party-giver), and almost everybody has something interesting to say. In fact, one can spend the entirety of a party on a mission to find the most interesting person in the room.

A Life Less Ordinary

The religious have the comfort of passing off the responsibility for their fate to a higher power. One of the disadvantages of secular life is that, by default, it dumps all responsibility for the way things turn out on the individual. That would be an enormous burden to carry even if we could manipulate all of the levers of reality to our liking, driving ourselves to just the destination we had in mind. But we can’t. The universe is random, dodgy and obstreperous in ways that are by turns infuriating and miraculous. There’s good news, though: coming to terms with the fact that it’s not all up to you is strangely liberating. Realizing that you’re embedded in systems beyond your control — and that you can learn to enjoy their company — means that it’s not all about you. It’s a powerful way of living lightly in the world.

Back at the beginning, I used the word “grace”. In Christian theology, it refers to expressions of God — basically blessings — in everyday life. In the absence of a divine entity, I think of grace as anything you can be grateful for that‘s not your direct responsibility. In the drive to achieve and keep focussed on goals, grace takes any number of forms that are easy to miss. As far as I’m concerned, staying alert to the opportunities that have so many different disguises, and dropping back from the chimera of full control and responsibility to invite serendipity in, is close to the essence of a graceful (grace-full) life.

This is what that fly crystallized for me: that a relentless forward path can be doomed to failure; how important a little arbitrary influence can be; and how education can come from the most surprising places — if you’re paying attention.

[1] Why the myth of a perfect meritocracy is so pernicious, vox.com

[2] The Levels of Satisfaction between Love and Arranged Marriages: A Comparative Study
