item.description: What are the basic drives of humanity? What gets us up in the morning, gets the juices flowing and steers our behavior through the day? Money? Power? Sex? Meaning? Status? Simple survival? Those are all renowned, and you can feel them surging through your life and the society aro…
item.content:encoded:
Express yourself!

What are the basic drives of humanity? What gets us up in the morning, gets the juices flowing and steers our behavior through the day? Money? Power? Sex? Meaning? Status? Simple survival? Those are all renowned, and you can feel them surging through your life and the society around you, but I would like to propose one more that pretty much flies under the radar: personal expression.

As used every day, “express” is a verb for saying something, and an “expression” is the thing said. But think of how far it goes. Consider the etymology of this simple idea: “ex” (out) + “press”, or push. To “push out.”

When we say “express”, we’re not just talking about putting something into words. We’re talking about taking something from inside ourselves, and pushing it out into the world. Again, sounds simple — until you think about it.

There aren’t many experiences more joyful than sitting across from another person, locked in rapport; words, ideas, and feelings springing forth and being received warmly and knowingly by the other. Knowing the elation of understanding and being understood, of the conviction that something alive in you now lives in them, and feeling the other person’s joy at being understood by you. The heart of that experience is the height of personal expression: making us feel alive.

If you’ve successfully “expressed” something — a desire, a thought, a feeling — you’ve taken something from inside your own head and brought it to life inside the head of another person. You’ve affected the world, and that effect is your own. Those effects can be trivial in scale and unimportant to the world (“I’ll pay with a credit card”), but the possibilities are endless, both to the world and the person so expressing.

Once we think of personal expression as the act of having our effect on the world, we start to realize how important it is to have such expressions, such personal effects on the world at large--and, conversely, how empty, lonely, and tragic is the life that slips by without touching anything.

When we’re suffering, we can go it alone, but if we’re lucky, and we have someone to share our misery with (literally, commiseration), how much solace do we get from the realization that a friend has found space in their head and heart for what was previously yours alone?

How much of our personal life revolves around our presentation in the world, defining who we are, for all the world to see? Matters of grooming aren’t just practical, they also tell the world that you’re a well-groomed person. Car ownership, bumper stickers, T-shirt slogans, hair style, and clothing choices in general only mean anything because they say something about the bearer — fostering an impression in others corresponding to the bearer’s expression. We want people to have a particular impression of us: of our personalities, of our charity, of our probity. We manage our reputations even among people who don’t have the slightest practical importance in our lives. Why? Because we want to have ourselves out there in the form that expresses who we are (or aspire to be).

How much of our social media presence is about presentation? From selfies in alluring locations to virtue signaling to staging bookshelves for Zoom calls, we spend much of the day trying to get the right ideas about ourselves into the heads of others.

What drives writers to toil on their expressions, but the goal of having their feelings, their ideas, find life in others out there?

What is art, but the willful act of taking something inside and “pushing it out” into the world — something that uniquely expresses its creator? Art, though its countless expressions, finally comes down to a simple message: “Here I am. I made this. I am real.” Even simple craftwork: if the craftsperson cares at all, they care that the object being crafted reflects the person who made it.

Of course our genes dictate that we reproduce, but once we have children, how many parents resist the urge to mold them in their image, with their values, to do things the way they do them?

What is power, but the act of forcibly bending the rest of the world to our idea of the way things should be? What could be a more tangible expression of who we are than imposing our will on the world? Even climbing to an executive position or running for an elective office is largely about getting some part of the world to see you in a particular way.

You can even see the call to expression behind behavior that seems to serve that need, but really only makes a mockery of it. How many social media feeds are tailored to presenting someone’s carefully curated version of themselves, the person they wish other people would see? Aren’t online phenomena like virtue signaling and Twitter mobs really about asserting a moral, upright picture of oneself in the world? And isn’t whole idea of status symbols, from cell phones to Macmansions to monster trucks, presenting an enhanced version of ourselves?

There’s an old essay by Lester Bangs that perfectly expresses (as it were) this distinction between authentic expression and its fake, performative corruption, in the difference between style and fashion. In Bangs’s formulation, style is adopted by an individual as an expression of who they are. By contrast, fashion comes top-down, from the group; conforming to fashion signals that one is a member in good standing of that group. Bangs called that the difference between originality and fascism. I call it the difference between genuinely engaging with a basic need, and just gesturing in that direction in a way that only frustrates the very desire it claims to serve. Junk food for the heart.

Coming to terms with what personal expression is really all about, and how many forms it takes, I’ve found myself viewing the world and people’s role in it through a particular kind of glasses. I’ve been wearing those glasses for a while now, and they’ve convinced me that the drive to express oneself, by any means necessary, is one of the fundamental imperatives of the human animal: right up there with the need for sustenance, comfort, and transcendence. It saturates our existence. The flow of expression, of people interacting over who they really are, is as central in the human, social sphere as the flow of money is in the economic one.

Try those glasses on, and see what you think. How many things would you stop doing if there was no one to see/hear you do it? How much of what you do is about pushing out something of yourself into the world? If that’s the goal, how well do your choices serve that goal? How many of the actions of others around you are all about expressing themselves? Are they fooling themselves about what those actions are really about? Where can you spot the urge for self-expression operating in the world at large? What is the effect when a person strives to present an aspirational or otherwise untrue version of his or her self?

The isolation imposed by COVID offers a unique chance to look at our personal expressions anew, to question how well each one actually serves the goal of putting ourselves out there.

item.content:encoded:
Why Dieting is Hard…also Climate Change…also Racism

Ever wonder why dieting is such a struggle? Why is it so difficult to attack climate change as a society? Why has it been so hard to get people to wear masks against the coronavirus? Each of these challenges has its own distinct features, of course, but there’s a common thread that runs between them — and many other issues that people face, both individually and collectively. And without coming to grips with that aspect, solutions will remain elusive, and we’ll stay frustrated because we don’t understand why — kind of like being hounded by invisible spirits.

To put it simply, that thread is a failure to understand, respect, and successfully cope with the difference between the individual and the collective. A decision vs. a policy. An act vs. a habit.

What is dieting? It’s long-term behavior (eating less, or better) directed at long-term goals (improved health, weight loss, etc.). But how is dieting practiced? As countless individual decisions of how much to eat this time. The key thing to realize is that any one of those individual decisions/acts has virtually no bearing on the long-term goal. When I am tempted by a fabulous piece of chocolate cake, it literally doesn’t matter whether I eat it or not. By itself, it has no measurable impact on the success of the diet plan I swore to on New Year’s Day. A long succession of such decisions definitely matters, but the individual act does not, in a very literal sense. And the gap between the two is a chasm into which the best-laid plans fall.

What I’m getting at is a blind spot in our worldview: an assumption that if we want the general outcome, then of course we’ll behave ourselves in the day-to-day. In other words, we walk around grindingly unaware that they’re not the same thing at all, and this confusion brings endless frustration at all levels of civilization from the personal to the global.

(If you can stomach a little math, this distinction is enshrined forcefully and starkly in the theory of sets, distinguishing between a member (individual), and a set, a collection of members. At a basic level members and sets are different logical types. They are thought of in different ways and subject to different treatment. Never the twain shall meet.)

An item is different from a collection. A decision is different from a policy. An act is different from a habit.

The struggle to keep to a diet is nothing more and nothing less than the struggle — mental, emotional and behavioral — to forge a link between the two, to make the act reflective of the policy. The reason it’s hard is that, at a basic level, no such link exists; we get frustrated and confused because we think the linkage is obvious, that we shouldn’t want to eat the chocolate cake if we want to lose weight. There we are, struggling with the gap between the two, with no idea that there even is a gap.

There are exceptions to this sad picture, and they’re worth a look because they highlight the issue. People do make plans, which amount to translating a longer-term goal (what I want out of life: career, education, budgets) into finer-grained steps (actions this year, or day-to-day). Once the plan is in place, the steps become part of a framework that helps them along more than, say, reading this book, then that book, and hoping they add up to something.

The case of budgeting is interesting because it breaks the broad goal of solvency or saving into categories, and those categories into small (day-to-day), salient boundaries, where overstepping the budget in a small way feels more like a violation of the grand plan, in a way that just buying that sticky bun in the absence of multilevel planning would not. Budgeting doesn’t always work (some people and circumstances — and budgets — are more amenable to success than others), but it is a lever that improves the odds of success.

Dieting is hard because it should be hard. There are workarounds in the budgeting sense (Weight Watchers, meal plan services, etc.), but the temptation to cheat is always there because a single act of cheating just doesn’t, as a matter of fact, affect the overall goal. The fact that we sometimes achieve it is the surprising thing, the unexpected thing, the thing that should be celebrated when it works rather than getting mad or frustrated or judgy when someone has difficulty linking the two.

It’s the same deal with procrastination. Why should I do this thing today? What difference does it make if I do it tomorrow instead? Well, no difference, actually. It’s only the aggregate of tomorrows that makes any real difference. Again with smoking cessation: that next cigarette has literally no long-term impact whatsoever. How do sensible people wind up with catastrophic credit-card debt? One purchase at a time.

Only in the aggregate…

Why has it been such a struggle to get Americans to take masks and social distancing seriously during the pandemic? After all, the numbers are clear, and the US has half a million corpses to show for it. But when you walk into a crowded store without a mask, the probability of a dire outcome is actually pretty low, kind of like playing Russian roulette with a thousand-chamber gun. You as an individual would have to play a lot of times for disaster to ensue — but that’s the level at which society operates, and suffers: it takes billions of careless acts produce that many deaths. We have largely failed as a society to make the requisite link between the individual decision and the outcomes at a societal level.

Big box stores and suburban malls have been hollowing out downtowns not because WalMart improves the local environment, but because there is just no salient connection between going to WalMart today for price and convenience, and the downstream consequences. Nobody voted for WalMart over Main Street, but their individual decisions had that collective outcome.

Heartland America hates jobs being shipped abroad, but who chooses the more expensive domestically manufactured item over the cheap Chinese knockoff? People complain about air travel being uncomfortable but they don’t think of the cumulative impact on quality from countless immediate decisions on price. Were they voting for a shitty travel experience? No, but that was the long-term outcome of such decisions over decades. Does anyone want a crisis in the availability and affordability of housing in the US? No, but they made millions of small decisions — in zoning, in regulations, in NIMBY behavior — each perfectly reasonable at a local level, and each making a negligible contribution to the end result.

Some acts get their meaning only at the level of statistics, which is to say, in the aggregate. That’s one reason why racism is so hard to eradicate. Suppose society managed to quell all vestiges of overt racism: perfect racial harmony on the surface. If a recruiter is interviewing job candidates and picks the white candidate over the Black one, it’s logically impossible to call that out as racist, assuming the absence of other signals. But if that recruiter, or their company as a whole, or the society in general show a pattern of exclusion and preference, then there’s a problem. This is what I fear is the hardest part of systemic racism: a pattern of oppression that emerges from a multitude of individually reasonable decisions even without expressed or even conscious hostility. If my life and my prospects were limited by something so diffuse, something so lacking in accountability, then I would be consumed by rage. And when there’s no obvious, tangible target of blame, I would acquire a hypersensitivity to anything that even looks like it has a tinge of racism. Sound familiar?

So there you have it: a broad range of human struggles, frustrations and outright anguish, just from falling into the gap between the individual and the collective. But what can be done about it?

A Couple of Ideas

Habit formation has been getting some love in the self-help world of late, which is interesting because habits are all about behavior in the aggregate. Of course, a habit is still made up of individual acts, so acquiring one is always going to be a challenge, but it’s encouraging to see habits addressed per se. James Clear’s book Atomic Habits has some clever hacks for working at the habit level, including:

  • starting small, with outright trivial behaviors, for example beginning on a habit of working out by just showing up at the gym for five minutes;
  • making a behavior more automatic by associating it with recurring triggers in the environment; and
  • reconceptualizing each individual act of X from a make-or-break success or failure, to “a vote for yourself as the kind of person who does X”.

For behaviors on a more public level, I notice that a good chunk of moral strictures are designed to conjure up link between the act and the habit, between the decision and the policy. There are obvious strictures based on the Golden Rule (“Act as you would be treated”) that address behaviors where every act is a violation (like the Commandments against killing, cheating, stealing and lying). But others are driven by aggregate-driven questions like “What if everybody did it?” (Even an atheist has to admit: you can’t beat moral injunctions backed by Divine authority for changing behavior at the individual level.)

Why do we recycle? Not because anyone’s household garbage has the slightest global impact. We do it either because it feels wasteful, or because we think everyone should do it. We’ve somehow forged that moral link between our behavior and everyone’s behavior.

Why is such shame attached to driving impaired, and why do we feel so wrong when we drive around without seatbelts? Not because the odds are very high of getting into trouble —once. It’s because if we do it repeatedly, or if many people do it, then there will be consequences. Somehow, and not very long ago, the society managed to make the connection salient and instill that ethic.

But there are plenty of public problems whose solution still eludes us, starting with that classic economic conundrum, the “tragedy of the commons”. The commons in question is a village commons, a tract of land open to grazing, shared by all the villagers: if everyone grazes it, it’s guaranteed to be over-grazed and finally exhausted. But it’s in every individual’s obvious interest to graze it because a piece of a failing resource is still better than nothing. Individually rational actions produce complete collective destruction.

The biggest commons of all is the natural world and its resources — depletion of fisheries being a pointed example. Exploitation of natural resources is an especially thorny commons problem because the consequences are so backloaded: when people first arrived in a place there was every reason to make the most of nature’s offerings and no reason not to. It’s only now, as the earth fills up, our lifestyles luxuriate and we realize that resources are finite, that stewardship has become an issue. I say the problem is backloaded because it’s not like we’re drawing down a bank account and trying to stay solvent. It’s that natural systems are subject to collapse: there may be a tipping point, beyond which the world plunges into disaster. That’s the crucial thing about climate change: once enough glaciers and ice caps melt, and tundra thaws, and the ocean reaches carbon saturation, we may have set off a downward spiral that we can’t even slow, much less reverse.

But however catastrophic, it’s still a commons problem, and we still don’t have either the will or the wisdom to connect individual behavior to global outcomes with any tools more effective than preaching and coaching.

This may be a harsh note to end on, but as you can see, all I have in hand is a highlighter. Individuals have fierce trouble accounting for the aggregate effects of their individual acts not because they’re selfishness, or unenlightened, or shortsighted, or otherwise flawed of character. We struggle with it because it is a hard problem in and of itself, and we should at least start addressing it as such. I don’t have any magic solutions, but I do submit that a good first step is to stop barking up the wrong tree.

item.description: If nothing else, the chaos in the US Capitol on Jan. 6 taught us that there really is no limit to the nonsense that people can be led to believe. Four years of mainlining bad information and riding high on outrage, gushing to a climax at the Capitol. But now the party is over: th…
item.content:encoded:
Facing the Elephant in the Room

If nothing else, the chaos in the US Capitol on Jan. 6 taught us that there really is no limit to the nonsense that people can be led to believe. Four years of mainlining bad information and riding high on outrage, gushing to a climax at the Capitol. But now the party is over: the place is a wreck, the fireworks have destroyed the fireplace, the virgin is de-flowered, and the Frat King has slunk away, leaving us to deal with the aftermath. The grownups are back, but the question lingers: did we learn anything?

Seriously, let’s be clear about what just happened:

People by the millions went off the deep end, and simple, obvious reality offered no resistance at all.

We’re talking about a metastasizing cancer of misinformation and disinformation. And we have a very good word for pernicious lies deliberately spread to masses of people for political purposes. We call it propaganda.

Contemporary propaganda has any number of agents, including right-wing talk radio, Fox News and its fellow travelers, the attention economy of the Internet in general, and the outrage machine of social media in particular. (I’ve written about this before in One Crisis to Rule Them All.) When “newspeople” with millions of viewers can get away with pushing the idea that “some people” think Antifa was involved in the Capitol riots; or the vast majority of Republicans become permanently convinced that the 2020 election was stolen, whatever sense of decency or shame that used to hold such forces in check is gone, baby gone.

The fact that it’s gotten this far is our red, flashing, wailing emergency signal that it’s time to, in the immortal words of W.C. Fields, take the bull by the tail and face the situation. If this kind of propaganda —propaganda that can turn a malignant narcissist into a messiah figure and sell a stressed but conspicuously sound election as a vast fraud — can have these kinds of consequences — civil unrest and violence at a national level — then if we don’t find a way to fix it, America is on the fast track to oblivion. If you think this crazy wave has reached some kind of crazy peak and will shortly subside with the departure of Donald Trump, I have two words for you: Think Again.

Propaganda vs. The First Amendment

Just as we resist the term “propaganda,” Americans panic at the very idea of managing information in any way: what about the First Amendment?!? We have grown comfortable with the idea that any restriction on speech is un-American. So we need to recall that “freedom of speech”, even enshrined in the Constitution, has never been absolute. Exceptions and limitations abound, so ingrained that we forget they even exist. As the relevant Wikipedia page puts it,

[C]ommon limitations or boundaries to freedom of speech relate to libel, slander, obscenity, pornography, sedition, incitement, fighting words, classified information, copyright violation, trade secrets, food labeling, non-disclosure agreements, the right to privacy, dignity, the right to be forgotten, public security, and perjury.

You can’t cry “fire” in a crowded theater. You can’t threaten the President. You can’t attack a person’s reputation with lies. You can’t incite violence against the government. And on and on. Clamping down on expression — especially political expression — is still somewhere between a third rail and a minefield. But it’s not unprecedented.

There is even a legal precedent, at least in the United States, for enforcing some fealty to the truth. The FCC’s Fairness Doctrine dictated that broadcast networks, by dint of licensing the public airwaves, had an obligation to present alternative viewpoints when discussing matters of opinion. The Fairness Doctrine had weaknesses aplenty, and in the new worlds of cable distribution and streaming media it has fallen by the wayside, but it is a real precedent for thinking of information integrity as a public good, and maybe a source of lessons learned?

A Re-framing: De-platforming vs. Censorship

Absolutism about the First Amendment isn’t the only misconception on the docket. There’s a widespread impulse to accuse commercial entities like news networks and social media platforms of attacking freedom of speech, of censorship. This idea may be sticky in the popular mind, but it has no legal standing at all. The First Amendment begins “Congress shall make no law…abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press…” In other words, only the government is constrained from constraining speech.

Practically speaking, freedom of the press has never applied to anyone without access to a printing press. Freedom of speech only means that the government can’t arrest you for standing on a soap-box and voicing your opinions in the park (and even then, only if you don’t violate the above-mentioned restrictions). No entity, public or private, is obligated to amplify your voice and broadcast it further than your voice (or pen) will reach. Social media companies have built engines of staggering power to spread all sorts of memes, including propaganda. Even the worst actors have come to assume that they are entitled to a free ride on these rocket ships of dissemination, with no cost or consequence whatsoever. How does that make sense?

Say it loud, say it again and again: The First Amendment isn’t even a speed bump in the way, should the social media giants come to grow a sense of ethics and responsibility for the uses to which their platforms are put and the epistemic devastation that follows.

A Modest Proposal

This essay started life as nothing more than a problem statement highlighting a Hard Problem of our day. But as it turns out, I do have a suggestion about a way we might tackle the problem of private propaganda. It’s based on the idea that speech has tangible consequences, with the speaker responsible, at least in part, for those consequences.

The doctrine of libel says that we can’t use false speech as a weapon against an individual. The doctrine of sedition says that we can’t use speech as a weapon against the State. Laws against perjury tell us that we can’t proffer untruths in a legal proceeding. We can’t even lie to an FBI investigation. The idea that speech — especially lies — can do real harm in the world is firmly established in law and precedent.

But propaganda lacks one thing that these cases have: an obvious, material victim, i.e., people or entities that are being harmed or materially threatened by the speech in question.

My suggestion: We need to develop the idea that truth itself can be a victim.

The truth is not a person or other entity in the material world, but it is a public good. It is the very lifeblood of a democratic society, and it has exploded in importance with the Information Age. It is the stuff of life on the Internet; the social media companies are all about building machines/networks of Biblical power for turning information toward good or evil ends. Not coincidentally, lies, misinformation and disinformation have acquired weapons-grade power. If the modern era has to get its shit together about one thing, it’s how it manages and respects quality of information.

(Full disclosure: I’m not a lawyer; I don’t even play one on TV. I only hope that actual legal minds will find a thread here that’s worth picking up.)

From my perspective as a civilian, libel law seems like a pretty good model to start with, in several respects:

First, libel law makes a clear distinction between fact and opinion. I am free to denounce anyone in the strongest terms, so long as that denunciation is based on my judgement and makes no false claims of fact.

A second important feature is that a libel proceeding does not try to make fine distinctions between truth and falsehood. The standard is not whether any given claim is true or false. The standard is whether it is an egregious, flagrant falsehood. Very different business. I think it’s incredibly important to stay well clear of any world in which some authority figure gets to rule on whether any random proposition is true or false. Instead, like libel, we want to confine attention to the extremes, filtering for the most egregious bullshit, in much the same way that criminal proceedings don’t hinge on whether a person is mostly innocent or guilty; the issue is whether they are clearly guilty. It’s the difference between a war on disinformation and a war on dissent.

Finally, libel law concerns itself mainly with another extreme: damage done. Nobody gets sued for libel for gossip, and, as far as I know, never without the involvement/amplification of mass media. Even in the media, even in the UK (where grounds for libel are much broader), proceedings are rare, and confined to the most damaging abuse. Initiating proceedings is just not worth it otherwise.

So, in as much detail as a non-lawyer can muster, the idea goes like this:

  • Recognize the truth as a public good that can be harmed.
  • Build a framework for civil proceedings to recover damages for willful, knowing harm to public information.
  • Set standards similar to libel law for identifying “willful disregard for the truth”, including not just malice but manipulative intent.
  • Provide for explicit exception where opinion is clearly separated from fact.

The biggest problem here is how to assess damages for redress. Individuals suing for libel can typically point to actual harms: to their business, to their social life, even to something as diffuse as their reputation. But there is such a thing as punitive damages, whose purpose is not to compensate the victim but to discourage the perpetrator from perpetrating further by making it unprofitable. That might be a good place to start.

A second problem is one of standing: who gets to sue? The damage of polluting the public information stream is distributed far and wide, in that it basically harms everybody in the society.

Now, before my “modest proposal” can find its way into reality, there are issues to overcome. First and foremost is the Don’t Tread On Me panic that surges in everyone’s gut at the idea of censorship. We may accept that some ideas may need management but our ideas are sacrosanct, and God forbid some bureaucrat should have veto power over our expressing them. There’s a basic issue of trust, and trust is, to put it mildly, in short supply nowadays.

This prospect makes a compelling boogeyman, but it doesn’t have to be a problem in practice. Libel law is not about monitoring the minutia of everyday discourse. Suits for libel only concern violations at scale: people get sued for libel only when lies are so egregious and widespread that they cause outstanding harm.

The second thing to avoid is a “watchdog effect” that comes if you make anyone responsible for issuing approvals. But I’m not talking about watchdogs, or censors; I’m talking about a Whack-a-Mole policy that responds only as matters break the bounds of decency. Again, my proposal isn’t about rendering a thumb-up or thumb-down on any given claim; it’s about looking for a consistent pattern of claims that are demonstrably out of bounds.

Finally, it might be objected that likening bullshit to libel, and thus focusing on only the most egregious abuse, sets the bar too high, and much abuse will go uncorrected. That is unquestionably the case, and I think it should be the case. Why? Because when someone is prosecuted for propagating private propaganda, it should mean something. The reaction of all parties to a successful prosecution shouldn’t be “Wow, sucks for them,” but rather “Man, I guess they really did go off the reservation.”

The idea is not to develop a predictable penalty for abusing truth. It’s to develop a possible penalty, one that comes to bear in the worst cases; to put a niggling thought in the back of the mind of the professional propagandist that they could be called to account for abusing their position. Yes, I want to have a chilling effect on the worst discourse society has to offer. It may not sound like much, but it’s better than nothing.

I vividly remember the joyful righteousness I felt on reading that Dominion Voting Machines was suing Sydney “Unleash the Kraken” Powell (and now Rudy Giuliani) for slander in the 2020 election misinformation campaign, and I rejoiced to see the dismal failure of Trump and his fellow travelers in a venue where reality actually mattered: the courts. Should we really have to wait until a corporate entity or individual suffers egregious, libelous harm before calling a halt? Should we really let a man with the power of the presidency use social media to wage war on reality without any option for pushback short of impeachment?

My message here is not that complicated: technology provides people awesome power in disseminating their ideas, and they need to be reminded of the Uncle Ben rule: “With great power comes great responsibility.” As it stands, they wield their power without the slightest responsibility, and if that doesn’t change, the modern world will literally drive itself insane.

The good news is that an artfully designed heuristic may be enough to put up guard rails without destroying freedom of speech. It might leave too much rabble-rousing on the table, but it would be a great improvement if we could just get back from Nutzville.

item.content:encoded:
A Question About the Insurrection

Ironic, isn’t it? The sentiment for which Hillary Clinton was pilloried the most, that may have cost her the Presidency, turns out to be a simple fact: a certain fraction of Donald Trump’s supporters really are deplorable. I refer, of course, to the MAGA mouth-breathers who stormed the Capitol this week, armed and bearing IEDs but without the wit to conceal their identities.

Call me a hopeless optimist, but I really want to believe that these goons don’t truly represent the body of Trump supporters. There must be a spectrum with the seditious mob on one end, and, on the other, their opposite number: respectable conservatives and patriots who voted for Trump, perhaps with nostrils pinched shut, because he has been the only available repository of their priorities.

The crucial question, then, is: How many of each? There must be a cadre of rational, calm, informed conservatives on the right who have been languishing, forgotten, in the shadow of the hyenas and QAnon cultists who get all the time on comedy news. But what’s the mix? Which group truly represents today’s Republican party?

The polls are not encouraging to the charitable mind. Something like 80% of Republicans still believe that the 2020 election was stolen, despite the idea’s dismal failure where the rubber hit the road: in court. And now, three times as many Republicans think that Joe Biden is “A great deal to blame” for the Capitol insurrection as Donald Trump is.

In this context, trying to maintain respect for Republican thinking is swimming upstream…but I’m still skeptical. Polling itself is losing ground rapidly as a source of data, and I have to ask myself if these responses are less a matter of actual conviction than an expression of tribal identification/virtue signaling. I’m still clinging to hope.

So, my call: open question. No good data to be had.

There’s a parallel question to be asked about the Republican leadership. For the last four years, the Republican party has been in thrall to Donald Trump. Why? One explanation, popular on the Left, is that they are just as corrupt, venal and power-mad as the man himself, and he has come along to provide their one, true voice. The explanation I prefer, though, is that he has dragged them down with him; that the Cruz’s and the Rubio’s meant what they said about him in the 2016 primaries; that there is a deep strain of ambivalence about Trump and the damage he has done to the Republic — said sentiment squelched by the fear he instils in his allies of turning his base against them.

Thus: another open question: willing collaborators or reign of terror?

Why am I raising these unanswered questions? Not just because the answers matter powerfully to the state of our nation, but because the insurrection in the Capitol offers a glittering, golden opportunity to answer both of them with surgical precision. How, you ask? By posing a third question to both the Republican leadership and Trump’s non-demented supporters:

Are you with us, or are you with them?

Do you favor giving a free pass to the man who fomented this insurrection and did nothing to stop it? Or do you support impeaching Donald Trump and removing him from office for his role in this horror?

This is the chance for respectable Republicans, who come to their conservatism honestly via values of mutual respect, patriotism and civic order — among others — and honest, sober reflection on priorities. This is their chance to show that the Capitol mob who couldn’t care less about those things does not speak for them, does not represent them. We’ve heard for years how unfair it is to lump them in with the deplorables who only share with them some willingness to support the President, however reluctantly. This is their chance to show that they’re actually different, that they’re the temperate “silent majority”: by rejecting the man who has exposed himself as an enemy of the America they purport to love.

It is also the chance for the Republican leadership to shed themselves of Donald Trump’s reign of terror, if they want to. By supporting Donald Trump’s impeachment and removal from office, they would dispel the shadow of a 2024 run — the certain shadow, assuming Trump’s fast-food diet doesn’t kill him first. Unlike in the prior impeachment, the prospect of giving Trump the mantle of martyr just doesn’t work here — at least not for the sane. A certain fraction of his supporters will follow him into exile, but they would no longer hold an iron fist over the Republican party, and it would cast a light of virtue and principle on the real patriots who remain.

It would also give the Republican leadership a chance to, you know, lead. Because leadership doesn’t mean following the will of the people as shaped by their views; it lies in inspiring the will of the people and working to shape those views. Those polls I reviewed earlier? They would be very different without Donald Trump shaping the opinions of his base. Get him out of the way — or at least stick him with his cultists in a back alley — and who knows how the clearheads of the party could guide its future?

As I said, it’s a question of numbers. If the Republican party really has been taken over by the mob, it will go one way. But if, as I, in my bottomless optimism, truly hope, the Grand Old Party of today really is a pony buried in poo**, then it will go the other way.

Stay tuned for later developments.

** For the young’uns, this is a Reagan reference: There’s Got to be a Pony in Here Somewhere

item.content:encoded:
The Best Worst Thing: The Upside of Disaster

Everyone knows Newton’s Third Law of Motion: “For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.” Newton was referring to physical dynamics, but we apply the principle far more widely, especially in human affairs. His law pertains to people because we react to what happens to us. You see a looming vehicle, you get out of the way. You see an economic downturn coming, you sell off your investments. A plane crash hits the news, people opt for terrestrial transport. A Democratic politician decries mass shooting, gun sales skyrocket. The Japanese bomb Pearl Harbor, the US enters WWII in the Pacific.

Missing the Obvious

Such interactions (inter-actions) are so commonplace and unremarkable that they’re easy to forget— you know, water, fish? This year I have been amazed to hear pundits fretting because half of Americans say they wouldn’t take a COVID vaccine. I say “amazed” because why would you even think about something that won’t even be an issue for at least a year, probably two, i.e. until after 1) there is more information about it because, you know, it actually exists, 2) it is widely available, and 3) the less skeptical half of the population has been vaccinated. In the interim we can expect any number of intervening events: news reports about the approval process, colloquial reports from acquaintances who get it, more and more COVID, insurance coverage, employer interactions and other social proof. People will react to all of these and more, so their predictions now of how they will feel about vaccinations then aren’t worth the bits used to encode them.

I’m also surprised when some looming event triggers forebodings of disaster that completely discount — or ignore entirely — the mitigating effects of reaction. How many dire warnings have you heard about an impending road closure bringing on a traffic apocalypse? A freeway in traffic-choked LA closes for repairs. Does the entire region tip over into gridlock? It almost never plays out that way. Far from chaos descending, traffic actually eases — enormously. Why? Because drivers react to the looming disaster in all sorts of ways, from re-routing to staying home. The reason Y2K wasn’t a crashing disaster was that it was so vividly and anxiously expected to be a crashing disaster.

(It’s amusing to realize that the doomsayers drumming up fear and loathing actually trigger the mitigating reaction. In other words, they play an essential role in making themselves wrong!)

Opposite, but not Equal

What’s more interesting about human reactions, though, concerns the other part of Newton’s law: we often get opposite reactions, but we rarely see equal ones. You would expect civilization to react to nuclear-power incidents like Three-Mile Island, Chernobyl and Fukushima, and indeed it did. The development of nuclear power is basically moribund in the wake of deaths numbered in the dozens, leaving a coal-fired infrastructure that kills hundreds of times as many every year. By contrast, climate change is bringing on a radically degraded terrestrial environment, and our actions to head it off aren’t nearly up to scratch.

In my experience, the scale of the human reaction to an event is unrelated to the scale of the event itself (that is, its effects). Which would be amusing, except for one thing about this emergent system (event + reaction): the ultimate outcome, the net effect, of an event, is the effect of the event itself, offset by the effect of the reaction. If the countervailing reaction to a negative event is “smaller” than the event, the event will be, on the whole, negative. But if a negative event triggers a larger compensatory reaction, its overall effect will be a net positive. Negative events, no matter how large and seemingly catastrophic, can turn out to be good news in the long run, depending on the reaction they foment. The killing of George Floyd and other fatal encounters between police and Black people, horrific as they are, fit right into the landscape of violent crime. But in the context of race relations as a whole, they have triggered a reaction — an entirely appropriate reaction — of profound importance, bringing to account the history and the presence of racism in America.

Where we are now

Which brings me to two of the most wretched realities we’re living with right now: the breakdown of civility and shared reality on social media; and the degradation of civil life under Donald Trump.

The Internet was around for some time before Facebook and Twitter arrived on the scene, and its denizens already had an, um, casual relationship to reality. But just as Fox News has weaponized right-wing counter-bias, the attention economy of “free” social services has brought us to the point of an existential crisis in how we as a society are with each other. As I wrote in One Crisis to Rule Them All, the best indicator of just how broken our shared reality is, is the preposterous ideas that are now taken seriously, in public, by thousands if not millions of people. QAnon, Flat Earth, the “link” between vaccines and autism, etc., together with the widespread disdain (on both Right and Left) for “the mainstream media” (i.e., professional journalism with standards of integrity and verification), are the bright red flashing emergency lights of an information ecosystem in collapse…

…so much so that the issue is getting unprecedented attention both inside and outside the companies responsible: within government, talk of breaking them up; within the companies themselves, actually banning threads of blatantly untrue and harmful content. To be clear, this is a very hard problem to tackle — and it strikes at the heart of a business model that has made many a billionaire. But that just tells you how dire the situation must be if it’s being addressed this seriously. Is it that hard to imagine a time in the not-too-distant future when people will shake their heads in wonderment and disdain at the bumpkins we must have been to allow such nonsense to spread so freely? Of course, it may not play out that way, but can you imagine it playing out that way if the Internet had loped along with its drip-feed diet of silly links and cat videos?

The Fruit of Trumpism?

At this point we are all embedded in the chaos that is Donald Trump. But there may come a time when the darkness lifts and we exit our caves, blinking, into a post-Trump day. What could that be like?

  • By attacking them at every turn, hasn’t Trump sharpened our appreciation (to put it mildly) for democratic norms, from financial transparency to the separation of powers? For the normal operation of government, in which professionals manage things like national security and criminal justice free of storms from above?
  • With his congenital lying, hasn’t he given us a new respect for truth and those who provide it, from civil servants to flawed but earnest media outlets?
  • Hasn’t his caustic Twitterocracy left a craving for leadership that makes us feel more included, united, and…decent?

But it’s not just Donald Trump. In recent years, Republicans have plumbed the depths of fealty before him and embraced a depraved, power-first, principal-be-damned stance toward governance. Heralded by Mitch McConnell’s express intent to deny Barack Obama any positive achievements, it descended this year to a head-snapping about-face over election-year Supreme Court nominations, and their program of undermining the 2020 election by word and deed. After making the Republican Party his thrall, Trump will leave it a disgraced husk that needs to earn its way back from the wilderness, perhaps adopting a tone of decency and reasonableness, a refreshed spirit of compromise, a morning-after sense of shame. Maybe not (I’m not holding my breath, though see this year’s upsurge in young-voter participation, or listen to these suburban women describe the shift in their attitudes), but it’s far more likely than it would have been after more years of business as usual.

In contrast, where would we have been after four years of a Hillary Clinton presidency? Four more years of Republican intransigence lightly papered over by conservative rhetoric. Four more years of scrabbling to eke out incremental improvements in health care or climate change policy. Racial tension and hostility to immigrants simmering along just under the surface. Another wan swing of the pendulum between middle-of-the-roaders in the two parties. Where’s the change in that?

Thanks to Donald Trump, the ideal of common governance; our fellow feeling as Americans; any sense of a shared destiny that we need to achieve together; any ability to work within a shared reality; even the idea of not giving in to naked impulse, selfishness and ill will; all that has its back against the wall. Can we, will we, react with a desperate lunge for the sweet refuge of a civil environment built on respect, a recovery of civic decency? Joe Biden seems to have grasped that thirst. If it is answered, Donald Trump will have done more good, in the most ironic possible way, than any boilerplate Democrat or Republican ever could have.

I am not making any predictions, much as I would love to see it play out this way. My point is that great change, real impetus in the world, doesn’t come spontaneously. It doesn’t always come just because it’s needed, either. It doesn’t happen when we just kind of want it, or think “I guess that would be a good idea”, but when we’re desperate, when there doesn’t seem to be any other way than to stand up and say “Enough!”. The pickle we’re in is horrific, but it also bears uniquely promising seeds of change precisely for being so dire. If the reaction to this current world is stronger than the hideousness of our situation, we really could redeem this darkness. And, ironic as it is, we will have Donald Trump to thank.

Remember, you read it here first.

item.title: One Crisis to Rule Them All

item.content:encoded:
One Crisis to Rule Them All

Civic life in the USA is at a boiling point. Incredibly, it has reached the point that the country may go to crisis about the legitimacy of the upcoming election. Does anyone think that civil war is out of the question? That question would have been unaskable four years ago.

There’s an understandable reflex to lay the blame at the feet of Donald Trump, that relentless agent of chaos. If Trump is the problem, it’s equally natural to look to the election for our salvation — and it certainly matters who takes office in 2021. Nonetheless, it’s time to realize that even a change of administration won’t save us. Much as I would love to blame Trump for everything wrong with America, it’s not true. Donald Trump would still be just a failing real estate developer in New York but for a host of circumstances that were swelling up when he came along to ride the wave. Donald Trump is as much an expression of what ails us as its cause.

So what does ail us? The circumstances that beget Trump are both multifarious and nefarious, but I am here to suggest a cause that lurks beneath them all, one crisis behind so many others. To get there, I need to start with an astonishing reality that we hardly even notice: the gobsmacking prevalence of truly preposterous beliefs in the public sphere.

A Carnival of Craziness

If the Internet and global communications were supposed to do anything, they were to democratize information, sweeping away propaganda, rumor and disinformation in a flood of Truth. Indeed, the supercomputer in our pockets offers us that option today.

But that’s not all. The Internet has also weaponized nonsense. There are thriving, if not viral, communities of people who sincerely believe things like:

  • The earth is flat and the moon landings were fake.
  • 9–11 was a putup job coordinated and executed by a cabal of thousands who operated without a single one ever defecting or leaving a trace, planting explosive charges in the Twin Towers and managing a dual airstrike to conceal the actual operation.
  • The leadership of the Democratic party is a pack of satanic, cannibalistic pedophiles who will be vanquished by Donald Trump working with Robert Mueller.
  • COVID-19 is a fabrication of the ruling elites to dominate the hoi polloi. Or a biological strike at the US by China. Or something.
  • Anthropogenic global warming is a hoax perpetrated by a conspiracy of scientists to hobble human progress.
  • The American healthcare system is the envy of the world.
  • Joe Biden is the new Red Menace whose guiding purpose is to destroy the suburbs, hand the economy back to China and transform the US into a Socialist autocracy.

Obviously, conspiracy theories and misinformation are nothing new. But the scope and scale of this infection would have been the stuff of dystopian fiction just a few years ago. The election under siege. Families riven by political division. Respectful dialogue a wistful memory. How can a country act on anything if it can’t even face in the same direction? And we’re seeing the answer: it can’t.

This United States of America of 2020 is literally going insane. And it’s not all Donald Trump’s fault.

How does this happen? There must be something seriously wrong for so many millions of brains to be infected like this — something new in the air.

The Meltdown

Think of public discourse like a nuclear chain reaction. In a reactor, uranium atoms decay, sending off neutrons that can kick more atoms into decay; if the chain reaction isn’t controlled somehow it enters a vicious cycle that ends in a meltdown — or an atomic explosion.

What controls a nuclear reactor is the presence of carbon rods mingled with the uranium. The rods absorb some fraction of the free neutrons, dampening the chain reaction and keeping it simmering along at a steady, productive, energy-producing pace rather than melting down or dying out.

In a sane society, ideas engage and spark off each other, producing both heat and light. But the most insidious memes are like the unconstrained neutrons of pure uranium: people and cohorts in close proximity can literally drive each other insane, with half-baked ideas, overheated rhetoric and deliberate misinformation that spark off more of the same. Without some inhibitory factor, a vicious cycle emerges, in which people believe crazier and crazier things, more and more vehemently.

In this analogy, the Internet has done two things: gathered uranium into tighter and tighter pockets, so that free neutrons have more reactive effect; and removed the buffering effect of information provided by people in the traditional media whose job is to put a damper on nonsense. Dismissing “the mainstream media” and encouraging everyone to live in their own reality just pulls out those carbon rods.

The “one crisis to rule them all” is a looming meltdown in how we gather information and intercommunicate, to the point that we no longer live in the same reality. The outcome of the 2020 election will do nothing to change this. As I said, civil war is no longer out of the question. This is why.

But what is special about this particular moment? There have always been information silos on the Internet, and Fox News started in the last century. Why is this meltdown happening now, of all times?

I do have a devil in mind, and this devil has a name, albeit a disarmingly boring one: The Attention Economy.

If you don’t pay for the product, you are the product

Think of the astronomical value of Facebook, Google/YouTube and Twitter. Did you contribute a single cent to any of them? Not if you’re a typical user you didn’t. And yet many of the founders of these companies are among the wealthiest people in history. Where did those vast fortunes come from?

Everyone knows the superficial answer: showing you ads. However, the important thing is not what rings the cash register, but what it takes to get to that point.

Consider another obvious fact: Facebook can’t show you an ad if you’re on YouTube. Google can’t deploy AdSense at you if you’re using DuckDuckGo — and none of them can make money if you’re out hanging with your friends or playing with your kids. For all of these companies, cashflow ceases if they don’t have your attention. For any “free” service, the game is played by securing the eyeballs of people by the millions. Everything revolves around showing them what gets, and keeps, their attention.

It’s hard to grasp the scope and scale of the technology devoted to this one goal; thinking about the money being made may help to imagine it. It’s no exaggeration to say that on the other side of your phone’s screen you have a supercomputer pointed at your brain armed with information about your past behavior and devoted to keeping your attention. On the other hand, our brains offer a rich set of handles to exploit: morbid curiosity; fear; tribal identity; righteous wrath; confirmation of prior beliefs: the whole toolbox of human manipulation.

Think of the movements full of people whose attention is a sure thing: QAnon; Flat Earthers; 911 truthers; climate deniers. You, dear reader, can sit in your armchair and describe how to enlist new recruits for any of these if you know a person’s prior inclinations. In fact, here’s a thought experiment: imagine you set out to play the world’s worst practical joke by recruiting someone you know well into a conspiracy theory or an extremist organization. You have continuous, complete control over what their phone suggests for them, whether on their Facebook timeline, their Twitter or News feeds, or their YouTube recommendations. You can experiment endlessly in a search for what actually grabs them and gets a click. Once interest is aroused, you can present them with content that entices them further: gives them a little bit more information, nudges them further down the rabbit hole. Baby step by baby step, you bring them into the company of like-minded others who bring them further into the fold. Before long, you’ve set up a vicious circle in which their identity becomes fused with their new fellows and reinforced by new information/spin/encouragement/discussion. And your new recruit never had to be aware of any of this. All they had to do was click on what seemed interesting.

But of course, this process isn’t being driven by amateur armchair recruiters. It’s being driven by algorithms of astronomical scale and precision, armed with all the information people have revealed about themselves online and controlling what gets suggested to them. What else do you need to know about the formation of QAnon, or the Flat Earth movement?

Naked in Public

Consider Google’s contributions to your life: Android, YouTube, gmail, Photos, Docs, Drive, Calendar, Contacts, Maps, not to mention Search. Every one is an absolute fount of information about you. To what purpose is that information put? Getting and holding your attention by using that information to exploit basic human drives.

In a way, Facebook is your most intimate friend: they are privy to all the information (the thoughts, the opinions, the recommendations, the incidents of your life) you’ve shared with all your other friends, as well as who those friends are and their information. If Facebook is going to show you ads, they need to keep your attention — by any means necessary.

To be clear: these companies did not set out to undermine Civilization As We Know It. The insanity around us is a distant, unintended effect of their fiscal need to sell ads by getting your attention. This whole nightmare is simply the outcome of AI systems figuring out how to maximize people’s attention. Even the AIs don’t have a theory of human mind. They just know what works.

It’s also worth noting that the outrage machine is not limited to social networks. You could sign off the Internet altogether and still get all the outrage you want from broadcast media. The founding charter of Fox News was to stir up the Right, and MSNBC serves a similar function for the Left. Indeed, the supporters of Donald Trump seem connected by a widespread, self-sustaining network that gets nourishment in a variety of ways.

I throw up my hands trying to convey the scale of what’s going on here, because 1) I actually can’t fit it into my own head; 2) you can’t succeed without sounding like a paranoid crank; and 3) these services really do go down so easy. You’re on Facebook for the personal connections. You’re on YouTube for the cat videos. You’re enmeshed with Google because Services! So many Services! All synchronized and working together!!! And yet…

What’s Really Going to Change?

So this is me giving up on properly communicating what’s actually going on. Instead, I can only remind you of the outcome: the absolutely ludicrous, delusional ideas that people have have come to embrace, and the meltdown of discourse as people get more tightly bound into hotter and hotter info-tribes. Something powerful made that happen. You don’t have to buy into, or even understand, the processes at work here. You only need to come to terms with the critical juncture we’re at, and make the connection back to what brought us here.

The election is still important. We shouldn’t imagine that there’s no difference between Donald Trump and Joe Biden. But in terms of where we are as a society, as a people who have to make decisions and move forward together, the bottom line is this:

As long as there are people and organizations whose livelihood depends on getting our attention by getting us angry at each other, America will continue heading for meltdown.

Now What?

Having highlighted a dire reality, I feel obliged to make suggestions for fixing it. Unfortunately, closed-form solutions are pretty thin on the ground. Even the outlines of the problem are just now coming into focus. So my suggestions are fairly vague, and centered around raising awareness.

First, come to terms with the existence of these systems. This essay is my contribution to the discussion, but it has been inspired by hearing Tristan Harris speak, and really fired up by The Social Dilemma, which is playing on Netflix. Absorbing it may not keep your next Trump-or-not-Trump “discussion” from going nuclear, but it will at least give you some understanding of why it does.

Second, realize that you are not immune. Get a grounding in the cognitive biases that make us all susceptible to conviction spirals and groupthink. Learn to recognize confirmation bias (filtering information for that which confirms your existing perspective) and the Dunning-Kruger Effect (in which the people who know the least about a subject think they’re an expert because they know so little), to name just two. I intend for my writing to focus on this sort of thing, but you could do worse than to dive into the work of David McRaney at You Are Not So Smart (podcast and website). Tim Urban at Wait But Why has an epic series of posts about how minds work together in a society, called The Story of Us.

Third, help make this kind of thing Not Okay. Society progresses when a phenomenon gets held up to the light of day and recognized as a Bad Thing. Child labor, overt racism and casual rape of the environment are just a few cases where society came to grips with an awful reality that had been invisible, taken for granted, “just the way things are”. And we can become more sophisticated about manipulation: just have a quick look back at the clumsy propaganda and laughably obvious advertising of only a few decades ago.

How does that work in everyday life? By talking about it. Noticing the symptoms when someone starts going down the rabbit hole, and calling it out. Pushing back when friends forward blatant bullshit that only works on their cohort. Awareness in public may not be enough, but it is definitely necessary.

There may be solutions in the political/regulatory realm, but there is no substitute for getting more sophisticated about what’s going on here: how it works, and what a serious pickle we’re in. America is barreling through a dark tunnel. We can all bring a little light.
